scenario: An application needs to ingest and process large volumes of streaming data — clickstream events, IoT telemetry, and log streams — with multiple consumers reading from the same stream at different paces. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SQS
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SNS
wrong_answer_3: AWS Glue
correct_explanation: Kinesis Data Streams ingests high-volume, ordered streaming data and retains it for a configurable period, allowing multiple consumers to read at their own pace from the same stream. It is the canonical AWS streaming service.
wrong_explanation_1: SQS is a worker queue. Once a message is consumed by one consumer it is deleted — it does not support multiple parallel consumers reading the same record stream.
wrong_explanation_2: SNS pushes messages to subscribers but does not retain them as a re-readable stream the way Kinesis does.
wrong_explanation_3: Glue is an ETL service for batch and streaming transformations. It is not the ingestion-and-fan-out streaming platform itself.

scenario: A company needs to run a high-performance computing (HPC) workload that requires low-latency, high-bandwidth communication between hundreds of EC2 instances. The instances must be physically close to each other to minimize network latency between nodes. Which EC2 feature should the solutions architect use?
correct_answer: Deploy the EC2 instances in a cluster placement group to place them on hardware that is physically close together within a single Availability Zone, minimizing network latency.
wrong_answer_1: Deploy the EC2 instances in a spread placement group to distribute them across distinct hardware for maximum availability.
wrong_answer_2: Deploy the EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones and use an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) to enable low-latency communication.
wrong_answer_3: Use EC2 Dedicated Instances to ensure the instances run on hardware dedicated to the account, reducing network contention.
correct_explanation: Cluster placement groups pack EC2 instances close together within a single AZ on high-bisection-bandwidth network hardware. This provides the lowest possible network latency and highest throughput between instances, which is critical for tightly coupled HPC workloads. Cluster placement groups also support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for MPI-based HPC applications.
wrong_explanation_1: Spread placement groups distribute instances across distinct underlying hardware to maximize fault tolerance. This is the opposite of what HPC workloads need — spread groups maximize physical distance between instances, increasing network latency.
wrong_explanation_2: Deploying across multiple AZs increases physical distance between instances, which increases network latency. EFA provides low-latency networking but requires instances to be in the same AZ and ideally in a cluster placement group to achieve maximum performance.
wrong_explanation_3: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to a single AWS account but do not guarantee physical proximity between instances. They address tenancy isolation requirements, not network latency optimization.

scenario: A company stores petabytes of objects in S3 Standard. As monthly storage usage crosses higher tiers, the per-GB price decreases. Which AWS pricing concept does this illustrate?
correct_answer: Volume-based discounts (tiered pricing)
wrong_answer_1: Savings Plans
wrong_answer_2: Spot pricing
wrong_answer_3: Compute Savings Plans
correct_explanation: Some AWS services, including S3 Standard, apply tiered pricing — the per-unit price decreases as monthly usage exceeds tier thresholds. This volume-based discount applies automatically without commitments.
wrong_explanation_1: Savings Plans apply to compute services (Lambda, Fargate, EC2). They do not apply to S3 storage.
wrong_explanation_2: Spot pricing is an EC2 purchasing option. It is not relevant to S3 storage pricing.
wrong_explanation_3: Compute Savings Plans cover Lambda, Fargate, and EC2 usage. S3 is outside their scope.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes how Amazon Bedrock typically charges customers for using foundation models on-demand?
correct_answer: Customers pay based on the number of input and output tokens processed per request
wrong_answer_1: Customers pay a flat monthly subscription regardless of usage
wrong_answer_2: Customers must purchase a 3-year commitment to use any model
wrong_answer_3: Bedrock is free for all model providers and any volume
correct_explanation: On-demand Bedrock pricing is token-based: customers pay per input token and per output token at a rate that varies by model and provider. (Provisioned Throughput offers an hourly commitment option for guaranteed capacity.)
wrong_explanation_1: There is no required flat subscription for on-demand Bedrock usage.
wrong_explanation_2: Multi-year commitments are not required; Provisioned Throughput is optional.
wrong_explanation_3: Bedrock usage is metered and billed; it is not free for paid models.

scenario: A company is building a serverless API using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The API is expected to receive highly variable traffic, with quiet periods and sudden bursts of up to 5,000 requests per second. The company wants to protect the backend Lambda functions from being overwhelmed during bursts while still serving as many requests as possible. Which feature should the solutions architect configure?
correct_answer: Configure usage plans and throttling limits on the API Gateway stage to set a burst limit and rate limit, smoothing traffic before it reaches Lambda.
wrong_answer_1: Set the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to 5,000 to match the expected burst traffic.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to pre-warm enough instances to handle 5,000 concurrent requests.
wrong_answer_3: Deploy the API Gateway in multiple AWS Regions and use Route 53 latency-based routing to distribute the burst traffic.
correct_explanation: API Gateway throttling (burst limit and rate limit) controls the rate at which requests are forwarded to Lambda. When traffic exceeds the configured limits, API Gateway returns 429 Too Many Requests to excess callers rather than passing all requests to Lambda simultaneously. This protects Lambda from concurrency exhaustion while still serving traffic up to the configured limits.
wrong_explanation_1: Setting Lambda reserved concurrency to 5,000 reserves that concurrency from the account pool but does not protect Lambda from being overwhelmed — it just ensures those 5,000 concurrent executions are available. Without throttling at the API Gateway, all 5,000 requests could hit Lambda simultaneously, potentially causing cold starts and latency spikes.
wrong_explanation_2: Provisioned Concurrency pre-warms Lambda instances to eliminate cold starts, which improves latency but does not protect against being overwhelmed by burst traffic. It addresses latency, not traffic volume control.
wrong_explanation_3: Multi-region deployment with Route 53 distributes traffic geographically but does not smooth burst traffic. A burst of 5,000 requests per second from a single region would still overwhelm the Lambda functions in that region.

scenario: A company runs a web application on EC2 instances. Traffic is highly variable, with quiet periods overnight and sudden spikes during business hours. The company wants the application to scale out within 60 seconds of a traffic spike to prevent performance degradation. Which combination of features achieves the fastest scale-out response?
correct_answer: Use a target tracking scaling policy with a low target value, and configure a warm pool on the Auto Scaling group to keep pre-initialized instances ready to launch immediately.
wrong_answer_1: Use a scheduled scaling policy to add instances at the start of business hours each day.
wrong_answer_2: Use a step scaling policy with a 5-minute CloudWatch alarm evaluation period to add instances when CPU exceeds 70%.
wrong_answer_3: Use predictive scaling to forecast traffic and pre-provision instances 10 minutes before anticipated spikes.
correct_explanation: A warm pool maintains a set of pre-initialized EC2 instances in a stopped or running state. When the Auto Scaling group needs to scale out, it pulls instances from the warm pool instead of launching and initializing new ones, dramatically reducing scale-out time. Combined with a target tracking policy that responds quickly to metric changes, this achieves sub-60-second scale-out.
wrong_explanation_1: Scheduled scaling adds instances at a fixed time each day, which is appropriate for predictable traffic patterns. It does not respond to sudden unexpected spikes that occur outside the scheduled window.
wrong_explanation_2: A 5-minute CloudWatch alarm evaluation period means the alarm must breach for 5 consecutive minutes before triggering scaling. This introduces at least 5 minutes of latency before any scaling action begins, far exceeding the 60-second requirement.
wrong_explanation_3: Predictive scaling forecasts traffic based on historical patterns and pre-provisions instances in advance. It works well for recurring predictable patterns but cannot respond to sudden unexpected spikes that deviate from historical patterns.

scenario: A data engineering team loads data into Amazon Redshift from Amazon S3. After loading, they want to validate that the number of rows loaded matches the number of rows in the source files and that key columns do not contain null values. Which approach provides automated post-load data quality validation in Redshift?
correct_answer: Run SQL queries in Redshift to count rows and check for nulls, then compare with source file metadata
wrong_answer_1: Use AWS Glue Data Quality rules on the S3 source files
wrong_answer_2: Enable Redshift automatic table optimization
wrong_answer_3: Use Amazon Athena to query the Redshift tables
correct_explanation: After loading data into Redshift, you can run SQL queries to validate row counts and check for null values in key columns. You can compare the row count in Redshift with the number of rows in the source files (tracked via S3 object metadata or Glue job metrics) to ensure completeness. This is the standard approach for post-load validation in Redshift.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Glue Data Quality rules validate data before loading into Redshift, not after. They operate on data in S3 or during ETL processing, not on data already loaded into Redshift tables.
wrong_explanation_2: Redshift automatic table optimization improves query performance by automatically sorting and distributing data. It does not validate data quality or check for null values.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Athena queries data in S3, not in Redshift tables. While you can use Athena Federated Query to query Redshift, it is not the standard approach for post-load validation within Redshift.

scenario: A team wants to compare three foundation models on the SAME task and dataset, with consistent metrics and side-by-side results. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is purpose-built for this comparative evaluation?
correct_answer: Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs with multiple models
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Bedrock Agents
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs let users compare multiple FMs on the same task and dataset with consistent metrics, producing side-by-side report cards to guide model selection.
wrong_explanation_1: Agents orchestrate tasks but do not produce comparative evaluation reports.
wrong_explanation_2: Knowledge Bases support RAG retrieval.
wrong_explanation_3: Guardrails filter content but do not compare models.

scenario: Which statement BEST captures AWS's commitment to its customers' security under the AWS shared responsibility model?
correct_answer: AWS is responsible for the security OF the cloud (infrastructure, hardware, facilities), and the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud
wrong_answer_1: AWS owns all security responsibilities, leaving the customer with none
wrong_answer_2: Customers own all security responsibilities, including the physical hardware
wrong_answer_3: Security is fully outsourced to AWS Support when a Business Support plan is purchased
correct_explanation: The shared responsibility model divides security into AWS's responsibility for the cloud (physical infrastructure, facilities, hardware, hypervisor, managed services) and the customer's responsibility in the cloud (data, IAM, OS configurations, networking choices). Both parties have ongoing obligations.
wrong_explanation_1: Customers retain meaningful responsibilities — data protection, identity, and configuration — that AWS cannot perform on their behalf.
wrong_explanation_2: Customers do not own the physical hardware or facilities. AWS is responsible for those.
wrong_explanation_3: Support plans provide help with operational issues but do not transfer security responsibility from the customer to AWS.

scenario: A company stores infrequently accessed archive data in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. A compliance audit requires that specific archived documents be made available within 5 minutes when requested. The company currently uses the default Bulk retrieval option. Which change should the solutions architect make to meet the 5-minute retrieval requirement?
correct_answer: Switch to Expedited retrievals for the compliance documents, which make data available within 1–5 minutes for archives up to 250 MB.
wrong_answer_1: Migrate the compliance documents from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which provides millisecond access.
wrong_answer_2: Use S3 Batch Operations to restore all Glacier objects to S3 Standard in advance of any audit requests.
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the Glacier objects to automatically move them to a faster access tier when retrieval is requested.
correct_explanation: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers three retrieval options: Expedited (1–5 minutes), Standard (3–5 hours), and Bulk (5–12 hours). Switching to Expedited retrievals for compliance documents meets the 5-minute requirement while keeping the data in Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Expedited retrievals can be provisioned for guaranteed capacity using Provisioned Retrieval Capacity.
wrong_explanation_1: Migrating to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval would meet the requirement (millisecond access) but at a higher storage cost than Glacier Flexible Retrieval. The question asks for a change to meet the 5-minute requirement, and Expedited retrieval achieves this without migrating storage tiers.
wrong_explanation_2: Pre-restoring all Glacier objects to S3 Standard is expensive and operationally complex. It requires knowing in advance which documents will be requested and incurs both retrieval fees and S3 Standard storage costs for the restored copies.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on access patterns, but it does not apply to objects already in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Intelligent-Tiering manages transitions between Standard, Standard-IA, Archive Instant Access, and Archive Access tiers within its own tier structure.

scenario: A company runs a transactional application on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ enabled. A cost review shows that the RDS instance is significantly over-provisioned — CPU averages 8% and memory usage is 20%. The company wants to reduce RDS costs without changing the database engine or losing Multi-AZ availability. Which action should the solutions architect take?
correct_answer: Downsize the RDS instance to a smaller instance class that matches the actual CPU and memory requirements, maintaining Multi-AZ for availability.
wrong_answer_1: Disable RDS Multi-AZ to eliminate the standby instance cost and rely on automated backups for recovery.
wrong_answer_2: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB to take advantage of on-demand pricing and eliminate over-provisioning.
wrong_answer_3: Convert the RDS instance to a Reserved Instance with a 3-year term to reduce the hourly cost of the over-provisioned instance.
correct_explanation: If the instance is significantly over-provisioned (8% CPU, 20% memory), downsizing to a smaller instance class directly reduces the hourly cost while maintaining the same database engine and Multi-AZ configuration. AWS Compute Optimizer or RDS Performance Insights can help identify the appropriate target instance size.
wrong_explanation_1: Disabling Multi-AZ eliminates the standby instance cost but removes automatic failover capability, increasing the RTO during a failure. The question specifies that Multi-AZ availability must be maintained.
wrong_explanation_2: Migrating from RDS PostgreSQL to DynamoDB requires a complete redesign of the data model and application queries. DynamoDB is a NoSQL database that does not support SQL, transactions in the same way, or relational schemas. This is a major architectural change, not a cost optimization.
wrong_explanation_3: Purchasing a Reserved Instance for an over-provisioned instance reduces the hourly rate but does not address the root cause — the instance is too large for the workload. Paying a discounted rate for unnecessary capacity still wastes money. Rightsizing first, then reserving, is the correct sequence.

scenario: A company wants to identify underutilized EC2 instances and over-provisioned EBS volumes across its AWS account to reduce costs. The company wants recommendations without building custom monitoring logic. Which AWS tool provides these recommendations automatically?
correct_answer: Use AWS Compute Optimizer, which analyzes CloudWatch metrics and provides rightsizing recommendations for EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and ECS services.
wrong_answer_1: Use AWS Cost Explorer with Reserved Instance utilization reports to identify underutilized instances.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize CPU and memory utilization across all EC2 instances.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to check for low-utilization EC2 instances based on CPU utilization thresholds.
correct_explanation: AWS Compute Optimizer uses machine learning to analyze historical CloudWatch utilization metrics and provides specific rightsizing recommendations — including recommended instance types, sizes, and EBS volume configurations — with projected cost savings. It requires no custom logic and covers EC2, EBS, Lambda, and ECS.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Cost Explorer's RI utilization reports show how well Reserved Instances are being used, not whether On-Demand instances are over-provisioned. It provides cost visibility but not specific rightsizing recommendations for instance types or EBS volumes.
wrong_explanation_2: CloudWatch dashboards visualize metrics but do not provide automated rightsizing recommendations. Building dashboards requires manual configuration and interpreting the data to identify optimization opportunities.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Trusted Advisor does check for low-utilization EC2 instances (CPU < 10% for 14 days), but it provides basic threshold-based checks rather than the ML-driven, specific rightsizing recommendations with projected savings that Compute Optimizer provides.

scenario: A data engineering team runs AWS Glue ETL jobs that process data from Amazon S3. The team wants to monitor job execution metrics such as the number of records processed, data processed in bytes, and job duration. They want to create custom CloudWatch dashboards to visualize these metrics. Which AWS Glue feature publishes job metrics to CloudWatch?
correct_answer: Enable job metrics in the Glue job configuration
wrong_answer_1: Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks
wrong_answer_2: Configure AWS Glue to write logs to CloudWatch Logs
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Glue Data Quality rules
correct_explanation: AWS Glue jobs can publish metrics to Amazon CloudWatch when job metrics are enabled in the job configuration. These metrics include records processed, bytes processed, and job duration. You can then create CloudWatch dashboards to visualize these metrics and monitor job performance.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed to avoid reprocessing. They do not publish job execution metrics to CloudWatch.
wrong_explanation_2: Configuring Glue to write logs to CloudWatch Logs provides log data for debugging and troubleshooting, but it does not publish structured metrics like records processed or bytes processed. Job metrics provide quantitative performance data.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue Data Quality rules validate data against defined constraints and publish data quality metrics. They do not publish job execution metrics like records processed or job duration.

scenario: A machine learning team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio to develop and train models. The security team requires that all SageMaker Studio traffic to AWS services (S3, ECR, SageMaker APIs) must route through the private AWS network and not traverse the public internet. Which configuration achieves this?
correct_answer: Deploy SageMaker Studio in a VPC with VPC-only mode and create interface VPC endpoints for the required AWS services
wrong_answer_1: Enable SageMaker Studio encryption and use AWS KMS customer-managed keys
wrong_answer_2: Attach an IAM policy to the SageMaker execution role that denies internet access
wrong_answer_3: Configure a NAT Gateway in the VPC to route all outbound traffic through a single IP
correct_explanation: SageMaker Studio VPC-only mode routes all traffic through the customer's VPC instead of the public internet. Interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for S3, ECR, and SageMaker APIs ensure that traffic to these services stays within the AWS private network, satisfying the security requirement.
wrong_explanation_1: KMS encryption protects data at rest and in transit but does not control network routing. It does not prevent Studio traffic from traversing the public internet.
wrong_explanation_2: IAM policies control API authorization (what actions are allowed) but do not control network routing. An IAM policy cannot prevent network traffic from routing through the public internet.
wrong_explanation_3: A NAT Gateway routes outbound traffic through a single IP but still sends traffic over the public internet. It does not keep traffic within the AWS private network as required.

scenario: A security team wants to identify any IAM roles, S3 buckets, KMS keys, or other resources in their accounts that are shared with external accounts or made public — without manually auditing each one. Which AWS service should the team use?
correct_answer: IAM Access Analyzer
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Inspector
wrong_answer_3: AWS Config
correct_explanation: IAM Access Analyzer continuously monitors resource-based policies and identifies resources shared with external principals (other accounts, public internet, federated identities). It produces findings the team can review and act on.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor has a small set of security checks but is not the dedicated cross-resource external-sharing analyzer.
wrong_explanation_2: Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities. It does not analyze resource sharing policies.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes; it does not specifically analyze access policies for external sharing the way Access Analyzer does.

scenario: Which LLM inference parameter restricts sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least P, encouraging diversity while excluding very low-probability tokens?
correct_answer: Top-P (nucleus sampling)
wrong_answer_1: Top-K
wrong_answer_2: Temperature
wrong_answer_3: Stop sequences
correct_explanation: Top-P (nucleus sampling) considers only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is ≥ P. This excludes very low-probability tokens while preserving diversity among reasonably likely ones.
wrong_explanation_1: Top-K restricts sampling to the K most probable tokens regardless of probability mass — a related but distinct parameter.
wrong_explanation_2: Temperature scales the probability distribution before sampling but does not cut off tails by cumulative probability.
wrong_explanation_3: Stop sequences end generation when matched; they do not control token sampling diversity.

scenario: Your team uses CloudFormation templates and CodePipeline to deploy infrastructure and application code. Manual changes through the console are forbidden, and all environments are reproduced from version-controlled definitions. Which Well-Architected design principle does this practice illustrate?
correct_answer: Perform operations as code
wrong_answer_1: Scale horizontally
wrong_answer_2: Decouple components
wrong_answer_3: Implement security at all layers
correct_explanation: "Perform operations as code" means defining infrastructure, runbooks, and deployments in version-controlled code so they can be tested, repeated, and audited. Using CloudFormation and CodePipeline with no manual console changes is the textbook implementation of this principle.
wrong_explanation_1: Horizontal scaling adds more small resources to handle load. It is about workload sizing, not about codifying operations.
wrong_explanation_2: Decoupling components reduces dependencies between services. It is a separate architectural design principle.
wrong_explanation_3: Defense in depth is a security principle. While important, it is not what is illustrated by using IaC for all deployments.

scenario: A company needs to transfer data from an on-premises Hadoop HDFS cluster to Amazon S3 as part of a cloud migration. The data is 20 TB and the on-premises environment has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection already provisioned. The team wants a managed service that handles data integrity verification and bandwidth throttling. Which AWS service should be used?
correct_answer: AWS DataSync
wrong_answer_1: AWS Snowball Edge
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
wrong_answer_3: AWS Storage Gateway
correct_explanation: AWS DataSync is a managed data transfer service that supports HDFS as a source and S3 as a destination. It performs automatic data integrity verification using checksums, supports bandwidth throttling to avoid saturating the Direct Connect link, and handles automatic retries — making it ideal for this managed migration scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Snowball Edge is a physical device for offline data transfer, used when network bandwidth is insufficient. With a 10 Gbps Direct Connect already in place, a network-based transfer via DataSync is faster and more appropriate than shipping a physical device.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload speeds by routing through CloudFront edge locations over the public internet. Since a Direct Connect connection is already available, DataSync over Direct Connect provides a more reliable and private path.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Storage Gateway provides hybrid cloud storage integration for on-premises applications to access AWS storage. It is designed for ongoing hybrid access patterns, not for one-time bulk data migration from HDFS.

scenario: A developer is building a web application where users log in with their Google accounts. After authentication, users need temporary AWS credentials to access specific AWS resources. The application uses Amazon Cognito. What is the correct flow to obtain AWS credentials for a Google-authenticated user?
correct_answer: Authenticate with Google to get a Google ID token, exchange it through a Cognito Identity Pool for temporary AWS credentials via STS.
wrong_answer_1: Authenticate with Google to get a Google ID token, then call the IAM CreateUser API to create a temporary IAM user.
wrong_answer_2: Authenticate with Google to get a Google ID token, then call STS AssumeRole directly using the Google token.
wrong_answer_3: Authenticate with Google to get a Google ID token, store it in the Cognito User Pool, and use the User Pool token for AWS API calls.
correct_explanation: Cognito Identity Pools support external identity providers including Google. The application authenticates with Google, receives a Google ID token, and passes it to the Cognito Identity Pool's GetId and GetCredentialsForIdentity APIs. Cognito validates the token with Google and returns temporary STS credentials scoped to the configured IAM role.
wrong_explanation_1: Creating IAM users dynamically for application end-users is an anti-pattern. IAM users are long-term identities intended for human operators and service accounts, not for application end-users. Cognito Identity Pools provide temporary credentials without creating persistent IAM users.
wrong_explanation_2: STS AssumeRole requires the caller to already have AWS credentials. A Google ID token is not an AWS credential and cannot be used directly with STS. The token must first be validated through Cognito Identity Pools, which then calls STS on behalf of the user.
wrong_explanation_3: Cognito User Pools are for managing your own user directory. They do not store third-party identity provider tokens. Additionally, Cognito User Pool tokens (JWTs) are not AWS credentials and cannot be used directly to call AWS APIs.

scenario: A team is evaluating a foundation model used for TEXT SUMMARIZATION and wants to compare model-generated summaries against human-written reference summaries by measuring overlap of words and n-grams. Which metric is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: ROUGE
wrong_answer_1: BLEU
wrong_answer_2: RMSE
wrong_answer_3: Accuracy
correct_explanation: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a set of metrics designed to compare machine-generated summaries with reference summaries by measuring overlap (recall, precision, F1) of n-grams and longest common subsequences.
wrong_explanation_1: BLEU is designed primarily for machine translation evaluation, focusing on precision of n-grams.
wrong_explanation_2: RMSE is a regression metric for numerical predictions, not text summarization.
wrong_explanation_3: Accuracy is a classification metric; summaries are open-ended generation.

scenario: Your team is building a CI/CD pipeline for a microservices application. Before deploying to production, the pipeline must run integration tests against a staging environment that mirrors production. The staging environment uses real AWS services including SQS and DynamoDB. Which approach best supports this integration testing stage in the pipeline?
correct_answer: Provision a dedicated staging AWS environment with real SQS queues and DynamoDB tables. Run integration tests in CodeBuild against the staging environment as a pipeline stage before the production deploy stage.
wrong_answer_1: Run integration tests locally on the developer's machine using LocalStack before committing code.
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS X-Ray in production to trace requests and identify integration failures after deployment.
wrong_answer_3: Mock all AWS service calls in the integration tests using the AWS SDK mock library to avoid needing real AWS resources.
correct_explanation: A dedicated staging environment with real AWS services provides the highest fidelity integration testing. CodeBuild can run the test suite against the staging environment as a pipeline stage, and the pipeline only proceeds to production if all tests pass. This catches integration issues that mocking or local emulation cannot detect.
wrong_explanation_1: Running tests locally before committing is a good developer practice but is not part of the automated CI/CD pipeline. It relies on individual developers running tests consistently and does not provide a pipeline gate that blocks bad deployments.
wrong_explanation_2: X-Ray traces requests in production after deployment. Using production as the integration test environment means failures affect real users. Integration testing must happen before production deployment, not after.
wrong_explanation_3: Mocking AWS service calls tests the application logic in isolation but does not test the actual integration with real AWS services. Mocks cannot detect issues like incorrect IAM permissions, wrong queue URLs, DynamoDB schema mismatches, or service-specific behavior differences.

scenario: A data analyst needs to query data stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database using standard SQL without connecting directly to the database. The analyst wants a serverless query interface that does not require managing database connections. Which AWS service enables this?
correct_answer: Amazon Athena Federated Query with the Aurora connector
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Redshift Spectrum
wrong_answer_2: AWS Glue Studio visual ETL
wrong_answer_3: Amazon QuickSight direct query mode
correct_explanation: Amazon Athena Federated Query allows running SQL queries against data sources outside S3, including Aurora MySQL, using pre-built connectors deployed as Lambda functions. The analyst can query Aurora data through Athena's serverless interface without managing database connections directly.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Redshift Spectrum queries data in S3 from within Redshift. It does not provide a connector for querying Aurora MySQL databases.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Glue Studio is a visual ETL authoring tool for building data transformation jobs. It is not a SQL query interface for ad-hoc analytics against Aurora.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon QuickSight in direct query mode connects to Aurora for BI visualizations but is a business intelligence tool, not a general-purpose SQL query interface with the same ad-hoc flexibility as Athena.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to allow an external partner's AWS account to read specific objects from an Amazon S3 bucket in the company's account. The partner should not need to create IAM users in the company's account. Which approach enables cross-account S3 access?
correct_answer: Attach an S3 bucket policy that grants the partner's AWS account ID read access to the specific prefix
wrong_answer_1: Create an IAM user in the company's account and share the credentials with the partner
wrong_answer_2: Make the S3 bucket public to allow the partner to access the objects
wrong_answer_3: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration to share the objects with the partner
correct_explanation: An S3 bucket policy can grant cross-account access by specifying the partner's AWS account ID as the principal. The partner's IAM users or roles can then access the specified S3 prefix using their own AWS credentials, without needing IAM users in the company's account.
wrong_explanation_1: Creating an IAM user in the company's account and sharing credentials with the partner is a security anti-pattern. It creates long-lived credentials outside the partner's control and violates the principle of using federated or cross-account access.
wrong_explanation_2: Making the S3 bucket public grants access to anyone on the internet, not just the partner. This is a significant security risk and violates the principle of least privilege.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload and download speeds by routing through CloudFront edge locations. It is not an access control mechanism and does not grant cross-account access.

scenario: A finance officer notices that the per-GB cost of S3 storage decreases as the company's monthly storage volume grows past several tiers. Which AWS pricing fundamental does this illustrate?
correct_answer: Pay less when you use more (tiered pricing)
wrong_answer_1: Always pay the same per-unit price regardless of volume
wrong_answer_2: Pay only with annual upfront commitments
wrong_answer_3: Pay more as you use more (penalty pricing)
correct_explanation: AWS tiered (volume-based) pricing reduces the per-unit price at higher monthly usage tiers for many services, including S3 storage and data transfer. Customers "pay less when you use more".
wrong_explanation_1: AWS pricing is tiered, not flat per-unit, so per-unit cost can fall as volume grows.
wrong_explanation_2: Annual upfront commitments are optional Savings Plans, not the only way to get lower prices.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS pricing does not include penalty pricing for high usage; it provides volume discounts.

scenario: Which responsible AI dimension is concerned with PROTECTING individuals' personal data within an AI system — including how data is collected, used, stored, and shared?
correct_answer: Privacy
wrong_answer_1: Fairness
wrong_answer_2: Veracity and robustness
wrong_answer_3: Explainability
correct_explanation: Privacy is the responsible AI dimension concerned with protecting personal data — how it is collected, used, stored, shared, and (when appropriate) deleted. Differential privacy, encryption, and access controls all support it.
wrong_explanation_1: Fairness concerns equitable outcomes across groups, not data protection.
wrong_explanation_2: Veracity and robustness is about correctness under adversarial or unexpected inputs.
wrong_explanation_3: Explainability is about understanding model outputs, not about data protection.

scenario: A regulator requires the company to demonstrate that all S3 buckets containing financial data are encrypted at rest and that any change to that encryption configuration is detected. Which combination of capabilities BEST supports this requirement?
correct_answer: AWS Config rules that detect non-compliant bucket configurations, combined with S3 default encryption enabled by KMS
wrong_answer_1: Amazon GuardDuty alone monitoring for suspicious encryption changes
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities on the buckets
wrong_answer_3: AWS CloudTrail logs reviewed manually each quarter
correct_explanation: S3 default encryption (using SSE-KMS or SSE-S3) ensures all new objects are encrypted at rest. AWS Config rules can continuously evaluate whether buckets remain compliant and generate findings if the configuration changes. Together they meet both the encryption and detection requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: GuardDuty focuses on threat detection (e.g., suspicious API behavior). It is not the primary tool for confirming bucket encryption configuration compliance.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and container images for vulnerabilities. It does not evaluate S3 bucket encryption configuration.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudTrail logs API events, but manual quarterly review is not continuous detection. The auditor's requirement implies near-real-time detection that AWS Config rules provide.

scenario: A company is designing a new application that requires a database capable of handling millions of requests per second with single-digit millisecond latency. The data model consists of simple key-value lookups with no complex joins or transactions. The dataset is expected to grow to hundreds of terabytes. Which AWS database service should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Amazon DynamoDB, which provides single-digit millisecond performance at any scale, supports key-value and document data models, and scales horizontally to handle millions of requests per second with no upper limit on dataset size.
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Aurora with multiple read replicas to distribute the millions of requests per second across the cluster.
wrong_answer_2: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with connection pooling via RDS Proxy to handle millions of concurrent connections.
wrong_answer_3: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as the primary database to handle millions of requests per second with sub-millisecond latency.
correct_explanation: DynamoDB is purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency key-value workloads at any scale. It handles millions of requests per second with consistent single-digit millisecond latency, scales automatically to hundreds of terabytes, and requires no capacity planning with on-demand mode. It is the correct choice when the data model is simple key-value lookups.
wrong_explanation_1: Aurora with read replicas can scale reads significantly, but relational databases have architectural limits on write throughput and connection counts. Achieving millions of requests per second with Aurora requires significant engineering effort and does not match DynamoDB's native scalability for key-value workloads.
wrong_explanation_2: RDS Proxy manages database connections but does not increase the underlying RDS instance's query throughput. RDS for PostgreSQL has inherent limits on concurrent queries and write throughput that make millions of requests per second impractical without extreme vertical scaling.
wrong_explanation_3: ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond latency and high throughput, but it is an in-memory cache, not a primary database. It does not provide durable storage for hundreds of terabytes of data and is not designed to be the sole data store for a production application.

scenario: A workload runs on a single large EC2 instance. To improve resilience and to spread load, the architects plan to replace it with a fleet of smaller instances behind a load balancer. Which design principle does this change illustrate?
correct_answer: Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability
wrong_answer_1: Scale vertically by upgrading the instance type
wrong_answer_2: Stop guessing capacity
wrong_answer_3: Test recovery procedures regularly
correct_explanation: Replacing one large server with multiple smaller ones behind a load balancer is horizontal scaling. It reduces blast radius (one failed instance affects only a fraction of capacity) and increases aggregate availability — a core reliability pillar principle.
wrong_explanation_1: Upgrading to a larger instance is vertical scaling. The scenario explicitly describes moving to many smaller instances — the opposite approach.
wrong_explanation_2: "Stop guessing capacity" addresses using elastic, demand-driven sizing. While related, the specific illustrative principle here is horizontal scaling.
wrong_explanation_3: Testing recovery procedures is a reliability principle, but it is about validating runbooks — not about how the workload is sized.

scenario: A machine learning team needs to continuously replicate changes from a production Amazon RDS MySQL database into Amazon S3 to keep their ML training dataset up to date. The replication must capture inserts, updates, and deletes with minimal lag and without impacting the production database performance. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
correct_answer: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with change data capture (CDC)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Glue ETL job scheduled every hour
wrong_answer_2: Amazon RDS automated backups restored to S3
wrong_answer_3: AWS Lambda triggered by RDS event notifications
correct_explanation: AWS DMS with CDC uses the database's transaction log to capture inserts, updates, and deletes in near real time without running queries against the production database. It continuously replicates changes to S3, keeping the ML training dataset current with minimal performance impact on the source database.
wrong_explanation_1: An hourly AWS Glue ETL job would introduce up to 60 minutes of lag and requires running queries against the production database on a schedule, which can impact performance during peak hours. It also cannot efficiently capture deletes without additional change tracking logic.
wrong_explanation_2: RDS automated backups create full database snapshots for disaster recovery purposes. They cannot be used for continuous incremental replication and would require restoring the entire database to extract changes.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Lambda triggered by RDS event notifications receives notifications about database instance events (e.g., failover, maintenance) but not row-level data changes. It cannot capture individual inserts, updates, and deletes from the database.

scenario: A security architect needs to centrally configure AWS WAF web ACLs, AWS Network Firewall rules, and Shield Advanced protections across many AWS accounts in an Organization. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this central security policy management?
correct_answer: AWS Firewall Manager
wrong_answer_1: AWS Security Hub
wrong_answer_2: AWS Config aggregator
wrong_answer_3: AWS Trusted Advisor
correct_explanation: AWS Firewall Manager centrally configures and manages WAF, AWS Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, and Shield Advanced protections across multiple accounts and resources in an AWS Organization. It is the dedicated cross-account security policy management service.
wrong_explanation_1: Security Hub aggregates security findings but does not centrally manage WAF or Network Firewall configurations.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Config aggregators consolidate configuration data across accounts but do not push firewall rules.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor offers recommendations; it does not centrally manage firewall configurations.

scenario: A machine learning team has deployed a binary classification model on a SageMaker endpoint. The model makes predictions on customer loan applications. The team wants to monitor whether the model's prediction quality (accuracy, precision, recall) is degrading over time as new data arrives, using ground truth labels that become available with a 2-week delay. Which SageMaker Model Monitor monitor type should be used?
correct_answer: Model quality monitoring
wrong_answer_1: Data quality monitoring
wrong_answer_2: Bias drift monitoring
wrong_answer_3: Feature attribution drift monitoring
correct_explanation: SageMaker Model Monitor's model quality monitoring compares model predictions against ground truth labels to track metrics like accuracy, precision, and recall over time. It supports delayed ground truth ingestion, making it suitable for scenarios where labels become available after a delay (e.g., 2 weeks after a loan decision).
wrong_explanation_1: Data quality monitoring detects statistical drift in the distribution of input features compared to the training baseline. It does not evaluate prediction quality against ground truth labels.
wrong_explanation_2: Bias drift monitoring (via SageMaker Clarify) tracks changes in bias metrics over time, such as disparate impact across demographic groups. It does not directly measure model accuracy, precision, or recall.
wrong_explanation_3: Feature attribution drift monitoring tracks changes in SHAP-based feature importance over time. It does not measure prediction quality metrics like accuracy or recall against ground truth labels.

scenario: A company brings several proprietary software licenses (Oracle, SQL Server, etc.) to AWS and wants centralized tracking and enforcement of license usage to avoid out-of-compliance situations. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS License Manager
wrong_answer_1: AWS Cost Explorer
wrong_answer_2: AWS Marketplace
wrong_answer_3: AWS Service Catalog
correct_explanation: AWS License Manager centralizes tracking and enforcement of software licenses (BYOL) across AWS and on-premises usage. Administrators define rules and limits, and License Manager prevents licensed deployments from exceeding the entitlement.
wrong_explanation_1: Cost Explorer analyzes spend, not license usage.
wrong_explanation_2: Marketplace sells third-party software but is not a license-tracking enforcement tool for BYOL.
wrong_explanation_3: Service Catalog publishes approved products; it is not a license-tracking service.

scenario: Which AWS infrastructure component is responsible for serving cached content closer to viewers and is the foundation of Amazon CloudFront's worldwide delivery network?
correct_answer: Edge locations
wrong_answer_1: AWS Outposts racks
wrong_answer_2: Availability Zones
wrong_answer_3: AWS Regions
correct_explanation: Edge locations form the CloudFront global network. There are hundreds of them worldwide — more than Regions — and they cache content close to end users to reduce latency for static and dynamic delivery.
wrong_explanation_1: Outposts racks are customer-located AWS hardware for hybrid workloads, unrelated to CloudFront edge caching.
wrong_explanation_2: AZs host customer compute and storage but are not CloudFront's edge-caching layer.
wrong_explanation_3: Regions are the geographic groupings of AZs. They host workloads but are not the CloudFront edge network.

scenario: An ML team has deployed a SageMaker model and wants to understand which input features are most influential in driving individual predictions for specific customers. The model is a black-box ensemble. Which SageMaker tool provides feature-level explanations for individual predictions?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Debugger
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Clarify uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to provide feature-level explanations for individual model predictions. It works with black-box models and can explain why a specific prediction was made for a given input, helping teams understand model behavior and identify potential bias.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon SageMaker Debugger monitors training jobs for issues like vanishing gradients and overfitting. It does not provide post-training feature importance explanations for individual predictions on deployed models.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor detects data drift and model quality degradation on deployed endpoints. It monitors statistical properties of inference inputs and outputs but does not provide SHAP-based feature explanations for individual predictions.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon SageMaker Experiments tracks and organizes training runs by logging metrics and parameters. It does not provide feature-level explanations for model predictions.

scenario: A developer is building a CI/CD pipeline using AWS CodePipeline for a Lambda function. The pipeline should deploy the function using AWS SAM and require a manual approval before deploying to production. Which CodePipeline action type provides the manual approval gate?
correct_answer: An Approval action in a CodePipeline stage, which pauses the pipeline and sends an SNS notification to reviewers who must approve or reject before the pipeline continues.
wrong_answer_1: A Lambda action that invokes a function to check approval status from an external ticketing system.
wrong_answer_2: A CodeBuild action configured to wait for a manual input before proceeding.
wrong_answer_3: A CloudFormation action with a manual change set execution step.
correct_explanation: CodePipeline has a built-in Approval action type that pauses pipeline execution and optionally sends an SNS notification to reviewers. A designated approver must log into the console (or use the CLI/API) to approve or reject the pipeline. Only after approval does the pipeline continue to the next stage.
wrong_explanation_1: A Lambda action can integrate with external systems, but building a custom approval workflow with Lambda adds unnecessary complexity when CodePipeline's native Approval action provides this functionality out of the box.
wrong_explanation_2: CodeBuild runs automated build and test commands. It does not support interactive manual input during execution — builds run to completion automatically. It cannot serve as a manual approval gate.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudFormation change sets require manual execution when using the MANUAL execution mode, which does provide a review step. However, this is specific to CloudFormation stack deployments and is not the general-purpose manual approval mechanism for CodePipeline stages.

scenario: A workload is batch-oriented, can tolerate interruption, and can be restarted from a checkpoint. The company wants to run it on EC2 as cheaply as possible. Which purchasing option provides the largest discount?
correct_answer: Spot Instances
wrong_answer_1: On-Demand Instances
wrong_answer_2: Reserved Instances (Standard, 1-year)
wrong_answer_3: Dedicated Hosts
correct_explanation: Spot Instances offer discounts up to 90% off On-Demand pricing in exchange for the possibility that AWS reclaims them with two minutes' notice. They are ideal for interruption-tolerant, checkpointable workloads.
wrong_explanation_1: On-Demand is the highest published price and offers no discount.
wrong_explanation_2: Reserved Instances provide significant discounts (up to ~72%) but less than Spot's potential 90%. They also require a 1- or 3-year commitment.
wrong_explanation_3: Dedicated Hosts address licensing or isolation requirements and are more expensive, not cheaper. They are the opposite of cost-optimal for this workload.

scenario: A company wants to share a centrally provisioned VPC subnet with several AWS accounts in its Organization, so that workloads in those accounts can deploy ENIs into the shared subnet. Which AWS service makes this resource sharing possible?
correct_answer: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Transit Gateway
wrong_answer_2: AWS PrivateLink
wrong_answer_3: AWS Direct Connect
correct_explanation: AWS RAM allows resources such as VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, License Manager configurations, and others to be shared across AWS accounts in an Organization. Sharing a subnet via RAM lets workloads in multiple accounts deploy ENIs into a common subnet.
wrong_explanation_1: Transit Gateway is a network hub for connecting VPCs and on-premises networks. It is not the mechanism for sharing a subnet across accounts.
wrong_explanation_2: PrivateLink provides private endpoint connectivity between VPCs and services. It does not share subnets between accounts.
wrong_explanation_3: Direct Connect is a dedicated link between on-premises networks and AWS. It does not handle cross-account resource sharing.

scenario: An application's front-end web tier currently calls the back-end database directly. The team wants to redesign the architecture so that the front-end can be deployed, scaled, and replaced independently of the back-end. Which design principle should guide this redesign?
correct_answer: Loose coupling
wrong_answer_1: Tight coupling
wrong_answer_2: Vertical scaling
wrong_answer_3: Single point of failure
correct_explanation: Loose coupling — typically achieved by inserting a message queue (Amazon SQS) or notification topic (Amazon SNS) between tiers — allows each component to be developed, deployed, and scaled independently. Failures or slowdowns in one tier do not directly cascade to the other.
wrong_explanation_1: Tight coupling is the opposite problem — components depend directly on each other. This is what the team is trying to move away from.
wrong_explanation_2: Vertical scaling increases the size of a single resource. It does not address the design coupling between tiers.
wrong_explanation_3: Single points of failure are reliability anti-patterns. They are not a design principle to follow.

scenario: A developer is deploying an application to Elastic Beanstalk and needs to run a database migration script after the new application version is deployed but before traffic is shifted to the new instances. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment hook should the developer use?
correct_answer: Use a container_commands: directive in .ebextensions with leader_only: true to run the migration script on a single instance after the application is deployed.
wrong_answer_1: Use a commands: directive in .ebextensions to run the migration script before the application is deployed.
wrong_answer_2: Use an EC2 user data script to run the migration script when the instance launches.
wrong_answer_3: Use an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Elastic Beanstalk environment event to run the migration.
correct_explanation: container_commands in .ebextensions run after the application source is extracted but before the application version is deployed to the web server. Setting leader_only: true ensures the command runs on only one instance (the leader), preventing duplicate migration runs when multiple instances are being updated simultaneously.
wrong_explanation_1: The commands: directive in .ebextensions runs before the application source is extracted and before the application is deployed. Database migrations should run after the new code is in place but before traffic is served — container_commands is the correct hook for post-extraction, pre-traffic operations.
wrong_explanation_2: EC2 user data runs only at instance launch, not during application deployments. If Elastic Beanstalk deploys a new application version to existing instances, user data does not re-execute. It is not suitable for deployment-time migration scripts.
wrong_explanation_3: Elastic Beanstalk environment events (via SNS) notify about environment state changes but do not provide fine-grained deployment lifecycle hooks. A Lambda function triggered by these events cannot reliably execute at the precise point between deployment and traffic shift.

scenario: A developer has a Lambda function that processes events from API Gateway. The function receives 20 requests per second and each execution takes a maximum of 30 seconds. The developer is worried about throttling. What action should the developer take?
correct_answer: No action is needed — Lambda will automatically scale to handle the load within the default concurrency limit.
wrong_answer_1: Request a concurrency limit increase from AWS Support.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to pre-warm enough instances.
wrong_answer_3: Set the function's reserved concurrency to 600 to guarantee capacity.
correct_explanation: Using the concurrency formula: 20 requests/second × 30 seconds = 600 concurrent executions. The default account-level Lambda concurrency limit is 1,000. Since 600 is well within this limit, Lambda will automatically scale to handle the load without any configuration changes or limit increase requests.
wrong_explanation_1: A limit increase is only necessary when the expected concurrent executions exceed the account-level limit of 1,000. At 600 concurrent executions, the function operates comfortably within the default limit.
wrong_explanation_2: Provisioned Concurrency eliminates cold start latency by pre-warming execution environments. It does not affect the account-level concurrency limit and is not needed to prevent throttling in this scenario.
wrong_explanation_3: Setting reserved concurrency to 600 would guarantee that capacity for this function but would also cap it at 600 concurrent executions. Since the function needs up to 600 and the account limit is 1,000, no reservation is necessary — and setting it could unnecessarily limit the function if demand spikes.

scenario: A company needs to archive data that is rarely accessed and may be retrieved only a few times per year, with retrieval times of 12 hours acceptable, at the LOWEST possible storage cost. Which S3 storage class should they choose?
correct_answer: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
wrong_answer_1: S3 Standard
wrong_answer_2: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
wrong_answer_3: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
correct_explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive offers the lowest storage price in S3, intended for long-term archival data accessed once or twice a year. Standard retrieval is within 12 hours, which matches the scenario's tolerance.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Standard is the most expensive per-GB option and is designed for frequently accessed data — not archival.
wrong_explanation_2: Intelligent-Tiering moves data between tiers automatically based on access patterns; for predictable archival use, Deep Archive is cheaper.
wrong_explanation_3: Glacier Instant Retrieval is for archives that need millisecond retrieval. The storage price is higher than Deep Archive.

scenario: A company needs to encrypt data stored in Amazon RDS and wants to use a key that is stored and managed entirely outside of AWS for maximum control. The company's security policy prohibits storing the master encryption key in any AWS service. Which encryption approach should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Use application-level encryption: encrypt sensitive data fields in the application before writing to RDS, using a key stored in the company's on-premises Hardware Security Module (HSM).
wrong_answer_1: Use RDS encryption with a customer managed KMS key, which gives the company full control over the key.
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS CloudHSM to store the encryption key and configure RDS to use CloudHSM for encryption.
wrong_answer_3: Use SSE-C on RDS by providing the encryption key with each database connection.
correct_explanation: When the security policy prohibits storing the master key in any AWS service — including KMS and CloudHSM — the only option is to encrypt data at the application layer before it reaches RDS, using a key stored entirely on-premises in a company-controlled HSM. The data arrives at RDS already encrypted and AWS never has access to the plaintext or the key.
wrong_explanation_1: A customer managed KMS key is stored and managed within AWS KMS, which is an AWS service. Even though the customer controls the key policy, the key material resides in AWS infrastructure, which violates the policy of not storing the master key in any AWS service.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS CloudHSM is a dedicated HSM appliance within AWS infrastructure. While the customer controls the HSM and AWS cannot access the keys, CloudHSM is still an AWS service and the key is stored within AWS's physical infrastructure, which may violate the stated policy.
wrong_explanation_3: SSE-C (Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys) is an Amazon S3 feature, not an RDS feature. RDS does not support SSE-C — RDS encryption uses KMS keys only.

scenario: A customer's workload is consistently on EC2 instances within a single family (m5) and a single Region. Which pricing model offers the LARGEST discount while still matching this specific commitment?
correct_answer: EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the m5 family in that Region
wrong_answer_1: Compute Savings Plan for any compute service
wrong_answer_2: On-Demand Instances
wrong_answer_3: Spot Instances
correct_explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit to a specific instance family in a specific Region and offer the largest Savings Plan discount (up to ~72%) — larger than Compute Savings Plans, which are broader in flexibility.
wrong_explanation_1: Compute Savings Plans cover all of EC2, Lambda, and Fargate. The broader flexibility comes at a smaller maximum discount than EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
wrong_explanation_2: On-Demand has no commitment and no discount.
wrong_explanation_3: Spot offers the largest possible EC2 discount but instances can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice — unsuitable for a consistently-on workload.

scenario: A company wants to build a document topic modeling system to automatically categorize thousands of unlabeled news articles into thematic groups. No labeled training data is available. Which Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithm is most appropriate for this task?
correct_answer: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)
wrong_answer_1: BlazingText (Text Classification mode)
wrong_answer_2: Sequence-to-Sequence
wrong_answer_3: Linear Learner
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker's Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is an unsupervised topic modeling algorithm that discovers latent topics in a collection of documents. It does not require labeled data and is specifically designed for categorizing text documents into thematic groups based on word co-occurrence patterns.
wrong_explanation_1: BlazingText in Text Classification mode is a supervised algorithm that requires labeled training examples for each category. Since no labeled data is available, supervised text classification cannot be applied.
wrong_explanation_2: Sequence-to-Sequence is a supervised algorithm designed for tasks like machine translation and text summarization that require labeled input-output sequence pairs. It is not applicable to unsupervised topic discovery.
wrong_explanation_3: Linear Learner is a supervised algorithm for regression and classification tasks. It requires labeled training data and is not designed for unsupervised topic modeling of text documents.

scenario: A company has multiple AWS accounts managed under AWS Organizations. A developer in a member account needs to assume a role in a different member account to access S3 resources. The developer's IAM user has sts:AssumeRole permission. What additional configuration is required in the target account?
correct_answer: The IAM role in the target account must have a trust policy that allows the developer's IAM user ARN (or the source account) to assume it.
wrong_answer_1: The target account must have an SCP that explicitly allows cross-account role assumption.
wrong_answer_2: The developer must create an IAM user in the target account with the same username.
wrong_answer_3: The target account must enable cross-account access in the AWS Organizations console.
correct_explanation: Cross-account role assumption requires two things: the caller must have sts:AssumeRole permission (already granted), and the target role must have a trust policy that explicitly allows the caller's principal to assume it. The trust policy is the access control mechanism on the role side that permits the cross-account assumption.
wrong_explanation_1: SCPs in AWS Organizations restrict what actions member account principals can perform — they do not grant permissions. An SCP cannot enable cross-account role assumption; that is controlled by the role's trust policy and the caller's IAM permissions.
wrong_explanation_2: Cross-account access works through role assumption, not through matching usernames. The developer assumes a role in the target account using their existing credentials — no user needs to be created in the target account.
wrong_explanation_3: There is no 'cross-account access' setting in the AWS Organizations console. Cross-account access is configured through IAM role trust policies and the caller's IAM permissions, not through an organizational setting.

scenario: A photo-sharing application needs to detect objects, scenes, and inappropriate content in user uploads, plus identify faces. Which AWS managed AI service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: Amazon Rekognition
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Textract
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Comprehend
correct_explanation: Amazon Rekognition uses pre-trained ML models for image and video analysis — object/scene detection, content moderation, face analysis, and celebrity recognition. It is the AWS managed service for these computer-vision tasks.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Canvas is a no-code ML builder for custom models on tabular data, not a vision API.
wrong_explanation_2: Textract extracts text and forms from documents — not general image analysis.
wrong_explanation_3: Comprehend works on text, not images.

scenario: Which statement BEST captures the difference between PRE-TRAINING and INFERENCE for a foundation model?
correct_answer: Pre-training learns general patterns from massive datasets over many compute-hours; inference uses the trained model to respond to user prompts
wrong_answer_1: Pre-training generates user responses; inference creates the model
wrong_answer_2: Pre-training and inference both happen at every user request
wrong_answer_3: Pre-training is optional; inference is the only required step
correct_explanation: Pre-training is the expensive, one-time process of learning general patterns from large datasets. Inference is the relatively lightweight, repeated use of the trained model on new prompts. Their costs and cadences differ dramatically.
wrong_explanation_1: Pre-training creates the model; inference generates responses — the question reverses this.
wrong_explanation_2: Pre-training happens once (or rarely); inference happens on each user request.
wrong_explanation_3: Pre-training is the essential step that produces the FM; inference is its use thereafter.

scenario: A company is deploying a CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. The security team requires that the ALB only accepts requests that originate from CloudFront — direct requests to the ALB's DNS name must be rejected. Which approach enforces this restriction?
correct_answer: Configure CloudFront to add a custom HTTP header with a secret value to all origin requests. Configure the ALB listener rule to only forward requests that contain the correct custom header value.
wrong_answer_1: Enable AWS WAF on the ALB with a rule that blocks requests not originating from CloudFront IP ranges.
wrong_answer_2: Configure the ALB security group to allow inbound traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list.
wrong_answer_3: Use an ACM certificate on the ALB and configure CloudFront to use HTTPS — only CloudFront knows the certificate details.
correct_explanation: CloudFront can be configured to inject a custom header (e.g., X-Origin-Verify: secret-value) into all requests sent to the origin. The ALB listener rule checks for this header and its value, rejecting requests that do not include it. Since the header value is a secret known only to CloudFront and the ALB configuration, direct requests to the ALB cannot forge it.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudFront IP ranges change over time as AWS adds and removes edge locations. Maintaining an up-to-date WAF rule based on CloudFront IP ranges is operationally complex and error-prone. AWS publishes the CloudFront IP ranges, but they are not static. The custom header approach is more reliable.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS does publish a managed prefix list for CloudFront edge locations that can be used in security groups. This is a valid approach, but the custom header method is more commonly recommended because it does not depend on maintaining IP-based rules that can change.
wrong_explanation_3: The ALB's ACM certificate is used for TLS termination and is not a secret — it is presented to any client that connects. Knowing the certificate details does not restrict who can connect to the ALB. TLS certificates authenticate the server to the client, not the client to the server.

scenario: A company is building a training dataset by labeling thousands of product images for a computer vision model. The labeling team is distributed across multiple locations. The company wants a managed service to coordinate the labeling workflow, track labeler agreement, and automatically label high-confidence examples to reduce manual effort. Which AWS service should be used?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels
wrong_answer_2: AWS Mechanical Turk (standalone)
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I)
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth is a fully managed data labeling service that supports distributed labeling workforces, tracks inter-annotator agreement, and uses active learning to automatically label high-confidence examples — reducing the total labeling cost by up to 70%. It integrates directly with SageMaker training jobs.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels trains custom image classification and object detection models using labeled images, but it does not provide a managed labeling workflow for coordinating distributed labelers or tracking annotator agreement.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Mechanical Turk can be used as a labeling workforce, but it is a standalone crowdsourcing marketplace. It does not provide workflow management, inter-annotator agreement tracking, or automated labeling — those capabilities are provided by SageMaker Ground Truth, which can use Mechanical Turk as one of its workforce options.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) is designed for human review of ML predictions in production (e.g., reviewing low-confidence model outputs). It is not designed for building initial training datasets through coordinated labeling workflows.

scenario: Which Amazon SageMaker feature helps administrators create least-privilege IAM personas (e.g., data scientist, MLOps engineer) by providing recommended permission templates?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Role Manager
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager
correct_explanation: SageMaker Role Manager helps administrators create role-based IAM personas for ML workloads — including templates for data scientists, MLOps engineers, and compute roles — to support least-privilege configurations.
wrong_explanation_1: Ground Truth handles data labeling.
wrong_explanation_2: JumpStart is the model and solution hub.
wrong_explanation_3: Edge Manager managed models on edge devices.

scenario: A retail company wants to ingest point-of-sale transaction events from 2,000 stores into AWS in real time. Each store generates up to 500 events per minute. The data must be available for ML feature computation within seconds of arrival and retained for 7 days for replay. Which AWS service is most appropriate for this ingestion layer?
correct_answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SQS FIFO queue
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 with event notifications
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Data Firehose
correct_explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is designed for real-time, high-throughput data ingestion with configurable retention up to 365 days. It supports multiple concurrent consumers, enabling parallel feature computation pipelines, and delivers data within milliseconds of ingestion — meeting both the latency and retention requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon SQS FIFO queues provide ordered, exactly-once message delivery but are designed for decoupling application components, not for high-throughput streaming analytics. Messages are deleted after consumption and cannot be replayed, which does not meet the 7-day retention requirement.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon S3 with event notifications triggers actions when objects are written to S3, but it is not a real-time streaming ingestion layer. It cannot handle continuous sub-second event streams from 2,000 stores and does not provide the millisecond-latency delivery required.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Data Firehose is designed for delivering streaming data to destinations like S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch. It buffers data for 60 seconds to 15 minutes before delivery, which does not meet the seconds-level latency requirement for real-time feature computation.

scenario: An application needs to convert text into natural-sounding speech in multiple languages, producing MP3 audio for an interactive voice response (IVR) system. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: Amazon Polly
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Transcribe
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Translate
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Lex
correct_explanation: Amazon Polly is the AWS text-to-speech service. It converts text to lifelike audio in many languages and voices, with output formats including MP3 — ideal for IVR and accessibility scenarios.
wrong_explanation_1: Transcribe is speech-to-text (the opposite direction).
wrong_explanation_2: Translate converts text between languages, not text to speech.
wrong_explanation_3: Lex is a conversational bot service that uses Polly for speech output, but the specific service that does TTS is Polly.

scenario: A company hosts a static website on Amazon S3 with a CloudFront distribution in front of it. The company wants to ensure the website remains available even if the primary S3 bucket becomes unavailable due to a regional outage. Which solution provides the highest availability for the static website?
correct_answer: Configure CloudFront with an origin group containing the primary S3 bucket and a secondary S3 bucket in a different region as the failover origin, with S3 Cross-Region Replication keeping the secondary bucket in sync.
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 Multi-AZ storage class to automatically replicate objects across Availability Zones within the same region.
wrong_answer_2: Create a second CloudFront distribution pointing to a backup S3 bucket and use Route 53 failover routing to switch between distributions.
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Versioning on the primary bucket so that previous versions of objects are available if current objects are corrupted.
correct_explanation: CloudFront origin groups support automatic failover: if the primary origin returns a configured error code (e.g., 5xx), CloudFront automatically retries the request against the failover origin. Combined with S3 Cross-Region Replication to keep the secondary bucket current, this provides seamless regional failover for the static website without any DNS changes or manual intervention.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 standard storage already stores data redundantly across multiple AZs within a region. There is no 'Multi-AZ storage class' as a separate option — S3 durability is built in. This does not protect against a full regional outage.
wrong_explanation_2: Using Route 53 failover routing between two CloudFront distributions adds DNS TTL-based failover latency and requires health checks to detect the failure. CloudFront origin groups provide faster, more seamless failover at the CDN layer without DNS propagation delays.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Versioning protects against accidental deletion or object corruption by preserving previous versions. It does not provide regional failover capability — if the S3 bucket's region is unavailable, all versions in that bucket are equally inaccessible.

scenario: A company's application writes items to a DynamoDB table and then publishes a notification to an SNS topic. Downstream services subscribe to the topic to react to new items. The team wants to simplify the architecture by eliminating the explicit SNS publish step from the application code. Which AWS feature can replace the manual publish step?
correct_answer: Enable DynamoDB Streams and configure an SNS topic or Lambda function as a downstream consumer of the stream.
wrong_answer_1: Enable DynamoDB auto scaling to automatically publish notifications when new items are written.
wrong_answer_2: Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to intercept write operations and forward notifications to SNS.
wrong_answer_3: Configure an S3 event notification on the DynamoDB table to trigger downstream services.
correct_explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes automatically without any application code changes. A Lambda function subscribed to the stream can publish to SNS or process the change directly, removing the explicit publish step from the application. The application only needs to write to DynamoDB — the stream handles downstream notification.
wrong_explanation_1: DynamoDB auto scaling adjusts read and write capacity in response to traffic. It has no capability to publish notifications or trigger downstream services when items are written.
wrong_explanation_2: DAX is an in-memory caching layer for DynamoDB that accelerates read performance. It does not intercept or forward write operations to other services — it is transparent to the application and has no event notification capability.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 event notifications are a feature of Amazon S3, not DynamoDB. DynamoDB is not an S3 bucket and does not support S3-style event notifications. DynamoDB Streams is the correct mechanism for change data capture on DynamoDB tables.
