scenario: A financial services company needs to ensure that all traffic between its EC2 instances and Amazon S3 stays within the AWS network and never traverses the public internet. The company also wants to restrict S3 access so that only requests originating from within the VPC are allowed. Which solution meets both requirements?
correct_answer: Create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3, update the route tables to direct S3 traffic through the endpoint, and add a bucket policy that denies access unless the request comes from the VPC endpoint.
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and configure the EC2 instances to use the acceleration endpoint.
wrong_answer_2: Deploy a NAT Gateway and route all S3 traffic through it to keep traffic within AWS infrastructure.
wrong_answer_3: Create a VPC Interface Endpoint for S3 and configure a security group that only allows traffic from the EC2 instances' security group.
correct_explanation: A VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 routes traffic from the VPC to S3 through the AWS private network without traversing the internet. Adding a bucket policy with a condition on aws:SourceVpce or aws:SourceVpc ensures that only requests originating from within the VPC (via the endpoint) are accepted, satisfying both the network isolation and access restriction requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes traffic through CloudFront edge locations to improve upload/download speeds. It routes traffic over the public internet to reach the edge locations and does not keep traffic within the AWS private network.
wrong_explanation_2: A NAT Gateway routes traffic to the internet gateway and then to S3 over the public internet. While the traffic originates from a private IP, it still traverses the public internet to reach S3, which does not meet the requirement.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 has both Gateway Endpoints (free, route-table based) and Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink, cost-based). While an Interface Endpoint also keeps traffic private, Gateway Endpoints are the standard and cost-effective solution for S3. More importantly, Interface Endpoints for S3 use security groups differently and the described configuration is not how S3 endpoint access restriction is enforced.

scenario: A company uses 100 GB of S3 storage in January and 500 GB in February. The February bill for storage is approximately five times the January bill. Which AWS pricing concept does this billing pattern illustrate?
correct_answer: Pay-as-you-go pricing
wrong_answer_1: Reserved Instance pricing
wrong_answer_2: Spot Instance pricing
wrong_answer_3: All Upfront pricing
correct_explanation: Pay-as-you-go pricing charges customers in direct proportion to consumed resources. Storing five times as much data leads to roughly five times the storage cost, with no commitments or upfront payments involved.
wrong_explanation_1: Reserved Instances apply to EC2, RDS, and a few other compute services. S3 storage is not purchased through Reserved Instances.
wrong_explanation_2: Spot Instances are a discounted EC2 purchase option. They do not apply to S3 storage.
wrong_explanation_3: All Upfront is a payment option for Reserved Instances or Savings Plans. S3 storage bills monthly based on usage, not upfront.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to synchronize files from an on-premises NAS device to Amazon S3 on an ongoing basis. New files are added daily and existing files are occasionally updated. The team wants automatic detection of changed files, bandwidth throttling to avoid saturating the corporate network, and encryption in transit. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
correct_answer: AWS DataSync
wrong_answer_1: AWS Snowball Edge
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
wrong_answer_3: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway
correct_explanation: AWS DataSync is designed for ongoing, scheduled file synchronization between on-premises storage and AWS. It automatically detects changed files using checksums, supports bandwidth throttling to limit network impact, and encrypts data in transit using TLS — satisfying all stated requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Snowball Edge is a physical appliance for large one-time bulk migrations. It is not designed for ongoing incremental synchronization of daily file changes.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads by routing through CloudFront edge locations but does not provide automatic change detection, scheduling, or bandwidth throttling. It is a transfer optimization feature, not a synchronization service.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway presents S3 as a local NFS/SMB file share for on-premises applications to write to. It is designed for applications that need to access S3 as a file system, not for scheduled synchronization of an existing NAS to S3.

scenario: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, a customer running Amazon EC2 instances is responsible for which of the following?
correct_answer: Patching the guest operating system on the EC2 instances
wrong_answer_1: Patching the hypervisor that runs the EC2 instances
wrong_answer_2: Replacing failed disks in the underlying physical hosts
wrong_answer_3: Maintaining the physical security of the AWS data centers
correct_explanation: For IaaS services like Amazon EC2, AWS is responsible for security "of" the cloud — the hardware, hypervisor, network, and facilities. The customer is responsible for security "in" the cloud, which includes patching the guest OS, configuring security groups, and managing data.
wrong_explanation_1: The hypervisor is part of the underlying virtualization layer that AWS manages. Customers have no access to the hypervisor.
wrong_explanation_2: Physical hardware including disks is AWS's responsibility. Customers never see or replace physical components.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS is solely responsible for the physical security of its data centers. Customers cannot access these facilities.

scenario: A workload is autoscaled so that the number of EC2 instances rises and falls with the daily traffic pattern. The customer pays only for the instance-hours actually consumed. Which AWS Cloud economic principle is illustrated?
correct_answer: Pay-as-you-go with elasticity
wrong_answer_1: Fixed-cost amortization
wrong_answer_2: All Upfront Reserved Instances
wrong_answer_3: On-demand capacity reservations
correct_explanation: Combining elasticity (scaling capacity with demand) and pay-as-you-go pricing (paying only for actual consumption) is one of the foundational AWS economic principles. Customers pay for exactly the capacity they use over time.
wrong_explanation_1: Fixed-cost amortization describes accounting for capital assets over time. It is not what is happening here.
wrong_explanation_2: All Upfront RIs involve paying for capacity in advance regardless of usage. The scenario describes per-hour, demand-driven billing.
wrong_explanation_3: On-demand capacity reservations reserve capacity at on-demand pricing. They are not about hourly autoscaling billing.

scenario: An engineering manager observes that the on-premises environment was either over-provisioned for occasional peaks (wasting money) or under-provisioned for those peaks (causing outages). Moving to AWS solved this dilemma. Which cloud benefit BEST describes the change?
correct_answer: Stop guessing capacity
wrong_answer_1: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
wrong_answer_2: Trade capital expense for variable expense
wrong_answer_3: Go global in minutes
correct_explanation: The "stop guessing capacity" benefit refers to the cloud's elasticity: customers add capacity when demand grows and shed it when demand falls, so they never need to predict peak load months in advance. This directly resolves the over/under-provisioning dilemma.
wrong_explanation_1: While moving off data centers is a related benefit, it does not directly address the capacity-planning dilemma the scenario describes.
wrong_explanation_2: CapEx-to-OpEx covers the financial classification of spend, not the operational capacity-planning problem.
wrong_explanation_3: Global deployment speed is not what the scenario is about; this is about local capacity planning, not geographic expansion.

scenario: A data engineering team is building a data lake on Amazon S3. They want to store data in a format that supports efficient columnar reads, predicate pushdown, and schema evolution (adding new columns without rewriting existing data). Which file format should they use?
correct_answer: Apache Parquet
wrong_answer_1: CSV
wrong_answer_2: JSON
wrong_answer_3: XML
correct_explanation: Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that enables efficient reads by scanning only the columns needed for a query. It supports predicate pushdown to skip row groups that don't match filter conditions, and schema evolution allows adding new columns to existing Parquet files without rewriting them.
wrong_explanation_1: CSV is a row-based text format that requires reading entire rows even when only a few columns are needed. It does not support predicate pushdown, columnar reads, or schema evolution — adding a new column requires rewriting all existing files.
wrong_explanation_2: JSON is a row-based text format with flexible schema support, but it does not provide columnar reads or predicate pushdown. It is significantly less efficient than Parquet for analytical queries that access a subset of columns.
wrong_explanation_3: XML is a verbose hierarchical text format that is inefficient for both storage and analytical querying. It does not support columnar reads, predicate pushdown, or efficient schema evolution.

scenario: A team wants to evaluate multiple foundation models on a STANDARD public dataset (such as MMLU or HellaSwag) so they can be compared on the same yardstick. Which kind of dataset does this describe?
correct_answer: Benchmark dataset
wrong_answer_1: Production telemetry log
wrong_answer_2: Vector store
wrong_answer_3: Embedding model
correct_explanation: Benchmark datasets are standard, public evaluation datasets used to compare different models on the same yardstick. MMLU, HellaSwag, BIG-bench, and HumanEval are well-known benchmark datasets for LLMs.
wrong_explanation_1: Production telemetry is logged usage data, not a public benchmark dataset.
wrong_explanation_2: Vector stores hold embeddings for retrieval, not standardized benchmarks.
wrong_explanation_3: Embedding models produce vectors; they are not benchmark datasets.

scenario: A developer is building a photo-sharing application. When a user uploads a photo to S3, a Lambda function is invoked to apply filters and store the result. The processing takes an average of 4 minutes. The application currently invokes Lambda synchronously, causing the API to hang until processing completes. What change should the developer make to prevent the API from becoming unresponsive?
correct_answer: Change the Lambda invocation type to Event to invoke the function asynchronously.
wrong_answer_1: Change the Lambda invocation type to DryRun to validate the request without waiting.
wrong_answer_2: Increase the API Gateway integration timeout to 15 minutes to match the Lambda execution time.
wrong_answer_3: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to reduce the function's execution time.
correct_explanation: Setting the invocation type to Event triggers asynchronous Lambda invocation. The API immediately receives a 202 Accepted response and Lambda processes the image in the background. The function's result is not returned to the caller, which is appropriate for fire-and-forget processing tasks like image filtering.
wrong_explanation_1: The DryRun invocation type validates parameters and permissions without executing the function. It does not process the image and is used only for testing IAM permissions, not for production workloads.
wrong_explanation_2: API Gateway has a maximum integration timeout of 29 seconds. It cannot be extended to 15 minutes, so synchronous invocation of a 4-minute Lambda function through API Gateway will always time out regardless of configuration.
wrong_explanation_3: Provisioned Concurrency pre-warms Lambda execution environments to eliminate cold start latency. It reduces initialization time but does not reduce the actual processing time of the filter operation, which is the cause of the 4-minute duration.

scenario: A company has an Amazon S3 bucket that receives millions of small objects daily from IoT devices. A cost analysis shows that S3 API request costs are unexpectedly high. The objects are written once and read infrequently. Which approach reduces S3 costs for this workload?
correct_answer: Aggregate multiple small IoT messages into larger batched objects before writing to S3, reducing the total number of PUT requests.
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 Requester Pays so that the IoT devices pay for the PUT request costs.
wrong_answer_2: Switch to S3 Glacier for all IoT data to reduce storage costs and eliminate PUT request charges.
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically reduce the cost of infrequently accessed objects.
correct_explanation: S3 charges per API request (PUT, GET, etc.). Millions of small individual PUT requests generate significant request costs. Aggregating multiple IoT messages into a single larger object before writing reduces the number of PUT requests proportionally, directly lowering API costs. This is a common pattern for IoT data ingestion pipelines.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Requester Pays shifts the cost of GET requests to the requester, not PUT requests. IoT devices writing data are the requesters for PUT operations, so enabling Requester Pays would not reduce the company's PUT request costs.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Glacier does not support direct PUT operations from standard S3 API calls in the same way — objects must be transitioned via lifecycle rules. Glacier also has minimum storage duration charges and retrieval fees that could increase total costs for this workload.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage costs based on access frequency but does not reduce API request costs. The high cost in this scenario is from PUT requests, not storage pricing.

scenario: You are building a real-time fraud detection system for a payment processing platform. Transaction events arrive via an API at a rate of thousands per second. Multiple independent systems — a rules engine, an ML scoring service, and an audit logger — must each process every transaction event. The solution must support each consumer reading at its own pace and must retain events for 24 hours for replay. Which AWS service is the MOST suitable ingestion layer?
correct_answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SQS Standard Queue
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SNS
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Data Firehose
correct_explanation: Kinesis Data Streams supports multiple independent consumers each maintaining their own position in the stream. Data is retained for up to 365 days (24 hours by default), enabling replay. Each consumer reads at its own pace without affecting others. This makes it the correct choice for fan-out real-time processing with replay capability.
wrong_explanation_1: SQS Standard queues deliver each message to only one consumer. Multiple services polling the same queue would each receive different messages — not the same message. SQS does not support the fan-out pattern where all consumers receive every event.
wrong_explanation_2: SNS delivers messages to all subscribers simultaneously at the time of publication but does not retain messages. If a subscriber is unavailable or needs to replay events, the messages are gone. SNS cannot support consumers reading at their own pace from a retained log.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Data Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations like S3 or Redshift for storage and analysis. It does not support multiple independent real-time consumers reading from the same stream and is not designed for sub-second fraud detection processing.

scenario: A company runs multiple SageMaker training jobs and inference endpoints across several teams. The finance team wants to allocate ML infrastructure costs to individual business units for chargeback purposes. Which approach enables cost allocation by team or project in AWS?
correct_answer: Apply AWS cost allocation tags to SageMaker resources and enable them in the AWS Billing console
wrong_answer_1: Create separate AWS accounts for each team and use AWS Organizations for consolidated billing
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon CloudWatch to track resource utilization and manually calculate costs per team
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to generate per-team cost reports
correct_explanation: AWS cost allocation tags allow you to label SageMaker resources (training jobs, endpoints, notebooks) with key-value pairs such as team or project. Once activated in the Billing console, these tags appear in Cost Explorer and detailed billing reports, enabling precise cost allocation and chargeback to individual business units.
wrong_explanation_1: Creating separate accounts per team is a valid isolation strategy but is a significant organizational change. Cost allocation tags achieve the same chargeback goal within a single account without requiring account restructuring.
wrong_explanation_2: CloudWatch tracks utilization metrics (CPU, GPU, memory) but does not directly map to AWS billing costs. Manually calculating costs from utilization data is complex and error-prone compared to using cost allocation tags.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Trusted Advisor provides recommendations for cost optimization, security, and performance. It does not generate per-team cost allocation reports or support chargeback workflows.

scenario: A data engineering team has multiple AWS Glue ETL jobs that read from and write to tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. After a schema change in a source table (a new column was added), downstream jobs start failing because they reference the old schema. Which Glue Data Catalog feature helps manage schema versions and track changes over time?
correct_answer: AWS Glue Data Catalog schema versioning
wrong_answer_1: AWS Glue job bookmarks
wrong_answer_2: AWS Lake Formation data filters
wrong_answer_3: Amazon S3 versioning on the underlying data files
correct_explanation: The AWS Glue Data Catalog maintains a version history of table schemas. When a crawler updates a table schema (e.g., adding a new column), the previous schema version is preserved. Teams can view schema history, compare versions, and roll back to a previous schema version if downstream jobs break due to schema changes.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed by a job to avoid reprocessing. They do not track schema changes or maintain schema version history in the Data Catalog.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Lake Formation data filters control access to specific columns and rows in Data Catalog tables. They do not manage schema versions or track schema change history.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon S3 versioning preserves previous versions of data files when they are overwritten. It does not track schema changes in the Glue Data Catalog or help manage table schema versions.

scenario: A company purchases physical servers for a five-year refresh cycle and pays for them up front through its capital budget. After moving the equivalent workload to AWS, the same dollars now appear as ongoing monthly charges. This shift in how IT spend is classified illustrates which transition?
correct_answer: Capital expenditure to operating expenditure
wrong_answer_1: Operating expenditure to capital expenditure
wrong_answer_2: Fixed cost to amortized cost
wrong_answer_3: Variable cost to depreciated cost
correct_explanation: Buying physical hardware is a capital expenditure (CapEx) — large upfront investment, depreciated over time. Pay-as-you-go cloud usage is operating expenditure (OpEx) — ongoing consumption costs. Moving to AWS shifts IT spend from CapEx to OpEx.
wrong_explanation_1: The direction is reversed. Cloud consumption is OpEx; on-premises hardware purchases are CapEx. The company is moving from CapEx to OpEx, not the other way around.
wrong_explanation_2: Amortized cost is a generic accounting term and does not specifically describe the cloud spending model. The relevant terminology is CapEx to OpEx.
wrong_explanation_3: Depreciation applies to capital assets being consumed over their useful life. Cloud spend is not depreciated — it is expensed in the period consumed.

scenario: A startup wants to launch a new SaaS product but cannot accurately predict how many customers will sign up in the first six months. The team wants to avoid purchasing servers that may sit idle if demand is low, but they also need the option to scale rapidly if demand surges. Which AWS Cloud value proposition addresses this concern most directly?
correct_answer: Trade capital expense for variable expense
wrong_answer_1: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
wrong_answer_2: Benefit from massive economies of scale
wrong_answer_3: Increase speed and agility
correct_explanation: The ability to trade capital expense for variable expense is the cloud value proposition that lets a business pay only for what it consumes, rather than committing capital up front for hardware that may be over- or under-utilized. The startup pays in proportion to actual customer demand.
wrong_explanation_1: Stopping data center spend is a real cloud benefit, but it primarily addresses operational overhead and physical infrastructure costs — not the specific risk of buying compute capacity for uncertain demand.
wrong_explanation_2: Economies of scale describe how AWS achieves lower per-unit pricing because of its scale, allowing customers to benefit from lower pay-as-you-go prices. It does not directly address right-sizing for unknown demand.
wrong_explanation_3: Speed and agility describe how quickly resources can be provisioned. It is a related benefit but does not specifically address the cost risk of provisioning capacity before demand is known.

scenario: A company has an AWS Direct Connect connection for its primary workloads. The company also runs a development environment that occasionally needs to connect to on-premises resources. The development team currently uses a separate Site-to-Site VPN for this connectivity, which incurs hourly VPN connection charges. The company wants to reduce connectivity costs for the development environment. Which solution eliminates the VPN charges while maintaining on-premises connectivity?
correct_answer: Route development environment traffic over the existing Direct Connect connection by adding the development VPC as an attachment to the Direct Connect gateway, eliminating the need for a separate VPN connection.
wrong_answer_1: Replace the Direct Connect connection with a higher-bandwidth VPN connection that can serve both production and development environments.
wrong_answer_2: Use VPC peering between the production VPC and the development VPC so that development traffic can reach on-premises resources through the production VPC's Direct Connect connection.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Transit Gateway with the Direct Connect gateway attachment and add both VPCs to the Transit Gateway to share the Direct Connect connection.
correct_explanation: A Direct Connect gateway can be associated with multiple VPCs across the same or different regions. By attaching the development VPC to the existing Direct Connect gateway, development traffic can reach on-premises resources over the same Direct Connect connection, eliminating the separate VPN connection and its hourly charges.
wrong_explanation_1: Replacing Direct Connect with VPN would degrade performance and reliability for production workloads. Direct Connect provides dedicated bandwidth and consistent latency that VPN over the internet cannot match. This is not a viable cost optimization for production environments.
wrong_explanation_2: VPC peering is non-transitive — traffic cannot flow from the development VPC through the production VPC to reach on-premises resources via Direct Connect. AWS explicitly does not support transitive routing through VPC peering connections.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Transit Gateway with Direct Connect gateway attachment is a valid solution and would work, but it introduces Transit Gateway hourly attachment charges and data processing fees. Simply attaching the development VPC directly to the existing Direct Connect gateway is simpler and avoids Transit Gateway costs.

scenario: Which phase of the ML lifecycle comes FIRST, before any data is collected or models are designed?
correct_answer: Business problem framing and goal identification
wrong_answer_1: Hyperparameter tuning
wrong_answer_2: Model deployment
wrong_answer_3: Inference
correct_explanation: The ML lifecycle starts with framing the business problem, identifying success criteria, and deciding whether ML is the right tool. Skipping this phase often leads to wasted effort on the wrong objective.
wrong_explanation_1: Hyperparameter tuning is a training-time activity, far downstream of problem framing.
wrong_explanation_2: Deployment comes after a model is trained and evaluated.
wrong_explanation_3: Inference is the use of a deployed model — even later.

scenario: A machine learning team is preparing a training dataset that was joined from three different source systems. After the join, the team suspects there are duplicate records caused by overlapping data exports. Which approach should the team use to detect and remove duplicates before training?
correct_answer: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile the dataset and apply a deduplication recipe step based on a composite key
wrong_answer_1: Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to detect duplicate records
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon Macie to scan the dataset for duplicate entries
wrong_answer_3: Use Amazon Rekognition to identify duplicate records in the dataset
correct_explanation: AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that includes dataset profiling and built-in recipe steps for deduplication. It can identify duplicate rows based on a composite key (combination of columns) and remove them as part of a repeatable data preparation pipeline.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon SageMaker Clarify is designed to detect bias in ML datasets and explain model predictions. It does not provide functionality for identifying or removing duplicate records.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Macie is a data security service that uses ML to discover and protect sensitive data such as PII in S3. It is not designed for data quality tasks like deduplication.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Rekognition is a computer vision service for image and video analysis. It has no capability to detect duplicate records in tabular datasets.

scenario: A data scientist trained a multi-class image classification model with 10 classes. After evaluation, the overall accuracy is 88%, but the business team reports that the model performs poorly on two specific classes. Which tool should the data scientist use to identify which specific classes are being confused with each other?
correct_answer: Confusion matrix
wrong_answer_1: Learning curve
wrong_answer_2: ROC curve
wrong_answer_3: Elbow plot
correct_explanation: A confusion matrix shows the counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives for each class in a multi-class problem. It directly reveals which classes are being confused with each other, allowing the data scientist to identify specific class pairs where the model struggles.
wrong_explanation_1: A learning curve plots training and validation performance as a function of training set size. It is used to diagnose underfitting and overfitting, not to identify which specific classes are being confused.
wrong_explanation_2: An ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at various thresholds. For multi-class problems, it requires one-vs-rest decomposition and does not directly show which specific classes are being confused with each other.
wrong_explanation_3: An elbow plot is used in unsupervised clustering (e.g., K-means) to determine the optimal number of clusters. It is not applicable to evaluating multi-class classification performance.

scenario: A large enterprise uses AWS Organizations with dozens of member accounts. The security team needs to ensure that no member account can disable AWS CloudTrail logging in any account. The requirement must be enforced centrally and cannot be overridden by account administrators. Which solution meets this requirement?
correct_answer: Create an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and cloudtrail:UpdateTrail for all principals, and attach it to the root of the organization.
wrong_answer_1: Enable CloudTrail in each member account and configure CloudWatch alarms to alert the security team if CloudTrail is disabled.
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS Config with the cloud-trail-enabled managed rule in each account and configure auto-remediation to re-enable CloudTrail if it is disabled.
wrong_answer_3: Grant the security team's IAM role in the management account permission to re-enable CloudTrail in any member account if it is found to be disabled.
correct_explanation: An SCP attached to the organization root applies to all member accounts and cannot be overridden by any IAM policy within those accounts, including the root user. Denying the specific CloudTrail API actions prevents any principal in any member account from disabling or deleting trails, providing a centrally enforced, non-bypassable control.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudWatch alarms detect and alert on CloudTrail being disabled but do not prevent it. There is a window between when CloudTrail is disabled and when the alert is acted upon during which audit logging is absent.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Config auto-remediation can re-enable CloudTrail after it is disabled, but there is a gap between the disable action and the remediation. This is a reactive control, not a preventive one. An SCP prevents the action from occurring at all.
wrong_explanation_3: Granting the security team permission to re-enable CloudTrail is a reactive remediation approach. It does not prevent account administrators from disabling CloudTrail in the first place and relies on manual or automated response after the fact.

scenario: A machine learning team needs to run weekly batch inference on 10 million customer records stored in S3 to generate personalized product recommendations. The inference job takes approximately 4 hours. The team does not need real-time responses. Which SageMaker deployment option is most cost-effective for this use case?
correct_answer: SageMaker Batch Transform
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker real-time inference endpoint
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference
wrong_answer_3: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference with a persistent endpoint
correct_explanation: SageMaker Batch Transform is designed for offline batch inference on large datasets. It spins up instances, processes the entire dataset, writes results to S3, and then terminates the instances — charging only for the duration of the job. For weekly batch jobs on millions of records with no real-time requirement, Batch Transform is the most cost-effective option.
wrong_explanation_1: A real-time inference endpoint keeps instances running continuously, incurring 24/7 costs even when not processing requests. For a weekly batch job, this would be significantly more expensive than Batch Transform.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference is designed for sporadic real-time requests, not for processing 10 million records in a single batch job. It has payload size limits and is not optimized for large-scale batch processing.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference handles individual requests asynchronously and is designed for long-running single predictions, not for processing millions of records as a batch. A persistent endpoint would also incur continuous costs.

scenario: A data engineering team runs a complex data pipeline with multiple AWS Glue jobs, Lambda functions, and Step Functions workflows. The team wants to visualize the end-to-end data flow and track how data moves through each stage of the pipeline. Which AWS service provides data lineage tracking and visualization?
correct_answer: AWS Glue Data Catalog with lineage tracking enabled
wrong_answer_1: Amazon CloudWatch ServiceLens
wrong_answer_2: AWS X-Ray
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Managed Grafana
correct_explanation: AWS Glue Data Catalog supports data lineage tracking, which captures metadata about how data flows through ETL jobs and transformations. You can visualize lineage in the Glue console to understand data dependencies and track data movement through the pipeline.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon CloudWatch ServiceLens provides a unified view of application performance and traces requests through distributed applications. It is designed for application monitoring, not data lineage tracking in data pipelines.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS X-Ray traces requests through distributed applications and provides performance insights. While it can trace Lambda and Step Functions executions, it does not provide data lineage visualization showing how data flows through ETL transformations.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Managed Grafana is a visualization service for creating dashboards from metrics and logs. While you can build custom dashboards, it does not natively provide data lineage tracking or visualization for data pipelines.

scenario: Which responsible AI dimension is about giving humans the ability to STEER, OVERRIDE, OR STOP an AI system's behavior when needed?
correct_answer: Controllability
wrong_answer_1: Latency
wrong_answer_2: Quantization
wrong_answer_3: Token throughput
correct_explanation: Controllability is the responsible AI dimension about supporting human oversight — letting humans steer, override, or stop AI behavior. It complements other dimensions by ensuring people retain meaningful control over deployed AI.
wrong_explanation_1: Latency is operational performance, not controllability.
wrong_explanation_2: Quantization is a model-compression technique.
wrong_explanation_3: Token throughput is a performance metric.

scenario: A machine learning team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio to develop and train models. The security team requires that all SageMaker Studio traffic to AWS services (S3, ECR, SageMaker APIs) must route through the private AWS network and not traverse the public internet. Which configuration achieves this?
correct_answer: Deploy SageMaker Studio in a VPC with VPC-only mode and create interface VPC endpoints for the required AWS services
wrong_answer_1: Enable SageMaker Studio encryption and use AWS KMS customer-managed keys
wrong_answer_2: Attach an IAM policy to the SageMaker execution role that denies internet access
wrong_answer_3: Configure a NAT Gateway in the VPC to route all outbound traffic through a single IP
correct_explanation: SageMaker Studio VPC-only mode routes all traffic through the customer's VPC instead of the public internet. Interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for S3, ECR, and SageMaker APIs ensure that traffic to these services stays within the AWS private network, satisfying the security requirement.
wrong_explanation_1: KMS encryption protects data at rest and in transit but does not control network routing. It does not prevent Studio traffic from traversing the public internet.
wrong_explanation_2: IAM policies control API authorization (what actions are allowed) but do not control network routing. An IAM policy cannot prevent network traffic from routing through the public internet.
wrong_explanation_3: A NAT Gateway routes outbound traffic through a single IP but still sends traffic over the public internet. It does not keep traffic within the AWS private network as required.

scenario: A company is running a containerized application on Amazon ECS with Fargate. The application experiences variable load throughout the day. The company wants to automatically scale the number of running ECS tasks based on CPU utilization, with a target of 60% average CPU across all tasks. Which scaling configuration should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Configure Application Auto Scaling for the ECS service with a target tracking scaling policy targeting ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization at 60%.
wrong_answer_1: Configure EC2 Auto Scaling for the ECS cluster with a target tracking policy based on CPU utilization.
wrong_answer_2: Configure an ECS service with a fixed desired count and use CloudWatch alarms to manually update the desired count when CPU exceeds 60%.
wrong_answer_3: Configure AWS Lambda to poll ECS task CPU metrics every minute and call the UpdateService API to adjust the desired count.
correct_explanation: Application Auto Scaling manages scaling for ECS services (among other services). A target tracking policy on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization automatically adjusts the number of running tasks to maintain the target CPU utilization. This is the native, fully managed scaling mechanism for ECS services on Fargate.
wrong_explanation_1: EC2 Auto Scaling manages EC2 instance fleets, not ECS task counts. With Fargate, there are no EC2 instances to scale — Fargate manages the underlying infrastructure. Application Auto Scaling is the correct service for scaling ECS task counts.
wrong_explanation_2: Manually updating the desired count in response to CloudWatch alarms requires human intervention and is not automatic scaling. It also introduces significant latency between when the threshold is breached and when the scaling action is applied.
wrong_explanation_3: Using Lambda to poll metrics and call UpdateService is a custom implementation of functionality that Application Auto Scaling provides natively. It adds operational complexity, potential polling latency, and requires managing Lambda execution and error handling.

scenario: A company needs to share encrypted Amazon EBS snapshots with a partner AWS account. The snapshots are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key in the company's account. The partner account needs to be able to create EBS volumes from the shared snapshots. What must the solutions architect do to enable this?
correct_answer: Share the EBS snapshot with the partner account and update the KMS key policy to grant the partner account kms:DescribeKey, kms:CreateGrant, and kms:Decrypt permissions.
wrong_answer_1: Re-encrypt the snapshot with an AWS managed key before sharing it with the partner account.
wrong_answer_2: Share the EBS snapshot with the partner account — no additional KMS configuration is needed because snapshot sharing automatically grants key access.
wrong_answer_3: Export the snapshot to an S3 bucket, share the S3 bucket with the partner account, and let them import the snapshot into their account.
correct_explanation: When an EBS snapshot is encrypted with a CMK, sharing the snapshot alone is not sufficient. The partner account must also be granted access to the KMS key used to encrypt the snapshot. The key policy must explicitly allow the partner account to use the key for decryption and grant creation, which is required when the partner creates an EBS volume from the snapshot.
wrong_explanation_1: Re-encrypting with an AWS managed key (aws/ebs) would make the snapshot unshareably encrypted — AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts. The snapshot would need to be re-encrypted with a CMK that has a cross-account key policy.
wrong_explanation_2: Sharing an encrypted snapshot does not automatically grant the partner account access to the KMS key. Without explicit key policy permissions, the partner account will receive an access denied error when attempting to create a volume from the snapshot.
wrong_explanation_3: Exporting snapshots to S3 and re-importing them is a complex, multi-step process that is not the standard approach for sharing encrypted snapshots. It also does not address the KMS key access requirement and introduces unnecessary data transfer steps.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to clean and normalize a dataset of 10 million customer records stored in Amazon S3. The transformations include standardizing phone number formats, removing duplicate rows, and splitting a full name column into first and last name. The team wants a visual, no-code interface to define and preview these transformations before running them at scale. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
correct_answer: AWS Glue DataBrew
wrong_answer_1: AWS Glue ETL job with PySpark
wrong_answer_2: Amazon EMR with Apache Spark
wrong_answer_3: AWS Lambda with S3 event triggers
correct_explanation: AWS Glue DataBrew provides a visual, no-code interface for defining data transformation recipes. Engineers can preview transformations on a sample of the data before running the recipe at scale on the full dataset. It includes over 250 built-in transformations including deduplication, string splitting, and format standardization.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Glue ETL with PySpark requires writing and maintaining Spark code. It does not provide a visual no-code interface for defining or previewing transformations.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon EMR with Apache Spark requires provisioning a cluster and writing Spark application code. It offers no visual transformation interface and has significantly more operational overhead.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Lambda is suited for lightweight, event-driven processing of individual records. It does not provide a visual transformation interface and is not designed for batch processing 10 million records with complex multi-step transformations.

scenario: A machine learning team has trained a regression model to predict housing prices. After evaluating on the test set, the model shows a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of $15,000 and an R² score of 0.62. The team wants to understand whether the model's errors are systematically biased toward over- or under-prediction. Which analysis should they perform?
correct_answer: Plot the residuals (predicted minus actual) against the predicted values to check for systematic bias
wrong_answer_1: Calculate the F1 score to measure the balance between precision and recall
wrong_answer_2: Run a confusion matrix analysis to identify misclassified samples
wrong_answer_3: Compute the AUC-ROC curve to evaluate the model's discrimination ability
correct_explanation: A residual plot (predicted minus actual values plotted against predicted values) reveals whether errors are randomly distributed or show systematic patterns. If residuals are consistently positive or negative across a range of predicted values, the model has a systematic bias toward over- or under-prediction that needs to be addressed.
wrong_explanation_1: F1 score is a classification metric that combines precision and recall. It is not applicable to regression problems and cannot reveal systematic bias in continuous predictions.
wrong_explanation_2: A confusion matrix is used for classification problems to show counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. It is not applicable to regression models predicting continuous values like housing prices.
wrong_explanation_3: AUC-ROC is a classification metric that measures a model's ability to discriminate between classes at various threshold settings. It is not applicable to regression problems.

scenario: A hospital wants to extract medical conditions, medications, and dosages from clinical notes — recognizing healthcare-specific terminology. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this domain?
correct_answer: Amazon Comprehend Medical
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Comprehend (standard)
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Lex
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Polly
correct_explanation: Amazon Comprehend Medical is a specialized NLP service for the healthcare domain. It detects medical entities (conditions, medications, dosages, anatomy) and ICD-10/RxNorm codes from unstructured clinical text.
wrong_explanation_1: Standard Comprehend handles general-purpose NLP but does not include the medical-specific entity types and code mappings.
wrong_explanation_2: Lex builds chatbots, not medical entity extractors.
wrong_explanation_3: Polly is text-to-speech.

scenario: A developer is building a mobile application using Amazon Cognito. Authenticated users need temporary AWS credentials to upload files directly to a private S3 bucket. The credentials should be scoped to only allow uploads to the user's own folder. Which Cognito feature provides temporary AWS credentials to authenticated users?
correct_answer: Amazon Cognito Identity Pools
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Cognito User Pools
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Cognito Sync
wrong_answer_3: AWS IAM Identity Center
correct_explanation: Cognito Identity Pools (Federated Identities) exchange Cognito User Pool tokens (or other identity provider tokens) for temporary AWS credentials via STS. The credentials are scoped by an IAM role associated with the identity pool, and IAM policy variables like ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} can restrict access to the user's specific S3 folder.
wrong_explanation_1: Cognito User Pools handle user authentication and issue JWT tokens (ID, access, and refresh tokens). They do not issue AWS credentials. To get AWS credentials, the JWT token from a User Pool must be exchanged through an Identity Pool.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Cognito Sync is a service for synchronizing user profile data and app preferences across devices. It does not issue AWS credentials or provide access to S3.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly SSO) is designed for workforce identity — employees accessing AWS accounts and business applications. It is not designed for mobile application end-user authentication or for issuing per-user scoped AWS credentials to app users.

scenario: A company is using AWS CodeDeploy to deploy a new version of a Lambda function. The deployment should shift all traffic to the new version immediately without any gradual rollout. If a CloudWatch alarm triggers within 5 minutes of deployment, CodeDeploy should automatically roll back. Which deployment configuration and setting should be used?
correct_answer: Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce and enable automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarm.
wrong_answer_1: Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes and enable automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarm.
wrong_answer_2: Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute and enable automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarm.
wrong_answer_3: Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce without enabling automatic rollback, and manually monitor CloudWatch alarms.
correct_explanation: LambdaAllAtOnce shifts 100% of traffic to the new version immediately in a single step. Enabling automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarm instructs CodeDeploy to redeploy the previous version if a configured alarm triggers after the deployment. This combination satisfies both requirements: immediate full traffic shift and alarm-triggered automatic rollback.
wrong_explanation_1: LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes shifts only 10% of traffic initially, then the remaining 90% after 5 minutes. This is a gradual rollout, not an immediate full traffic shift. The requirement specifies all traffic should shift immediately.
wrong_explanation_2: LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute shifts traffic in 10% increments every minute, taking 10 minutes to complete. This is a gradual linear rollout, not an immediate full traffic shift.
wrong_explanation_3: Disabling automatic rollback means a CloudWatch alarm would only notify the team — it would not trigger an automatic redeployment of the previous version. Manual monitoring and rollback introduces human response time and does not meet the requirement for automatic rollback.

scenario: A platform team commits to managing every change to their AWS environment through a code-reviewed CloudFormation pipeline. Manual console changes are not permitted. Which Well-Architected design principle is BEST illustrated by this practice?
correct_answer: Perform operations as code
wrong_answer_1: Adopt a consumption model
wrong_answer_2: Make frequent, small, reversible changes
wrong_answer_3: Stop guessing capacity
correct_explanation: Forbidding manual changes and codifying every change through code-reviewed templates is the canonical "perform operations as code" principle of operational excellence. Code is reviewable, repeatable, and auditable.
wrong_explanation_1: Consumption model is a cost-optimization principle about paying for what you use.
wrong_explanation_2: Small reversible changes is also operational excellence, but it focuses on deployment frequency and rollback ability, not on codification specifically.
wrong_explanation_3: Capacity planning is unrelated to manual-vs-code change management.

scenario: A data engineering team is designing a schema for an Amazon DynamoDB table that stores user session data. Each session has a user_id and a session_id. The team needs to efficiently retrieve a specific session by both user_id and session_id, and also query all sessions for a specific user. Which key design supports both access patterns?
correct_answer: Use user_id as the partition key and session_id as the sort key
wrong_answer_1: Use session_id as the partition key with no sort key
wrong_answer_2: Use a composite string of user_id#session_id as the partition key
wrong_answer_3: Create a Global Secondary Index with session_id as the partition key and user_id as the sort key
correct_explanation: Using user_id as the partition key and session_id as the sort key supports both access patterns: a GetItem call with both keys retrieves a specific session, and a Query call with only the partition key retrieves all sessions for a user. This is the optimal DynamoDB key design for these requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Using session_id as the partition key with no sort key allows efficient retrieval of a specific session by session_id, but querying all sessions for a user would require a full table Scan — which is inefficient and expensive.
wrong_explanation_2: Using a composite string as the partition key allows retrieval of a specific session but prevents querying all sessions for a user without knowing all their session IDs. It also distributes data less evenly across partitions.
wrong_explanation_3: A GSI with session_id as the partition key allows querying by session_id, but the primary table design with user_id as partition key already supports both required access patterns without needing a GSI.

scenario: A data scientist is training a deep learning model on Amazon SageMaker using a single ml.p3.2xlarge instance. Training is taking 48 hours, which is too slow for the team's iteration cycle. The model architecture uses standard dense layers and the dataset is 500 GB stored in S3. Which approach will most effectively reduce training time?
correct_answer: Use SageMaker distributed data parallel training across multiple GPU instances
wrong_answer_1: Switch to a CPU-based instance type with more vCPUs
wrong_answer_2: Reduce the dataset size by randomly sampling 10% of the training data
wrong_answer_3: Increase the batch size to the maximum that fits in GPU memory
correct_explanation: SageMaker's distributed data parallel (DDP) library splits the training data across multiple GPU instances and synchronizes gradients, enabling near-linear scaling of training throughput. For a 500 GB dataset and a model that is already GPU-bound, distributing across multiple instances is the most effective way to reduce wall-clock training time.
wrong_explanation_1: Switching to a CPU-based instance would significantly slow down deep learning training. Deep learning models rely on GPU parallelism for matrix operations — CPUs are orders of magnitude slower for this workload.
wrong_explanation_2: Randomly sampling 10% of the training data would reduce training time but at the cost of model quality. The model would train on far less data, likely resulting in worse generalization. This is not a recommended approach when the goal is to maintain model quality.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing batch size can improve GPU utilization and reduce the number of gradient update steps per epoch, but it has diminishing returns and can negatively affect model convergence and generalization. It does not address the fundamental bottleneck of a single GPU instance.

scenario: An on-call engineer wants to see the operational status of AWS services AND any account-specific events that might affect their workloads (e.g., scheduled maintenance on an EC2 host hosting their instances). Which AWS resource provides both views?
correct_answer: AWS Health Dashboard (with Service Health and Your account health views)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor
wrong_answer_2: Amazon CloudWatch
wrong_answer_3: AWS CloudTrail
correct_explanation: The AWS Health Dashboard combines a public Service Health view (general AWS service status) and a Your account health view that surfaces account-specific events — including scheduled maintenance, instance retirements, and certificate expirations.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor highlights best-practice issues but does not provide service operational status or account health events.
wrong_explanation_2: CloudWatch monitors customer metrics, alarms, and logs. It does not report AWS service-side health information.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudTrail logs API calls. It does not report service status or AWS-initiated maintenance events.

scenario: A team wants to test their Lambda function locally before deploying to AWS. The function is triggered by an SQS event and reads from a DynamoDB table. The team wants to simulate the SQS event payload and invoke the function in a local environment that matches the Lambda runtime. Which tool enables this?
correct_answer: AWS SAM CLI using sam local invoke with a local event JSON file that simulates the SQS event payload.
wrong_answer_1: The AWS Lambda console's test event feature with a custom SQS event template.
wrong_answer_2: AWS CodeBuild with a local build environment configured to run Lambda functions.
wrong_answer_3: The AWS CLI lambda invoke command with a local payload file.
correct_explanation: The SAM CLI's sam local invoke command runs the Lambda function in a Docker container that replicates the Lambda execution environment. A local JSON file containing the SQS event payload is passed as input. This enables fully local testing before deployment, with no AWS account interaction required for the function execution itself.
wrong_explanation_1: The Lambda console test event feature invokes the function in AWS — it requires the function to already be deployed. It does not provide local pre-deployment testing.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS CodeBuild runs build and test commands in a managed build environment in AWS. It does not provide a local Lambda execution environment and requires network access to AWS services.
wrong_explanation_3: The AWS CLI lambda invoke command invokes a deployed Lambda function in AWS. Like the console test feature, it requires the function to already be deployed and does not support local execution.

scenario: A company wants to build a serverless data pipeline that automatically processes new files uploaded to S3, transforms the data using Python, and loads the results into Amazon Redshift every hour. The files vary in size from 1 MB to 5 GB. The company wants minimal operational overhead. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Use AWS Glue with a scheduled trigger to run an ETL job every hour that reads new S3 files, applies Python transformations using Glue's PySpark or Python Shell job type, and loads results into Redshift using the COPY command.
wrong_answer_1: Use AWS Lambda triggered by S3 Event Notifications to process each file as it arrives and load results into Redshift.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon EMR with a scheduled step to process files hourly, running a PySpark job to transform and load data into Redshift.
wrong_answer_3: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream S3 file contents into Redshift with inline Lambda transformation.
correct_explanation: AWS Glue is a fully managed serverless ETL service that handles job scheduling, scaling, and infrastructure automatically. It supports Python Shell jobs for smaller files and PySpark jobs for larger ones, natively integrates with S3 and Redshift, and can be triggered on a schedule. There are no servers to manage and it scales to handle files up to 5 GB without configuration changes.
wrong_explanation_1: Lambda has a 15-minute execution timeout and 10 GB memory limit. A 5 GB file cannot be fully processed within these constraints, especially with transformation logic. Lambda is appropriate for lightweight event-driven processing, not large-scale ETL.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon EMR requires provisioning and managing a cluster, even with auto-termination. Cluster startup time adds latency to the hourly schedule, and managing EMR adds operational overhead that contradicts the minimal overhead requirement.
wrong_explanation_3: Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for streaming data delivery, not for processing existing files in S3. It cannot read files from S3 on a schedule and its inline Lambda transformation has the same size and timeout limitations as Lambda.

scenario: A retail company needs to analyze clickstream data from its website in near-real-time to detect fraud patterns and personalize recommendations. The data arrives as a continuous stream of millions of events per hour. The analytics team wants to run SQL queries on the streaming data with sub-minute latency. Which AWS service should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the clickstream data and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) to run continuous SQL queries on the stream.
wrong_answer_1: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver clickstream data to Amazon S3, then use Amazon Athena to query the data.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon SQS to buffer clickstream events and trigger a Lambda function to process each event individually.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Glue streaming ETL to ingest and transform the clickstream data, then load it into Amazon Redshift for SQL analysis.
correct_explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides real-time ingestion of streaming data. Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink enables continuous SQL queries on streaming data with sub-minute latency, supporting windowed aggregations and pattern detection. This combination is purpose-built for real-time stream analytics.
wrong_explanation_1: Kinesis Data Firehose with S3 and Athena is a batch analytics pattern. Firehose buffers data for a minimum of 60 seconds before delivering to S3, and Athena queries are run on-demand against static files. This introduces minutes of latency, not sub-minute, and does not support continuous streaming queries.
wrong_explanation_2: SQS with Lambda processes individual events but does not support SQL-based windowed aggregations or pattern detection across a stream of events. Lambda functions process events in isolation and cannot maintain state across millions of events per hour efficiently.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue streaming ETL can process streaming data but is designed for ETL transformation, not for interactive SQL analytics. Loading into Redshift adds additional latency and Redshift is optimized for batch analytical queries, not sub-minute streaming analysis.

scenario: Over the past several years, AWS has lowered its prices on EC2 and S3 multiple times. Which underlying economic principle BEST explains how AWS is able to do this?
correct_answer: Massive economies of scale lower AWS's per-unit costs, which it passes to customers
wrong_answer_1: AWS subsidizes pricing through advertising revenue
wrong_answer_2: AWS resells third-party hardware at cost
wrong_answer_3: AWS prices are set by government regulators
correct_explanation: AWS achieves massive economies of scale through aggregated demand across millions of customers, allowing lower per-unit infrastructure costs. AWS has consistently passed these savings on through repeated price reductions on core services.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS does not subsidize pricing through advertising. Pricing reductions are driven by economies of scale.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS designs and operates its own custom infrastructure at scale rather than reselling third-party hardware at cost.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS service prices are not regulated by governments. They are set by AWS in response to scale efficiencies and competitive markets.

scenario: A data scientist wants to discover, browse, and quickly deploy pre-trained models and prebuilt ML solutions across many task types — including foundation models — from a curated hub inside Amazon SageMaker. Which feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
correct_explanation: SageMaker JumpStart is a model and solution hub curated by AWS. It includes built-in algorithms, prebuilt solutions, and foundation models with one-click deployment options inside SageMaker.
wrong_explanation_1: Model Monitor watches deployed endpoints for drift, not a model hub.
wrong_explanation_2: Ground Truth is a data-labeling service.
wrong_explanation_3: Pipelines orchestrate ML workflows, not model browsing and deployment.

scenario: A company is running a suite of internal tools on EC2 instances that are used by employees during business hours only. The instances run a mix of Linux and Windows workloads across several instance families. The company has been using On-Demand pricing and wants to reduce costs with a flexible commitment that applies across all instance families and operating systems without locking into specific instance types. Which purchasing option should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Purchase Compute Savings Plans, which provide up to 66% discount over On-Demand pricing and automatically apply to any EC2 instance regardless of instance family, size, OS, tenancy, or region.
wrong_answer_1: Purchase EC2 Instance Savings Plans for each instance family used, which provide a higher discount than Compute Savings Plans for specific instance families.
wrong_answer_2: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for each instance type currently in use to lock in the maximum discount.
wrong_answer_3: Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for each instance family, which allow changing instance attributes while maintaining a discount.
correct_explanation: Compute Savings Plans offer the most flexibility of any commitment-based pricing option — they apply automatically to any EC2 instance usage regardless of instance family, size, operating system, tenancy, or AWS region. For a mixed workload spanning multiple instance families and operating systems, Compute Savings Plans eliminate the need to manage separate commitments per instance type.
wrong_explanation_1: EC2 Instance Savings Plans provide a higher discount (up to 72%) than Compute Savings Plans but are locked to a specific instance family within a region. For a mixed workload across multiple instance families, separate Instance Savings Plans would be needed for each family, reducing flexibility and increasing management overhead.
wrong_explanation_2: Standard Reserved Instances provide the highest discount but are locked to a specific instance type, OS, tenancy, and region. For a mixed workload that may change over time, Standard RIs are inflexible and require purchasing separate reservations for each instance type in use.
wrong_explanation_3: Convertible Reserved Instances allow changing instance attributes but are still tied to a specific region and require managing separate reservations per instance family. They provide less flexibility than Compute Savings Plans and a lower discount than Standard RIs, making them a middle-ground option that is less suitable here than Compute Savings Plans.

scenario: An application needs the LLM to return a very short, single-line answer. Which inference parameter is the MOST direct control for limiting output length?
correct_answer: Maximum response length (max tokens)
wrong_answer_1: Temperature
wrong_answer_2: Top-K
wrong_answer_3: Top-P
correct_explanation: Maximum response length (sometimes called max tokens) directly caps the number of tokens generated. Setting a small max tokens enforces a short output. Stop sequences can also help, but max tokens is the most direct cap.
wrong_explanation_1: Temperature controls randomness, not length.
wrong_explanation_2: Top-K controls token-sampling diversity at each step, not total output length.
wrong_explanation_3: Top-P controls diversity, not total length.

scenario: Why does a typical ML workflow split data into separate training, validation, and test sets?
correct_answer: To tune hyperparameters on the validation set while keeping the test set untouched for an unbiased final performance estimate
wrong_answer_1: To speed up training by processing the three sets in parallel
wrong_answer_2: To enable ensemble methods that train different models on each subset
wrong_answer_3: To apply different preprocessing techniques to each subset
correct_explanation: The training set fits the model, the validation set tunes hyperparameters and informs model selection, and the test set provides an unbiased final estimate of generalization. Keeping the test set untouched until the end prevents leakage.
wrong_explanation_1: Parallelism is unrelated to the purpose of the split.
wrong_explanation_2: Ensembles do not require this three-way split.
wrong_explanation_3: Preprocessing decisions should be consistent across splits to avoid leakage; they are not the reason for the split.

scenario: In a RAG application, what is the role of the "AUGMENTATION" step?
correct_answer: Inserting retrieved context into the prompt sent to the foundation model so the FM grounds its answer in that context
wrong_answer_1: Adding more training data to the foundation model
wrong_answer_2: Adding additional GPUs to the inference endpoint
wrong_answer_3: Adding new tokens to the model's vocabulary
correct_explanation: The augmentation step injects retrieved context (relevant chunks from the vector store) into the prompt sent to the FM. The FM then generates a response that is grounded in that context, rather than relying solely on its parametric knowledge.
wrong_explanation_1: RAG operates at inference time and does not add training data to the FM.
wrong_explanation_2: GPU capacity is an infrastructure concern, not a RAG step.
wrong_explanation_3: Vocabulary expansion is a tokenizer-level change, not part of RAG.

scenario: A company runs a batch processing workload that requires 500 vCPUs for 4 hours each night. The workload is fault-tolerant and can be restarted if interrupted. The company wants to minimize compute costs. Which EC2 purchasing option should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Use EC2 Spot Instances with a Spot Fleet or Auto Scaling group configured to maintain the required capacity, taking advantage of the up to 90% discount over On-Demand pricing.
wrong_answer_1: Purchase 500 vCPUs worth of Reserved Instances with a 1-year term to cover the nightly batch workload.
wrong_answer_2: Use On-Demand Instances and schedule them to run only during the 4-hour batch window each night.
wrong_answer_3: Use Dedicated Hosts to ensure consistent hardware availability for the nightly batch workload.
correct_explanation: Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount over On-Demand pricing and are ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch workloads. Since the workload can be restarted if interrupted, Spot interruptions are acceptable. A Spot Fleet or Auto Scaling group with multiple instance types and AZs maximizes availability of Spot capacity at the lowest cost.
wrong_explanation_1: Reserved Instances provide a discount for steady-state workloads that run continuously. A workload that runs only 4 hours per night uses Reserved Instances for only 17% of the time, making the reservation inefficient. The unused hours are wasted spend.
wrong_explanation_2: On-Demand Instances are the most flexible option but the most expensive per hour. For a cost-sensitive batch workload that runs nightly, On-Demand pricing is significantly more expensive than Spot pricing.
wrong_explanation_3: Dedicated Hosts provide physical server isolation for licensing or compliance requirements. They are the most expensive EC2 option and provide no cost benefit for a batch workload that has no dedicated hardware requirements.

scenario: A telecommunications carrier wants to deploy an application that processes mobile device traffic directly inside the carrier's 5G network for ultra-low latency. Which AWS offering is purpose-built for this scenario?
correct_answer: AWS Wavelength
wrong_answer_1: AWS Direct Connect
wrong_answer_2: AWS Snowball Edge
wrong_answer_3: AWS Global Accelerator
correct_explanation: AWS Wavelength embeds AWS compute and storage at the edge of 5G telecommunications networks, enabling applications to process mobile traffic without it traversing to a Region. This is the AWS offering specifically designed for 5G edge workloads.
wrong_explanation_1: Direct Connect is a dedicated, private connection from on-premises networks to AWS. It is not deployed inside carrier 5G networks.
wrong_explanation_2: Snowball Edge is a portable data transfer and edge compute appliance for remote or disconnected locations, not for 5G carrier-network deployment.
wrong_explanation_3: Global Accelerator routes user traffic to the optimal AWS endpoint over the AWS network. It does not place compute inside 5G networks.

scenario: A developer needs to configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers only when all three data points in the most recent three consecutive evaluation periods exceed a threshold. The metric is checked every minute. How should the developer configure the alarm?
correct_answer: Set the Evaluation Period to 3 and Datapoints to Alarm to 3.
wrong_answer_1: Set the Period to 3 minutes and Datapoints to Alarm to 3.
wrong_answer_2: Set the Evaluation Period to 3 and use high-resolution metrics with a 10-second period.
wrong_answer_3: Set the Evaluation Period to 1 and Datapoints to Alarm to 3.
correct_explanation: Evaluation Period defines how many of the most recent data points to evaluate. Datapoints to Alarm defines how many of those data points must be breaching for the alarm to trigger. Setting both to 3 means all three of the most recent consecutive 1-minute data points must exceed the threshold before the alarm fires. This prevents false alarms from transient spikes.
wrong_explanation_1: Period defines the length of time (in seconds) for each individual data point — it is not the number of periods to evaluate. Setting Period to 3 minutes would create one data point every 3 minutes, not evaluate 3 consecutive 1-minute data points. The correct setting is Evaluation Period, not Period.
wrong_explanation_2: High-resolution metrics with a 10-second period would create data points every 10 seconds, not every minute. This changes the metric resolution and is not needed to configure the 3-consecutive-period alarm behavior described in the scenario.
wrong_explanation_3: Setting Evaluation Period to 1 means only the most recent data point is evaluated. With Datapoints to Alarm set to 3, the alarm would require 3 breaching data points out of 1 evaluated period, which is impossible. The Evaluation Period must be at least equal to Datapoints to Alarm.

scenario: A startup needs to handle highly unpredictable load. The CTO wants to avoid both buying servers up front and over-paying for a fixed monthly capacity. Which approach BEST aligns with AWS Cloud economic principles?
correct_answer: Use elastic services like Auto Scaling and Lambda, paying only for what is consumed
wrong_answer_1: Buy three-year Reserved Instances at All Upfront pricing for predicted peak load
wrong_answer_2: Co-locate hardware in a third-party data center and connect to AWS
wrong_answer_3: Provision a single very large EC2 instance to handle worst case
correct_explanation: AWS's elastic services let capacity track demand, and pay-as-you-go billing converts what would have been over-provisioning waste into actual usage cost. For unpredictable load, this is the most economically aligned approach.
wrong_explanation_1: Three-year All Upfront RIs sized for peak load defeat the goal: capacity is paid for regardless of actual demand, and capital is committed up front.
wrong_explanation_2: Co-location reintroduces capital expense and operational overhead — the opposite of the cloud economic model.
wrong_explanation_3: A single very large instance over-provisions for worst case all the time, wasting money on idle capacity during normal load.

scenario: A data engineering team uses AWS Glue crawlers to automatically discover and catalog datasets stored in Amazon S3. The S3 bucket contains partitioned Parquet files organized by year, month, and day. After running the crawler, the team notices that the Data Catalog table does not include partition columns. What is the most likely cause?
correct_answer: The crawler did not detect the partition structure because the S3 path does not follow the Hive-style partitioning format (key=value)
wrong_answer_1: The Glue crawler does not have permission to read partition metadata from S3
wrong_answer_2: The Parquet files do not include partition columns in their schema
wrong_answer_3: The Glue Data Catalog has reached its maximum number of partitions
correct_explanation: AWS Glue crawlers automatically detect partitions when S3 paths follow the Hive-style partitioning format (e.g., s3://bucket/table/year=2024/month=01/day=15/). If the paths use a different format (e.g., s3://bucket/table/2024/01/15/), the crawler will not recognize them as partitions. You can manually add partitions or restructure the S3 paths to follow Hive-style partitioning.
wrong_explanation_1: If the Glue crawler did not have permission to read S3 data, it would fail entirely and not create a table in the Data Catalog. The issue is not permissions but the partition path format.
wrong_explanation_2: Partition columns are derived from the S3 path structure, not from the Parquet file schema. Parquet files in partitioned datasets typically do not include partition columns in their schema because those values are encoded in the directory structure.
wrong_explanation_3: The Glue Data Catalog supports millions of partitions per table. Reaching the partition limit is extremely unlikely and would result in an error message, not silently omitting partition columns from the table definition.

scenario: A company has multiple VPCs in the same AWS Region that need to communicate with each other and with an on-premises network connected via AWS Direct Connect. The company expects to add more VPCs in the future. The solutions architect wants a hub-and-spoke network topology that minimizes the number of connections to manage. Which service should the architect use?
correct_answer: Deploy AWS Transit Gateway and attach all VPCs and the Direct Connect gateway to it, creating a centralized hub for all network traffic.
wrong_answer_1: Create VPC peering connections between every pair of VPCs and configure the on-premises router to connect to each VPC individually.
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS PrivateLink to create interface endpoints in each VPC to enable cross-VPC communication.
wrong_answer_3: Deploy a transit VPC using EC2-based VPN appliances to route traffic between all VPCs and the on-premises network.
correct_explanation: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a regional network hub that connects multiple VPCs and on-premises networks through a single gateway. Each VPC and the Direct Connect gateway attach to the Transit Gateway once, and routing is managed centrally. Adding new VPCs requires only a single new attachment, making it highly scalable for growing environments.
wrong_explanation_1: VPC peering requires a separate peering connection between every pair of VPCs (N*(N-1)/2 connections for N VPCs). Peering connections are also non-transitive — traffic cannot flow through an intermediate VPC. This approach does not scale and becomes unmanageable as the number of VPCs grows.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS PrivateLink enables private access to specific services across VPCs but is not designed for general-purpose VPC-to-VPC routing. It requires creating individual endpoints for each service and does not support transitive routing or on-premises connectivity.
wrong_explanation_3: A transit VPC using EC2-based VPN appliances was a common pattern before Transit Gateway existed. It requires managing EC2 instances, VPN software, routing configurations, and high availability — significantly more operational overhead than Transit Gateway.

scenario: A team needs the LLM to respond ONLY with valid JSON conforming to a specific schema, so the response can be parsed programmatically. Which prompt engineering practice BEST supports this?
correct_answer: Specify the exact JSON schema and an example in the prompt, optionally combined with output indicators and JSON-mode features
wrong_answer_1: Increase temperature so JSON is more creative
wrong_answer_2: Increase Top-P to widen the candidate pool
wrong_answer_3: Switch to Amazon Polly
correct_explanation: Specifying the expected JSON schema (and an example) in the prompt — combined with output indicators or model-specific JSON-mode features — significantly improves the likelihood the LLM returns parseable JSON.
wrong_explanation_1: Higher temperature increases randomness and reduces structural reliability.
wrong_explanation_2: Higher Top-P also increases diversity and can break strict structural output.
wrong_explanation_3: Polly is a text-to-speech service, not an LLM JSON tool.

scenario: A startup wants to evaluate whether generative AI is suitable for a task before investing in a full implementation. Which factor argues AGAINST using a foundation model when accuracy and reproducibility are paramount?
correct_answer: Generative AI outputs can be probabilistic and non-deterministic, varying between identical requests
wrong_answer_1: Generative AI models cannot accept user input
wrong_answer_2: Generative AI cannot produce text in English
wrong_answer_3: Generative AI requires zero compute resources
correct_explanation: By design, generative LLMs produce probabilistic outputs that can vary between identical requests (especially at non-zero temperature). For workflows requiring strict reproducibility or numerical precision, this variability is a limitation to account for.
wrong_explanation_1: Generative AI explicitly responds to user input.
wrong_explanation_2: Generative AI commonly produces text in many languages including English.
wrong_explanation_3: Generative AI is compute-intensive at inference and training.

scenario: A company wants to receive automated alerts when their SageMaker inference endpoint's average latency exceeds 500 milliseconds over a 5-minute period. Which AWS service should be used to configure this alert?
correct_answer: Amazon CloudWatch Alarms
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
wrong_answer_2: AWS Health Dashboard
wrong_answer_3: Amazon GuardDuty
