correct_answer: Enable Redshift result caching, which stores the results of queries in memory and returns cached results for identical subsequent queries without re-executing them against the cluster.
wrong_answer_1: Enable Redshift Concurrency Scaling to automatically add cluster capacity when multiple analysts run queries simultaneously.
wrong_answer_2: Create Redshift materialized views for the most common query patterns and schedule them to refresh hourly.
wrong_answer_3: Enable Redshift Spectrum to offload query processing to S3, reducing the load on the main cluster.
correct_explanation: Redshift result caching stores query results in memory on the leader node. When an identical query is submitted (same SQL text, same parameters, same user permissions, and the underlying data has not changed), Redshift returns the cached result immediately without executing the query. This eliminates the 10–30 minute execution time for repeated queries entirely.
wrong_explanation_1: Redshift Concurrency Scaling adds transient cluster capacity to handle bursts of concurrent queries, reducing queue wait times. It does not cache results or reduce execution time for individual queries — each query still executes fully against the cluster.
wrong_explanation_2: Materialized views pre-compute and store query results, which can speed up queries that use them. However, they require identifying query patterns in advance, creating and maintaining the views, and scheduling refreshes. Result caching is automatic and requires no schema changes.
wrong_explanation_3: Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 using the Redshift cluster's compute nodes. It extends Redshift's query capability to S3 data but does not cache results or reduce execution time for repeated queries against the main cluster.

scenario: A company needs to register a domain name, provide authoritative DNS resolution, and route traffic to AWS resources with health checks and failover. Which AWS service provides all of these capabilities?
correct_answer: Amazon Route 53
wrong_answer_1: AWS CloudFront
wrong_answer_2: Elastic Load Balancing
wrong_answer_3: AWS Global Accelerator
correct_explanation: Amazon Route 53 is the AWS DNS web service. It supports domain registration, authoritative DNS hosting, multiple routing policies (latency, failover, weighted, geolocation), and health checks for failover.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudFront is a CDN that caches content at edge locations. It does not register domains or perform authoritative DNS resolution.
wrong_explanation_2: ELB distributes traffic to back-end targets but is not a DNS service and cannot register domains.
wrong_explanation_3: Global Accelerator improves global application traffic routing using the AWS network but does not register domains or host authoritative DNS records.

scenario: A Lambda function processes S3 events and is expected to receive 30 requests per second. Each execution takes an average of 60 seconds to complete. The team is planning capacity and wants to know the expected concurrent execution count. What is the correct value?
correct_explanation: Lambda concurrent executions are calculated as: invocations per second × average execution duration in seconds. In this case: 30 × 60 = 1,800 concurrent executions. Since the default account-level concurrency limit is 1,000, the team must request a limit increase from AWS to prevent throttling at this load.
wrong_explanation_1: 30 is the invocations per second — one factor in the formula. Concurrent executions accumulate over time as long-running functions overlap with new invocations. The formula multiplies invocations per second by average duration.
wrong_explanation_2: 60 is the average execution duration in seconds — the other factor in the formula. It is not the concurrent execution count.
wrong_explanation_3: 90 would result from adding the two values (30 + 60) rather than multiplying them. The correct formula is multiplication: invocations/sec × avg duration = concurrent executions.

scenario: A fraud-detection dataset has 998 normal transactions for every 2 fraudulent transactions. A model trained on this data achieves 99.8% accuracy by always predicting "normal," yet it is useless. What is the underlying problem?
correct_answer: Class imbalance
wrong_answer_1: Data residency violation
wrong_answer_2: Vanishing context window
wrong_answer_3: Excessive feature engineering
correct_explanation: Class imbalance occurs when one class vastly outnumbers others. Trivial models that always predict the majority class can score very high accuracy while completely failing on the minority class. Techniques like resampling, class weighting, and metrics like F1 score or AUC are common mitigations.
wrong_explanation_1: Data residency concerns geographic data location, not class distribution.
wrong_explanation_2: Context window is an LLM property, not relevant to tabular fraud detection.
wrong_explanation_3: Feature engineering is not the cause of the always-majority prediction here.

scenario: An ML team has deployed a SageMaker model and wants to understand which input features are most influential in driving individual predictions for specific customers. The model is a black-box ensemble. Which SageMaker tool provides feature-level explanations for individual predictions?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Debugger
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Clarify uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to provide feature-level explanations for individual model predictions. It works with black-box models and can explain why a specific prediction was made for a given input, helping teams understand model behavior and identify potential bias.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon SageMaker Debugger monitors training jobs for issues like vanishing gradients and overfitting. It does not provide post-training feature importance explanations for individual predictions on deployed models.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor detects data drift and model quality degradation on deployed endpoints. It monitors statistical properties of inference inputs and outputs but does not provide SHAP-based feature explanations for individual predictions.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon SageMaker Experiments tracks and organizes training runs by logging metrics and parameters. It does not provide feature-level explanations for model predictions.

scenario: A company runs a stateless web application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones. During a recent AZ failure, the Auto Scaling group launched replacement instances in the remaining AZ, but the application experienced degraded performance because the remaining AZ did not have enough capacity to handle the full load. How should the solutions architect address this?
correct_answer: Implement the N+1 or N*2 capacity model by ensuring each AZ runs enough instances to handle the full expected load independently, so that losing one AZ does not degrade performance.
wrong_answer_1: Add a third Availability Zone to the Auto Scaling group so that the load is distributed across more AZs.
wrong_answer_2: Enable predictive scaling on the Auto Scaling group to forecast traffic and pre-provision instances before demand increases.
wrong_answer_3: Increase the maximum instance count in the Auto Scaling group so that more instances can be launched during an AZ failure.
correct_explanation: For true fault tolerance, each AZ should be capable of handling the full expected load on its own (N+1 model) or the combined load should be distributed such that the remaining AZs can absorb the failed AZ's traffic without degradation. This means running more instances than strictly necessary during normal operation — the cost of over-provisioning is the price of resilience.
wrong_explanation_1: Adding a third AZ distributes the load across more zones, which reduces the impact of a single AZ failure, but does not guarantee that the remaining AZs can handle the full load. The root cause — insufficient per-AZ capacity — is not addressed by simply adding more AZs.
wrong_explanation_2: Predictive scaling forecasts traffic based on historical patterns and pre-provisions instances. It helps with anticipated load increases but does not address the sudden capacity requirement caused by an AZ failure, which is not a predictable traffic pattern.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing the maximum instance count allows more instances to be launched, but Auto Scaling takes time to detect the AZ failure, launch new instances, and pass health checks. During this period, the application experiences degraded performance. The solution is to have sufficient capacity already running, not to rely on reactive scaling.

scenario: A compliance officer wants to CONTINUOUSLY assess their AWS environment — including generative AI usage on Bedrock — against frameworks such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST, and a prebuilt framework for generative AI on AWS. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS Audit Manager
wrong_answer_1: AWS Artifact
wrong_answer_2: Amazon GuardDuty
wrong_answer_3: AWS Trusted Advisor
correct_explanation: AWS Audit Manager continuously collects evidence from the customer's AWS environment and maps it to controls in frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST) including a prebuilt framework for generative AI on AWS. It produces audit-ready evidence packs.
wrong_explanation_1: Artifact distributes AWS's own compliance reports but does not continuously audit a customer's own AWS usage against frameworks.
wrong_explanation_2: GuardDuty performs threat detection, not framework-driven compliance assessment.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor offers best-practice recommendations and does not produce framework-mapped evidence.

scenario: A data engineering team uses AWS Glue DataBrew to profile a dataset before processing. The profiling report shows that 15% of values in a required 'customer_id' column are null. The team wants to automatically reject records with null customer_id values during ETL processing. Which AWS Glue feature enforces this data quality rule?
correct_answer: AWS Glue Data Quality rules with a completeness check
wrong_answer_1: AWS Glue DataBrew recipe with a filter transformation
wrong_answer_2: AWS Glue DynamicFrame with a filter() transformation
wrong_answer_3: AWS Glue job bookmarks
correct_explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality rules support completeness checks that validate whether required columns contain non-null values. You can define a rule that requires customer_id to be non-null and configure the Glue job to reject or flag records that fail the check.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Glue DataBrew recipes can filter out records with null values, but this is a transformation step, not a data quality validation. DataBrew does not provide the same automated quality rule enforcement and reporting as Glue Data Quality.
wrong_explanation_2: Using a DynamicFrame filter() transformation can remove records with null customer_id values, but it does not enforce a data quality rule or provide quality metrics. It silently filters records without reporting quality violations.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed to avoid reprocessing. They do not validate data quality or enforce rules about null values.

scenario: A healthcare company needs to store and query time-series data from IoT medical devices. The data includes patient vitals collected every second from 100,000 devices. Queries will aggregate data by device ID and time range. The database must automatically scale storage and provide fast query performance for time-based aggregations. Which AWS database service is most appropriate?
correct_answer: Amazon Timestream
wrong_answer_1: Amazon DynamoDB
wrong_answer_2: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Redshift
correct_explanation: Amazon Timestream is a purpose-built time-series database that automatically scales storage and compute independently. It is optimized for time-series data with built-in functions for time-based aggregations, interpolation, and smoothing. Timestream stores recent data in memory for fast queries and automatically moves older data to a cost-optimized storage tier.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon DynamoDB can store time-series data using composite keys, but it is not optimized for time-based aggregations and does not provide the built-in time-series functions that Timestream offers. Queries requiring aggregations across time ranges would be less efficient and more complex to implement.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL can store time-series data, but it requires manual schema design, indexing, and partitioning to achieve good performance at scale. It does not automatically scale storage independently of compute or provide built-in time-series optimizations.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse optimized for analytical queries on large datasets. While it can store time-series data, it is designed for batch analytics rather than continuous ingestion of high-frequency IoT data. Timestream is more cost-effective and better suited for this use case.

scenario: A business team without coding skills wants to experiment with generative AI by chaining prompts and building small AI "mini-apps" in a browser, powered by foundation models on AWS. Which AWS offering is purpose-built for this no-code generative-AI experimentation?
correct_answer: PartyRock, an Amazon Bedrock Playground
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab
wrong_answer_2: AWS DeepRacer
wrong_answer_3: AWS Cloud9
correct_explanation: PartyRock is an Amazon Bedrock-powered playground that lets users create small generative-AI applications in a browser by composing prompts and widgets without writing code — built for hands-on experimentation.
wrong_explanation_1: Studio Lab is a free environment for running Jupyter notebooks; it is code-based, not no-code app building.
wrong_explanation_2: DeepRacer teaches reinforcement learning with autonomous race cars — unrelated to no-code gen-AI mini-apps.
wrong_explanation_3: Cloud9 is a developer IDE, not a no-code gen-AI playground.

scenario: A company wants to allow its on-premises users to access an internal web application running on EC2 instances in a private VPC subnet without exposing the application to the public internet. The company already has an AWS Direct Connect connection. Which solution provides private access to the application for on-premises users?
correct_answer: Deploy an internal Application Load Balancer in the VPC and use Direct Connect with a private virtual interface (VIF) to route on-premises traffic to the ALB.
wrong_answer_1: Assign public IP addresses to the EC2 instances and create a security group rule allowing traffic from the on-premises IP range.
wrong_answer_2: Create an internet-facing ALB and restrict access using a WAF rule that only allows requests from the on-premises public IP range.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Client VPN to allow on-premises users to connect to the VPC and access the application.
correct_explanation: An internal ALB has no public IP address and only accepts traffic from within the VPC or connected networks. With Direct Connect and a private VIF, on-premises traffic is routed directly into the VPC over the private AWS backbone. On-premises users reach the internal ALB without any traffic touching the public internet.
wrong_explanation_1: Assigning public IPs to EC2 instances exposes them to the internet, even if security group rules restrict access to specific IP ranges. This violates the requirement to not expose the application to the public internet and introduces unnecessary attack surface.
wrong_explanation_2: An internet-facing ALB has a public DNS name and public IP addresses, meaning the application is technically exposed to the public internet. WAF IP restrictions reduce the attack surface but do not make the application private — the endpoint is still publicly resolvable and reachable.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Client VPN is designed for individual remote users connecting from laptops or devices using VPN client software. It is not the appropriate solution for connecting an entire on-premises network — that is the use case for Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.

scenario: A company stores customer data in an S3 bucket. The security team requires that all objects uploaded to the bucket be encrypted at rest using AES-256, and that any upload request that does not include server-side encryption headers be automatically rejected. Which combination of S3 configurations enforces this?
correct_answer: Enable default bucket encryption with SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS, and add a bucket policy that denies s3:PutObject requests where the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is absent or set to an unapproved value.
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode to prevent unencrypted objects from being stored.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Amazon Macie on the bucket to detect and quarantine unencrypted objects after upload.
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Versioning and configure a lifecycle rule to delete unencrypted object versions automatically.
correct_explanation: Default bucket encryption automatically encrypts objects that are uploaded without explicit encryption headers. The bucket policy with a Deny condition on s3:PutObject where the encryption header is missing or incorrect acts as a preventive control, rejecting non-compliant uploads before they are stored. Together these two controls ensure all objects are encrypted and non-compliant uploads are blocked.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Object Lock prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a retention period — it is an immutability feature, not an encryption enforcement mechanism. It has no capability to detect or reject unencrypted uploads.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Macie uses ML to discover and classify sensitive data in S3. It can detect unencrypted objects after they are stored, but it is a detective control — it does not prevent unencrypted uploads from occurring in the first place. The requirement is to reject non-compliant uploads, not to detect them after the fact.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Versioning preserves multiple versions of objects and lifecycle rules manage object transitions and expiration. Neither feature can inspect encryption status at upload time or reject unencrypted uploads. Deleting unencrypted versions after the fact still allows them to be stored briefly, which does not satisfy the requirement.

scenario: A company is redesigning its checkout service to handle traffic spikes during holiday sales. The current architecture calls a payment processor API synchronously during checkout. When the payment processor is slow, checkout requests time out and customers see errors. The company wants to ensure checkout requests are never lost even if the payment processor is temporarily unavailable. Which architecture change should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: Place an SQS queue between the checkout service and the payment processor. The checkout service enqueues payment requests and returns an immediate acknowledgment to the customer. A worker service processes payments from the queue at the rate the payment processor can handle.
wrong_answer_1: Increase the checkout service's HTTP timeout to 5 minutes to wait for slow payment processor responses.
wrong_answer_2: Add an ElastiCache layer in front of the payment processor to cache payment responses and reduce API calls.
wrong_answer_3: Deploy the payment processor behind an Auto Scaling group so it scales up during traffic spikes.
correct_explanation: Decoupling the checkout service from the payment processor with an SQS queue eliminates the synchronous dependency. Payment requests are durably stored in SQS and processed at the rate the payment processor can handle. If the processor is temporarily unavailable, messages remain in the queue and are processed when it recovers. No checkout requests are lost.
wrong_explanation_1: Increasing the HTTP timeout keeps the synchronous coupling intact. Customers would wait up to 5 minutes for a response, which is an unacceptable user experience. It also ties up server threads and connections for the duration of the wait.
wrong_explanation_2: Payment responses cannot be cached — each payment is a unique transaction with a unique outcome. Caching payment responses would return stale or incorrect results for new transactions.
wrong_explanation_3: Auto Scaling the payment processor helps with capacity but does not address the fundamental problem of synchronous coupling. If the payment processor is unavailable for any reason (not just capacity), checkout requests still fail. The queue provides durability that scaling alone cannot.

scenario: A machine learning engineer needs to group millions of unlabeled customer support tickets into thematic clusters to help the operations team identify common issue categories. No labeled examples exist. Which type of algorithm is appropriate for this task?
correct_answer: K-means clustering
wrong_answer_1: XGBoost
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Sequence-to-Sequence
correct_explanation: K-means clustering is an unsupervised algorithm that groups data points into k clusters based on feature similarity. Since no labeled examples exist, an unsupervised approach is required. SageMaker's built-in K-means algorithm scales to millions of records and can cluster text embeddings of support tickets into thematic groups.
wrong_explanation_1: XGBoost is a supervised learning algorithm that requires labeled training data. Since no labeled examples exist for the support tickets, XGBoost cannot be applied to this unsupervised grouping task.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner is a supervised algorithm for regression and classification. It requires labeled data and is not applicable to unsupervised clustering of unlabeled support tickets.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon SageMaker Sequence-to-Sequence is designed for supervised sequence transformation tasks such as machine translation and text summarization. It requires labeled input-output sequence pairs and is not applicable to unsupervised clustering.

scenario: Which SageMaker capability provides a single-tenant Jupyter notebook environment, useful for ad-hoc data exploration and model development?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker notebook instances
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Neo
correct_explanation: SageMaker notebook instances are managed Jupyter notebook environments. While SageMaker Studio is the unified IDE, classic notebook instances remain a simple, single-tenant option for ad-hoc data exploration.
wrong_explanation_1: Ground Truth is a labeling service, not a notebook environment.
wrong_explanation_2: Edge Manager managed models on edge devices.
wrong_explanation_3: Neo compiles models to run efficiently on specific hardware targets; it is not a notebook environment.

scenario: A data engineering team is building a pipeline to load daily batch exports from an on-premises Oracle database into Amazon S3 for ML training. The exports are large CSV files totaling 500 GB per day. The team wants a managed service that handles schema mapping, incremental loads, and automatic retries without writing custom code. Which AWS service best meets these requirements?
correct_answer: AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)
wrong_answer_1: AWS DataSync
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
wrong_answer_3: AWS Transfer Family
correct_explanation: AWS DMS is designed to migrate and replicate data from relational databases including Oracle. It supports ongoing replication with change data capture (CDC), handles schema mapping, and provides automatic retries — making it well-suited for managed incremental loads from on-premises databases to S3 for ML pipelines.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS DataSync is optimized for transferring files between on-premises file systems and AWS storage services. It does not connect to relational databases or handle SQL-based incremental extraction.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for streaming data delivery, not batch database exports. It does not connect to Oracle databases or perform schema-aware incremental loads.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTP/FTPS endpoints for file transfer into S3. It does not integrate with relational databases or support incremental database replication.

scenario: A team configures EC2 Auto Scaling, scheduled scaling for predictable peaks, and target-tracking scaling for variable load. Which Well-Architected design principle is the team applying?
correct_answer: Implement elasticity
wrong_answer_1: Implement a single static instance per workload
wrong_answer_2: Avoid using managed services
wrong_answer_3: Centralize all workloads on one EC2 instance
correct_explanation: Implementing elasticity — adding capacity when demand grows and removing it when demand falls — is core to the performance efficiency and reliability pillars. Auto Scaling with scheduled and target-tracking policies is a canonical implementation.
wrong_explanation_1: A single static instance is the opposite of elasticity.
wrong_explanation_2: Managed services are encouraged by Well-Architected, not avoided.
wrong_explanation_3: Concentrating all workloads on one EC2 instance creates a single point of failure and the opposite of elasticity.

scenario: A company stores ML training data in Amazon S3. The security team requires that the data be encrypted at rest using a customer-managed key so the company retains full control over key rotation and revocation. Which AWS service and configuration should be used?
correct_answer: Use AWS KMS with a customer-managed key (CMK) and configure S3 server-side encryption with SSE-KMS
wrong_answer_1: Use S3 server-side encryption with SSE-S3 (Amazon S3-managed keys)
wrong_answer_2: Use client-side encryption with a key stored in the application code
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 default encryption with SSE-S3 and rotate the key annually
correct_explanation: AWS KMS customer-managed keys (CMKs) give the company full control over key policies, rotation schedules, and the ability to revoke access by disabling or deleting the key. Configuring S3 SSE-KMS with a CMK ensures training data is encrypted at rest using the company-controlled key.
wrong_explanation_1: SSE-S3 uses Amazon S3-managed keys where AWS controls the key material. The company has no control over key rotation schedules or the ability to revoke access by disabling the key — which does not meet the requirement for customer-controlled key management.
wrong_explanation_2: Client-side encryption with a key stored in application code is a security anti-pattern. Hardcoded keys are difficult to rotate, can be exposed in code repositories, and do not leverage AWS's managed key infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_3: SSE-S3 with annual rotation still uses Amazon-managed keys. The company cannot control the rotation schedule or revoke access, which does not satisfy the requirement for full customer control over key management.

scenario: A developer is running a Lambda function that processes events from Amazon S3. The function is expected to receive 80 requests per second, and each execution takes an average of 40 seconds to complete. The developer is concerned about hitting Lambda concurrency limits. What is the expected number of concurrent executions for this function?
correct_explanation: Lambda concurrent executions are calculated using the formula: concurrent executions = invocations per second × average execution duration in seconds. In this case: 80 requests/second × 40 seconds = 3,200 concurrent executions. Since the default account-level concurrency limit is 1,000, the developer must request a limit increase from AWS to prevent throttling.
wrong_explanation_1: 80 is simply the invocations per second — it does not account for the duration of each execution. Concurrent executions accumulate over time as long-running functions overlap with new invocations.
wrong_explanation_2: 40 is the average execution duration in seconds. It is one factor in the concurrency formula but not the result of the calculation.
wrong_explanation_3: 320 would result from a calculation error such as dividing instead of multiplying (80 × 40 = 3,200, not 320). The correct formula multiplies invocations per second by average duration.

scenario: A company hosts a web application on EC2 instances in a private subnet. The instances need to download software packages from the internet during bootstrapping. The security team requires that all outbound internet traffic from the instances be inspected and filtered to allow only traffic to approved domains. Which solution meets this requirement?
correct_answer: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the VPC with domain-based filtering rules that allow only approved domains, and route outbound traffic from the private subnet through the Network Firewall before reaching the NAT Gateway.
wrong_answer_1: Use a NAT Gateway with security group rules that restrict outbound traffic to approved IP addresses.
wrong_answer_2: Configure VPC Flow Logs to monitor outbound traffic and use Lambda to automatically block unapproved destinations.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer to filter outbound traffic to unapproved domains.
correct_explanation: AWS Network Firewall is a managed stateful firewall that supports domain-based filtering (FQDN filtering) for outbound traffic. By routing private subnet traffic through Network Firewall before the NAT Gateway, all outbound internet traffic is inspected and only traffic to approved domains is permitted. This provides the domain-level filtering the security team requires.
wrong_explanation_1: NAT Gateway security groups cannot be modified — NAT Gateways do not have associated security groups. Even if they did, security groups operate on IP addresses and ports, not domain names. Domain-based filtering requires a layer-7 inspection capability.
wrong_explanation_2: VPC Flow Logs capture connection metadata (IPs, ports, bytes) but do not perform real-time traffic inspection or blocking. Using Lambda to react to Flow Log entries introduces significant latency and cannot block traffic in real time.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS WAF is designed to filter inbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to web applications, not to filter outbound traffic from EC2 instances. It cannot be applied to outbound traffic from private subnets.

scenario: A company wants to fine-tune a pre-trained foundation model from Amazon Bedrock on a proprietary dataset of 10,000 labeled customer service transcripts to improve response quality for their specific domain. Which approach should the ML team use?
correct_answer: Use Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning to customize the foundation model with the labeled dataset
wrong_answer_1: Train a new foundation model from scratch using the 10,000 transcripts on SageMaker
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon Bedrock Agents to inject the transcripts as context at inference time
wrong_answer_3: Use Amazon Comprehend to extract entities from the transcripts and use them as features for a separate classifier
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock supports fine-tuning of foundation models using custom labeled datasets. Fine-tuning adapts the pre-trained model's weights to the specific domain using the 10,000 transcripts, improving response quality for customer service use cases without the cost and complexity of training from scratch.
wrong_explanation_1: Training a foundation model from scratch requires billions of tokens and massive compute resources. 10,000 transcripts are far too few to train a foundation model from scratch, and the cost would be prohibitive. Fine-tuning a pre-trained model is the appropriate approach.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks using tools and APIs. Injecting transcripts as context at inference time is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach, not fine-tuning. RAG does not update the model's weights and may not achieve the same domain adaptation as fine-tuning.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Comprehend is a managed NLP service for entity recognition and sentiment analysis. Using it to extract entities for a separate classifier does not leverage the generative capabilities of the foundation model and would not improve the model's response quality for customer service.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to migrate 200 TB of archived files from an on-premises tape library to Amazon S3 Glacier. The on-premises environment has a 500 Mbps internet connection shared with production workloads. The migration must complete within 5 days and must not impact production traffic. Which approach is most appropriate?
correct_answer: AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized
wrong_answer_1: AWS DataSync over a dedicated Direct Connect connection
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 multipart upload via the AWS CLI
wrong_answer_3: AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint
correct_explanation: At 200 TB over a shared 500 Mbps connection, a network transfer would take well over 30 days at full utilization — far exceeding the 5-day window and impacting production traffic. AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized ships a physical appliance that can hold up to 80 TB per device (multiple devices can be used in parallel), completing the migration offline without consuming any network bandwidth.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and would still require transferring 200 TB over the wire. Even at 1 Gbps dedicated throughput, 200 TB would take approximately 18 days — well beyond the 5-day requirement.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 multipart upload via the CLI uses the existing internet connection. At 500 Mbps shared with production, the effective throughput would be far too low to transfer 200 TB in 5 days without impacting production workloads.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints for transferring files to S3. It still relies on the existing internet connection and would face the same bandwidth constraints as a direct upload.

scenario: A team is training a model to predict tomorrow's temperature in degrees Celsius based on historical weather data. The target is a continuous numeric value. Which type of ML problem does this represent?
correct_answer: Regression
wrong_answer_1: Binary classification
wrong_answer_2: Multi-class classification
wrong_answer_3: Clustering
correct_explanation: Regression predicts a continuous numeric target (e.g., temperature, price, sales volume). The scenario's target — temperature in degrees Celsius — is a continuous variable, making this a regression task.
wrong_explanation_1: Binary classification predicts one of two discrete labels (yes/no). Temperature is continuous, not binary.
wrong_explanation_2: Multi-class classification predicts one of several discrete labels. Temperature is continuous, not categorical.
wrong_explanation_3: Clustering is unsupervised and groups similar items without a target variable. The scenario has a clear continuous target.

scenario: A company runs a steady-state production workload on 20 EC2 instances that must run continuously 24/7 for the next 3 years. The workload is predictable with no significant traffic variation. The company wants to minimize EC2 costs. Which purchasing option provides the greatest discount?
correct_answer: Purchase 3-year Compute Savings Plans or EC2 Instance Savings Plans, which provide up to 66% discount over On-Demand pricing for committed usage.
wrong_answer_1: Use On-Demand Instances and rely on AWS Cost Explorer recommendations to identify savings opportunities quarterly.
wrong_answer_2: Use Spot Instances for all 20 production instances to take advantage of up to 90% discounts.
wrong_answer_3: Purchase 1-year Reserved Instances with a partial upfront payment for a moderate discount.
correct_explanation: For steady-state workloads running continuously for 3 years, Savings Plans provide the highest discount (up to 66% for Compute Savings Plans) with more flexibility than Reserved Instances. Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, sizes, regions, and even Fargate and Lambda, making them more versatile than instance-specific reservations.
wrong_explanation_1: On-Demand Instances are the most expensive option for steady-state workloads. Relying on quarterly Cost Explorer reviews means paying full On-Demand rates in the interim and missing months of potential savings.
wrong_explanation_2: Spot Instances can be interrupted with 2-minute notice and are not suitable for production workloads that must run continuously. Using Spot for critical production instances introduces unacceptable availability risk.
wrong_explanation_3: 1-year Reserved Instances provide a discount (up to 40% with partial upfront), but 3-year Savings Plans provide a higher discount (up to 66%). For a known 3-year commitment, the longer term provides significantly better savings.

scenario: A company is deploying a new version of their application to an Elastic Beanstalk environment. The deployment must not take any instances out of service simultaneously — each instance should be updated one at a time, and the deployment should pause if any instance fails its health check. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy should be used?
correct_answer: Rolling deployment policy, which updates instances in batches and pauses if health checks fail.
wrong_answer_1: All at once deployment policy, which deploys to all instances simultaneously for the fastest deployment.
wrong_answer_2: Immutable deployment policy, which launches a new set of instances with the new version before terminating the old ones.
wrong_answer_3: Blue/Green deployment, which creates an entirely new environment and swaps the CNAME.
correct_explanation: The Rolling deployment policy updates instances in configurable batches (minimum batch size of 1). It performs health checks after each batch and pauses the deployment if instances fail health checks, preventing a bad deployment from propagating to all instances. At any point during the deployment, some instances run the old version and some run the new version.
wrong_explanation_1: All at once deploys to all instances simultaneously, taking the entire environment out of service briefly. It is the fastest deployment method but does not meet the requirement of updating one instance at a time.
wrong_explanation_2: Immutable deployment launches a new Auto Scaling group with the new version alongside the existing instances. It provides zero downtime and easy rollback but does not update existing instances one at a time — it replaces them entirely with new instances.
wrong_explanation_3: Blue/Green deployment creates a completely new Elastic Beanstalk environment and swaps the CNAME after validation. It provides zero downtime and instant rollback but involves creating an entirely new environment, not updating existing instances one at a time.

scenario: A data engineer is writing an AWS Glue PySpark job that joins two large datasets stored in Amazon S3. The first dataset is 5 TB and the second is 200 MB. The job is slow due to a shuffle operation. The engineer wants to optimize the join by broadcasting the smaller dataset to all executors. Which PySpark function should be used?
correct_answer: Use the broadcast() function from pyspark.sql.functions to broadcast the 200 MB dataset
wrong_answer_1: Use the repartition() function to redistribute the 5 TB dataset across more partitions
wrong_answer_2: Use the coalesce() function to reduce the number of partitions in the 200 MB dataset
wrong_answer_3: Use the cache() function to cache the 5 TB dataset in memory
correct_explanation: The broadcast() function sends a copy of the smaller dataset (200 MB) to every executor, eliminating the shuffle operation during the join. This is the standard optimization for joining a large dataset with a small dataset that fits in executor memory, and can reduce join time by orders of magnitude.
wrong_explanation_1: Repartitioning the 5 TB dataset increases parallelism but does not eliminate the shuffle caused by the join. The shuffle will still occur across all executors, just with more partitions. Broadcasting the small dataset is more effective.
wrong_explanation_2: The coalesce() function reduces the number of partitions in a DataFrame, which can reduce overhead for small datasets. However, it does not eliminate the shuffle during the join or broadcast the dataset to all executors.
wrong_explanation_3: Caching the 5 TB dataset in memory would require enormous memory capacity and is not feasible for a dataset of this size. More importantly, caching does not eliminate the shuffle during the join — broadcasting the small dataset does.

scenario: A company wants to prevent its developers from accidentally exposing sensitive data by making S3 buckets or objects publicly accessible. The company wants a single control that blocks all current and future public access configurations across all S3 buckets in the account, regardless of bucket policies or ACLs. Which feature should the solutions architect enable?
correct_answer: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the AWS account level, which overrides any bucket-level or object-level public access settings.
wrong_answer_1: Create an SCP that denies s3:PutBucketPolicy and s3:PutBucketAcl for all member accounts.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Amazon Macie to detect publicly accessible S3 buckets and send alerts to the security team.
wrong_answer_3: Create an AWS Config rule that checks for public S3 buckets and triggers a Lambda function to remove public access when detected.
correct_explanation: S3 Block Public Access at the account level is a single toggle that overrides all bucket policies, bucket ACLs, and object ACLs that would grant public access. It prevents any bucket in the account from being made public, regardless of what individual bucket configurations say. This is the simplest and most comprehensive preventive control for this requirement.
wrong_explanation_1: An SCP denying s3:PutBucketPolicy and s3:PutBucketAcl prevents new public access configurations from being created but does not retroactively block existing public buckets. It also prevents legitimate bucket policy changes, which may be too restrictive.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Macie detects publicly accessible buckets and alerts the security team, but it is a detective control. It does not prevent buckets from being made public in the first place.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config with auto-remediation is a reactive approach — there is a window between when a bucket is made public and when the remediation runs. S3 Block Public Access is a preventive control that eliminates this window entirely.

scenario: After fine-tuning an LLM heavily on a narrow new dataset, a team observes that the model is much worse at general tasks it used to do well. What is this phenomenon called?
correct_answer: Catastrophic forgetting
wrong_answer_1: Quantization
wrong_answer_2: Tokenization
wrong_answer_3: Hallucination
correct_explanation: Catastrophic forgetting is the phenomenon where a model, when fine-tuned heavily on new data, loses previously learned general capabilities. Techniques like PEFT, mixing in original data, or careful learning-rate schedules help mitigate it.
wrong_explanation_1: Quantization compresses model weights; it is unrelated to the forgetting phenomenon.
wrong_explanation_2: Tokenization is unrelated to forgetting.
wrong_explanation_3: Hallucination is the LLM-specific term for fabricated content, not loss of prior abilities.

scenario: A machine learning team is building a SageMaker training pipeline that requires a custom preprocessing step using a library not available in any SageMaker managed container. The team wants to run this step as a SageMaker Processing job. What is the correct approach to provide the custom environment?
correct_answer: Build a custom Docker image with the required library, push it to Amazon ECR, and specify it as the image URI in the SageMaker Processing job configuration
wrong_answer_1: Use a SageMaker notebook instance to run the preprocessing step before submitting the training job
wrong_answer_2: Install the library using pip in the processing script's entry point before importing it
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Lambda to run the preprocessing step with the custom library installed as a Lambda layer
correct_explanation: SageMaker Processing jobs support custom Docker containers. You build an image with the required library, push it to ECR, and reference the ECR image URI in the ProcessingJob configuration. This is the standard BYOC pattern for SageMaker Processing jobs with custom dependencies.
wrong_explanation_1: Running preprocessing in a notebook instance is not a scalable or reproducible approach for a production pipeline. Notebook instances are interactive environments, not managed processing job infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_2: Installing packages via pip at runtime in the processing script's entry point is unreliable in isolated container environments and may fail due to network restrictions or missing build tools. Dependencies should be baked into the Docker image at build time.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Lambda has a 15-minute execution limit, a 10 GB memory cap, and is not designed for data-intensive ML preprocessing workloads. SageMaker Processing jobs provide managed, scalable compute specifically designed for ML preprocessing.

scenario: A regulated company needs to enforce that SageMaker training jobs run inside a customer-controlled VPC with NO internet access — even for image downloads or package installation. Which capability addresses this?
correct_answer: Run SageMaker training jobs in network-isolation mode within a private VPC subnet
wrong_answer_1: Disable IAM
wrong_answer_2: Enable Top-P sampling
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS DeepRacer for training
correct_explanation: SageMaker supports VPC mode and network isolation, where training jobs run inside private subnets with no internet egress. Combined with VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, and SageMaker APIs, this provides full network isolation for sensitive workloads.
wrong_explanation_1: Disabling IAM is impossible and would not address network isolation; IAM is required for any AWS access.
wrong_explanation_2: Top-P is an inference parameter, not a networking control.
wrong_explanation_3: DeepRacer is an RL learning tool, not a network-isolation feature.

scenario: A company wants to enforce HTTPS for all traffic between users and their CloudFront distribution. HTTP requests should be automatically redirected to HTTPS rather than rejected. Which CloudFront setting achieves this?
correct_answer: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS on the cache behavior.
wrong_answer_1: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy to HTTPS Only on the cache behavior.
wrong_answer_2: Configure an AWS WAF rule on the CloudFront distribution to block HTTP requests.
wrong_answer_3: Set the Origin Protocol Policy to HTTPS Only to force encrypted communication.
correct_explanation: The Viewer Protocol Policy controls how CloudFront handles HTTP and HTTPS requests from viewers. Setting it to 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' automatically issues a 301 redirect to the HTTPS version of the URL for any HTTP request, providing a seamless user experience without rejecting the request.
wrong_explanation_1: Setting the Viewer Protocol Policy to 'HTTPS Only' rejects HTTP requests with a 403 Forbidden response rather than redirecting them. This is more restrictive than required — the company wants automatic redirection, not rejection.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS WAF can block requests based on rules, but using WAF to block HTTP requests would return a 403 error rather than redirecting to HTTPS. WAF is also an additional cost and complexity for a use case that CloudFront's native Viewer Protocol Policy handles directly.
wrong_explanation_3: The Origin Protocol Policy controls encryption between CloudFront and the origin (e.g., ALB or S3), not between viewers and CloudFront. Setting it to HTTPS Only ensures CloudFront fetches content from the origin over HTTPS but has no effect on how CloudFront handles viewer requests.

scenario: A team needs a private, managed Git repository service hosted within AWS so the source code never leaves AWS. Which AWS service was historically purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS CodeCommit
wrong_answer_1: AWS CodeBuild
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 versioning
wrong_answer_3: AWS CodeArtifact
correct_explanation: AWS CodeCommit is a managed Git repository hosted in AWS. It supports standard Git workflows, IAM-based access control, and HTTPS/SSH access, keeping source code inside the AWS account.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeBuild compiles and tests source code. It is not a Git host.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 versioning provides object-level history but is not a Git server.
wrong_explanation_3: CodeArtifact is a package repository for build artifacts like npm, Maven, and PyPI packages — not a source-code Git host.

scenario: A startup is building its first AWS environment. The solutions architect wants to ensure that the AWS account root user is protected and never used for day-to-day operations. Which combination of actions should the architect take to secure the root user? (Choose the most complete answer.)
correct_answer: Enable MFA on the root user, do not create access keys for the root user, and create individual IAM users or use IAM Identity Center for all day-to-day administrative tasks.
wrong_answer_1: Create a strong password for the root user, share it only with senior administrators, and use it only for billing-related tasks.
wrong_answer_2: Create root user access keys with read-only permissions and store them in AWS Secrets Manager for emergency use.
wrong_answer_3: Enable AWS CloudTrail to monitor root user activity and set up a CloudWatch alarm to notify the security team if the root user signs in.
correct_explanation: AWS best practices for root user security include: enabling MFA to prevent unauthorized console access even if the password is compromised, not creating access keys to prevent programmatic root access, and using IAM users or IAM Identity Center for all operations. The root user should only be used for the small number of tasks that specifically require it (e.g., closing the account, changing support plans).
wrong_explanation_1: Sharing the root password with multiple administrators increases the risk of compromise. Even for billing tasks, an IAM user with billing permissions is more appropriate. A shared password also makes it impossible to attribute actions to a specific individual.
wrong_explanation_2: Creating root user access keys — even read-only ones — is explicitly against AWS security best practices. Root access keys provide programmatic access that bypasses many security controls and cannot be restricted by IAM policies.
wrong_explanation_3: Monitoring root user activity with CloudTrail and CloudWatch is a good detective control but does not prevent unauthorized use. It should be implemented in addition to the preventive controls (MFA, no access keys), not instead of them.

scenario: A data engineer is writing a Python script to process records from an Amazon DynamoDB table and load them into Amazon S3 as JSON files. The script runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. Which AWS SDK should the engineer use to interact with both DynamoDB and S3 from Python?
correct_answer: boto3
wrong_answer_1: AWS CLI
wrong_answer_2: AWS CDK
wrong_answer_3: AWS SDK for Java
correct_explanation: boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. It provides client and resource interfaces for all AWS services including DynamoDB and S3, enabling the engineer to read from DynamoDB tables and write objects to S3 within a Python script.
wrong_explanation_1: The AWS CLI is a command-line tool for interacting with AWS services from a terminal. While it can be invoked from Python using subprocess, it is not a Python SDK and is not the appropriate tool for programmatic AWS service interactions within application code.
wrong_explanation_2: The AWS CDK (Cloud Development Kit) is an infrastructure-as-code framework for defining AWS resources. It is not used for runtime data operations like reading from DynamoDB or writing to S3.
wrong_explanation_3: The AWS SDK for Java provides Java bindings for AWS services. Since the script is written in Python, the Java SDK is not applicable.

scenario: An enterprise wants to run some workloads on AWS while keeping latency-sensitive workloads in its on-premises data center, with both environments managed in a connected fashion. Which deployment model does this describe?
correct_answer: Hybrid cloud
wrong_answer_1: All-in cloud
wrong_answer_2: On-premises only
wrong_answer_3: Multi-Region cloud
correct_explanation: A hybrid cloud deployment combines cloud and on-premises resources, connected so workloads can run where they best fit. AWS supports hybrid through services like AWS Outposts, AWS Storage Gateway, and AWS Direct Connect.
wrong_explanation_1: All-in cloud means moving all workloads to AWS, which contradicts the scenario's requirement to keep some workloads on-premises.
wrong_explanation_2: On-premises only means no cloud, also contradicting the scenario.
wrong_explanation_3: Multi-Region cloud spans multiple AWS Regions but does not include on-premises infrastructure.

scenario: A machine learning team trained a time-series forecasting model using Amazon SageMaker DeepAR. The model achieves low Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the test set, but the business team reports that large prediction errors on peak demand days are causing operational problems. Which metric should the team add to their evaluation to better capture the impact of large errors?
correct_answer: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
wrong_answer_1: Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
wrong_answer_2: R² (coefficient of determination)
wrong_answer_3: Precision at K
correct_explanation: RMSE squares the errors before averaging, which penalizes large errors more heavily than small ones. Since the business impact is concentrated in large prediction errors on peak days, RMSE is more sensitive to these outlier errors than MAE or MSE alone, making it a better metric for capturing the operational impact of large forecasting mistakes.
wrong_explanation_1: Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) measures errors as a percentage of actual values. It can be unstable or undefined when actual values are near zero (common in demand forecasting) and does not specifically penalize large absolute errors more than small ones.
wrong_explanation_2: R² measures the proportion of variance in the target explained by the model. It is a relative measure of fit and does not directly quantify the magnitude of large errors on specific peak days.
wrong_explanation_3: Precision at K is a ranking metric used in recommendation systems and information retrieval. It is not applicable to time-series forecasting evaluation.

scenario: An image-generation model keeps producing images that include text labels in them, but the team wants images WITHOUT any text labels overlaid. Which prompt engineering technique BEST addresses this with the least operational effort?
correct_answer: Use a negative prompt that lists "text" and "labels" as content to avoid
wrong_answer_1: Fine-tune the model on a custom dataset that has no text labels
wrong_answer_2: Train a brand-new diffusion model from scratch
wrong_answer_3: Lower the temperature parameter to zero
correct_explanation: Negative prompts let users specify content the model should avoid generating. Listing "text" and "labels" as negative-prompt entries is a low-effort, prompt-engineering-only way to suppress that content in image generation.
wrong_explanation_1: Fine-tuning is heavy operational work for what can be accomplished with a negative prompt.
wrong_explanation_2: Training a brand-new model is even heavier and unnecessary.
wrong_explanation_3: Temperature controls randomness; it does not specifically suppress "text" in image output.

scenario: A company runs a multi-tier application where the web tier writes user activity events to a backend processing service. During peak hours, the backend cannot keep up with the volume of events and starts dropping them. The company wants to ensure no events are lost and the backend can process them at its own pace. The events do not need to be processed in strict order. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Introduce an Amazon SQS Standard queue between the web tier and the backend. The web tier enqueues events and the backend polls the queue, processing events at its own pace.
wrong_answer_1: Introduce an Amazon SQS FIFO queue to ensure events are processed in the exact order they are received.
wrong_answer_2: Increase the backend service's instance size to handle the peak event volume without dropping events.
wrong_answer_3: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a single shard to buffer events between the web tier and the backend.
correct_explanation: SQS Standard queues provide virtually unlimited throughput, durable message storage, and at-least-once delivery. The web tier can enqueue events at any rate without loss, and the backend processes them at its own pace. Since strict ordering is not required, Standard queues are the appropriate and more cost-effective choice over FIFO queues.
wrong_explanation_1: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict ordering but have a throughput limit of 3,000 messages per second with batching. For high-volume event ingestion where ordering is not required, FIFO queues add unnecessary constraints and cost.
wrong_explanation_2: Scaling up the backend instance handles current peak load but does not provide a buffer for future spikes. The fundamental problem is tight coupling between the web tier's write rate and the backend's processing rate — a queue decouples these rates durably.
wrong_explanation_3: Kinesis Data Streams with a single shard supports only 1,000 PUT records per second and 1 MB/s throughput. For high-volume event ingestion, a single shard would quickly become a bottleneck. SQS Standard queues have no throughput limits and are simpler to operate for this use case.

scenario: A data analyst needs to run ad-hoc SQL queries against 2 TB of Parquet files stored in Amazon S3, partitioned by year and month. The analyst wants to minimize query costs and execution time. Which best practice should be applied when writing queries in Amazon Athena?
correct_answer: Include partition filters in the WHERE clause to limit data scanned
wrong_answer_1: Use SELECT * to retrieve all columns and filter in the application layer
wrong_answer_2: Convert Parquet files to CSV before querying to improve compatibility
wrong_answer_3: Increase the Athena query timeout to allow full table scans
correct_explanation: Amazon Athena charges per TB of data scanned. Including partition filters (e.g., WHERE year = 2024 AND month = 3) allows Athena to skip partitions that don't match, dramatically reducing the amount of data scanned and lowering both cost and query execution time.
wrong_explanation_1: Using SELECT * retrieves all columns from every scanned row, maximizing data scanned and cost. Parquet's columnar format allows Athena to read only the columns needed — selecting specific columns reduces data scanned significantly.
wrong_explanation_2: Converting Parquet to CSV would increase storage costs and worsen query performance. CSV is a row-based format that requires reading entire rows, while Parquet's columnar format enables Athena to read only the columns needed.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing the query timeout does not reduce data scanned or improve performance. It only extends how long Athena waits before timing out a query.

scenario: A bank wants to build a voice-driven phone assistant that lets customers check balances and pay bills through conversational interactions, including automatic speech recognition and intent understanding. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this conversational interface?
correct_answer: Amazon Lex
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Polly
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Transcribe
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Comprehend
correct_explanation: Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces (chat and voice) using automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding. It powers chatbots and IVR systems that can capture intents, slots, and dialog flow.
wrong_explanation_1: Polly is text-to-speech only; it does not understand intents or manage conversations.
wrong_explanation_2: Transcribe converts audio to text but does not handle conversational logic or intents.
wrong_explanation_3: Comprehend analyzes text for entities and sentiment; it does not manage chatbot dialog.

scenario: Which of the following is NOT one of the six advantages of cloud computing typically cited by AWS?
correct_answer: Manual capacity planning at fixed annual intervals
wrong_answer_1: Trade capital expense for variable expense
wrong_answer_2: Benefit from massive economies of scale
wrong_answer_3: Increase speed and agility
correct_explanation: Manual fixed-interval capacity planning is the OLD on-premises model. The six AWS-cited advantages are: trade CapEx for variable expense; benefit from economies of scale; stop guessing capacity; increase speed and agility; stop spending money on data centers; and go global in minutes. Manual annual planning is the opposite of these benefits.
wrong_explanation_1: Trading CapEx for variable expense is one of the six benefits.
wrong_explanation_2: Benefiting from massive economies of scale is one of the six benefits.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing speed and agility is one of the six benefits.

scenario: Which AWS-published resource is specifically intended to help customers understand the intended use cases, limitations, fairness considerations, and design choices of an AWS AI service?
correct_answer: AWS AI Service Cards
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor reports
wrong_answer_2: AWS Health Dashboard events
wrong_answer_3: Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
correct_explanation: AWS AI Service Cards document AWS AI services' intended use cases, fairness considerations, design choices, and limitations. They are AWS's transparency-and-accountability resource for AI offerings.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor offers cost/performance/security best-practice recommendations, not AI transparency documentation.
wrong_explanation_2: Health Dashboard reports service availability, not AI transparency.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudWatch dashboards show operational metrics.

scenario: A developer has an application that uses a Lambda function connected to an Aurora MySQL database in a VPC. Under high load, the database returns a 'Too many connections' error. The developer has already set the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to 100. What is the MOST suitable solution?
correct_answer: Provision an RDS Proxy between the Lambda function and the Aurora database to pool and reuse database connections.
wrong_answer_1: Increase the max_connections parameter on the Aurora instance to match the Lambda concurrency limit.
wrong_answer_2: Increase the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to reduce the number of concurrent executions.
wrong_answer_3: Increase the Lambda function's memory allocation to reduce execution time and free connections faster.
correct_explanation: RDS Proxy maintains a warm connection pool to the database and multiplexes many Lambda connections onto a smaller set of long-lived database connections. Lambda functions connect to the proxy endpoint instead of Aurora directly. The proxy handles connection management transparently, resolving the 'too many connections' error without requiring changes to the database or Lambda concurrency settings.
wrong_explanation_1: Increasing max_connections raises the limit but does not solve the architectural problem. As Lambda scales, the connection count will continue to grow. RDS Proxy addresses the root cause by pooling connections rather than simply raising the ceiling.
wrong_explanation_2: Reducing reserved concurrency would limit the number of simultaneous Lambda executions, which reduces connections but also reduces throughput. This trades one problem for another. RDS Proxy solves the connection problem without sacrificing Lambda's ability to scale.
wrong_explanation_3: Faster execution does reduce the time each connection is held open, but under sustained high load, connections are still opened at a rate that can exceed the database limit. RDS Proxy is the correct architectural solution for Lambda-to-RDS connection management.

scenario: A data engineering team runs AWS Glue ETL jobs that process data from Amazon S3 and load results into Amazon Redshift. The jobs run on a schedule, but occasionally fail due to transient network errors or temporary Redshift unavailability. The team wants failed jobs to automatically retry up to 3 times before sending an alert. Which AWS Glue configuration enables automatic retries?
correct_answer: Configure the job's 'Number of retries' parameter to 3 in the Glue job settings
wrong_answer_1: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect job failures and restart the job
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS Step Functions with a retry policy to orchestrate the Glue job
wrong_answer_3: Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks to resume from the last successful checkpoint
correct_explanation: AWS Glue jobs have a built-in 'Number of retries' parameter that automatically retries failed jobs up to the specified number of times. This is the simplest and most direct way to handle transient failures without requiring external orchestration or custom logic.
wrong_explanation_1: While an EventBridge rule can detect job failures and trigger a restart, this requires additional configuration and does not provide built-in retry counting or exponential backoff. The native Glue retry parameter is simpler and more appropriate for this use case.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Step Functions can orchestrate Glue jobs with retry policies, but this adds unnecessary complexity when Glue's built-in retry mechanism can handle the requirement directly. Step Functions is more appropriate for complex multi-step workflows.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed to avoid reprocessing in subsequent runs. They do not automatically retry failed jobs or handle transient errors.

scenario: A company is running a multi-account AWS environment. The security team wants a centralized view of security findings across all accounts, including GuardDuty findings, IAM Access Analyzer findings, and Security Hub checks. They want a single pane of glass without logging into each account individually. Which service provides this capability?
correct_answer: AWS Security Hub with a delegated administrator account configured to aggregate findings from all member accounts.
wrong_answer_1: AWS Config aggregator configured to collect configuration data from all member accounts.
wrong_answer_2: Amazon CloudWatch cross-account observability configured to share metrics and logs across accounts.
wrong_answer_3: AWS Trusted Advisor with organizational view enabled to display recommendations across all accounts.
correct_explanation: AWS Security Hub aggregates, normalizes, and prioritizes security findings from multiple AWS services including GuardDuty, IAM Access Analyzer, Inspector, and Macie. When configured with a delegated administrator in AWS Organizations, it automatically collects findings from all member accounts into a single centralized view without requiring individual account access.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Config aggregator collects resource configuration and compliance data across accounts, but it does not aggregate security findings from GuardDuty, IAM Access Analyzer, or Security Hub checks. It is focused on configuration state, not security findings.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon CloudWatch cross-account observability shares metrics, logs, and traces across accounts for operational monitoring. It does not aggregate security findings from GuardDuty or IAM Access Analyzer.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Trusted Advisor provides best practice recommendations across cost, performance, security, and fault tolerance. While it has an organizational view, it does not aggregate GuardDuty findings or IAM Access Analyzer findings.

scenario: An auditor has requested a current copy of the SOC 2 Type II report covering AWS services. Which AWS service should the company use to download this compliance report?
correct_answer: AWS Artifact
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor
wrong_answer_2: AWS Config
wrong_answer_3: AWS Audit Manager
correct_explanation: AWS Artifact is the central, self-service portal for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports such as SOC 1/2/3, ISO certifications, and PCI reports. It is the standard way auditors obtain AWS's compliance documentation.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and recommends improvements. It does not deliver third-party compliance reports.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Config records configuration history of AWS resources. It does not provide AWS's own compliance reports.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Audit Manager helps customers continuously audit their own AWS usage. It does not deliver AWS's external SOC reports — those come from Artifact.

scenario: A data scientist wants to capture a sample of inference requests and responses from a SageMaker real-time endpoint for offline analysis and model monitoring. The captured data should be stored in Amazon S3. Which SageMaker feature enables this?
correct_answer: SageMaker Data Capture
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker Debugger
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
wrong_answer_3: AWS CloudTrail
correct_explanation: SageMaker Data Capture is a feature of SageMaker real-time endpoints that records a configurable sample of inference requests and responses to an S3 bucket. The captured data serves as input for SageMaker Model Monitor and offline analysis of model behavior in production.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Debugger captures tensor data during model training to detect training issues. It does not capture inference requests and responses from deployed endpoints.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a streaming data delivery service. While it can deliver data to S3, it is not a native SageMaker feature and would require custom integration to capture endpoint inference data.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS CloudTrail records API calls made to AWS services for auditing purposes. It captures API-level events (e.g., InvokeEndpoint calls) but does not capture the actual payload content of inference requests and responses.

scenario: A data engineering team uses Amazon Athena to query partitioned data in Amazon S3. Queries are slow because Athena scans entire partitions even when filters are applied. The team wants to improve query performance by enabling Athena to skip irrelevant data within partitions. Which approach improves query performance?
correct_answer: Store data in Parquet format with predicate pushdown enabled
wrong_answer_1: Increase the number of partitions in the dataset
wrong_answer_2: Enable Athena query result caching
wrong_answer_3: Use S3 Select to pre-filter data before querying
correct_explanation: Parquet is a columnar storage format that supports predicate pushdown. Athena can read only the columns needed for a query and skip row groups that do not match filter predicates, significantly reducing the amount of data scanned and improving query performance.
wrong_explanation_1: Increasing the number of partitions can improve query performance by allowing Athena to skip entire partitions, but it does not help Athena skip irrelevant data within partitions. Predicate pushdown with Parquet provides finer-grained filtering.
wrong_explanation_2: Athena query result caching returns cached results for identical queries, reducing query time and cost. However, it does not improve performance for new queries or queries with different filters. Predicate pushdown improves performance for all queries.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Select allows you to retrieve a subset of data from an object using SQL expressions, but it is not integrated with Athena's query execution. Athena's native predicate pushdown with Parquet is more efficient and requires no additional configuration.

scenario: A company needs an ENCRYPTED tunnel between an on-premises network and an AWS VPC over the public internet. The setup must be quick, with no dedicated circuit required. Which AWS service is the appropriate choice?
correct_answer: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
wrong_answer_1: AWS Direct Connect
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Route 53
wrong_answer_3: AWS PrivateLink
correct_explanation: AWS Site-to-Site VPN establishes an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet between an on-premises VPN gateway and an AWS VPN gateway. Setup is fast and does not require ordering a dedicated circuit.
wrong_explanation_1: Direct Connect requires ordering a dedicated physical circuit through a partner, which is not quick. Direct Connect by itself is also not encrypted; encryption can be layered on top.
wrong_explanation_2: Route 53 is DNS; it does not provide encrypted on-premises connectivity.
wrong_explanation_3: PrivateLink provides private connectivity to specific AWS services and endpoints within AWS; it does not establish an on-premises VPN tunnel.

scenario: A company is required by regulators to ensure that all Amazon S3 objects in a specific bucket are encrypted at rest. New objects uploaded without encryption must be automatically encrypted, and unencrypted objects must not be stored. The company wants to enforce this without requiring application changes. Which solution meets these requirements?
correct_answer: Enable default S3 bucket encryption with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key. S3 will automatically encrypt any object uploaded without explicit encryption settings using the bucket's default encryption configuration.
wrong_answer_1: Create a bucket policy that denies s3:PutObject requests that do not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Amazon Macie on the bucket to detect unencrypted objects and trigger a Lambda function to encrypt them after upload.
wrong_answer_3: Use an S3 Inventory report to identify unencrypted objects weekly and run a batch encryption job using S3 Batch Operations.
correct_explanation: S3 default bucket encryption automatically applies the configured encryption to any object uploaded without explicit encryption headers. Since April 2023, all new S3 objects are encrypted by default (SSE-S3 minimum), but configuring SSE-KMS with a CMK ensures company-controlled key encryption is applied automatically to all uploads without requiring application changes.
wrong_explanation_1: A bucket policy denying PutObject without the encryption header prevents unencrypted uploads but requires applications to explicitly set the encryption header. The question specifies no application changes should be required — default bucket encryption handles this transparently.
wrong_explanation_2: Encrypting objects after upload means there is a window where unencrypted objects exist in S3. This violates the requirement that unencrypted objects must not be stored. Reactive encryption after the fact does not satisfy the compliance requirement.
wrong_explanation_3: Weekly inventory reports and batch encryption jobs create a compliance gap of up to 7 days during which unencrypted objects exist in the bucket. This does not meet the requirement that unencrypted objects must not be stored.

scenario: A data scientist is preparing a dataset for a gradient boosting model. The dataset contains a numeric feature representing the number of days since a customer's last purchase, with values ranging from 0 to 1,825 (5 years). The distribution is heavily right-skewed with most values below 90 days. Which preprocessing step is most appropriate to reduce the skew before training?
correct_answer: Apply a log transformation to the feature
wrong_answer_1: Apply one-hot encoding to the feature
wrong_answer_2: Drop the feature because it is skewed
wrong_answer_3: Apply min-max normalization without any prior transformation
correct_explanation: A log transformation compresses the long right tail of a skewed distribution, making it more symmetric and reducing the influence of extreme values (e.g., customers who haven't purchased in 5 years). This helps gradient boosting models learn more effectively from the feature by reducing the dominance of outliers.
wrong_explanation_1: One-hot encoding is used for categorical features, not continuous numeric features. Applying it to a continuous variable like days since last purchase would destroy the ordinal and magnitude information in the feature.
wrong_explanation_2: Dropping a skewed feature is not appropriate — skewness is a distributional property that can be corrected through transformation. The feature likely contains valuable predictive signal about customer recency.
wrong_explanation_3: Min-max normalization scales values to a [0,1] range but does not address skewness. The transformed values would still be heavily concentrated near 0, preserving the skewed distribution and its impact on model training.

scenario: Which of the following statements about AWS Regions is correct?
correct_answer: Every AWS Region has a minimum of three Availability Zones
wrong_answer_1: Each AWS Region contains exactly one Availability Zone
wrong_answer_2: Availability Zones in different Regions are interconnected through a single shared subnet
wrong_answer_3: All AWS Regions are physically located inside the United States
correct_explanation: AWS Regions are designed with multiple, isolated, and physically separated AZs — a minimum of three in current Regions — so that multi-AZ architectures can achieve high availability with meaningful fault isolation.
wrong_explanation_1: A single AZ per Region would preclude multi-AZ resilience. AWS Regions are explicitly designed with multiple AZs.
wrong_explanation_2: AZs in different Regions are not connected through a shared subnet. Regions are fully isolated, and cross-Region traffic uses AWS's backbone with explicit constructs like inter-Region VPC peering.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS operates Regions globally across many countries. They are not US-only.

scenario: Which of the following statements about Amazon SQS FIFO queues is NOT correct?
correct_answer: FIFO queues support unlimited throughput with no messages-per-second limit.
wrong_answer_1: FIFO queues guarantee that messages are processed exactly once.
wrong_answer_2: FIFO queues preserve the order in which messages are sent and received.
wrong_answer_3: FIFO queues use a message deduplication ID to prevent duplicate message delivery within a 5-minute window.
correct_explanation: FIFO queues have a throughput limit of 3,000 messages per second with batching (300 without batching) per API action. They do not support unlimited throughput — that is a characteristic of SQS Standard queues. Standard queues sacrifice ordering and exactly-once delivery in exchange for nearly unlimited throughput.
