correct_answer: A large, general-purpose model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
wrong_answer_1: A small model trained for a single, specific task and not useful elsewhere
wrong_answer_2: A rule-based system written by hand that does not use neural networks
wrong_answer_3: A type of relational database optimized for time-series queries
correct_explanation: Foundation models are large models pre-trained on broad, diverse data (text, code, images). They develop general capabilities that can be adapted (via prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning) to many downstream tasks rather than being trained per-task from scratch.
wrong_explanation_1: FMs are explicitly general-purpose and reusable, the opposite of single-task narrow models.
wrong_explanation_2: FMs are neural-network-based models, not hand-coded rule systems.
wrong_explanation_3: FMs are not databases.

scenario: A genomics research company needs to store petabytes of raw sequencing data that is generated daily. The data is accessed intensively for the first 30 days during analysis, then rarely accessed for 1 year for compliance, and must be retained for 7 years total at the lowest possible cost. Which S3 storage strategy should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Store new data in S3 Standard for 30 days, transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year, and configure a lifecycle rule to expire objects after 7 years.
wrong_answer_1: Store all data in S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically optimize costs across all access patterns.
wrong_answer_2: Store all data in S3 Standard for the full 7 years to ensure consistent access performance.
wrong_answer_3: Store new data in S3 Standard for 30 days, then transition directly to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for the remaining 6 years and 11 months.
correct_explanation: This lifecycle policy matches each storage tier to the access pattern: S3 Standard for active analysis (high performance, higher cost), S3 Standard-IA for the compliance period (lower cost, infrequent access), and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for long-term archival (very low cost). The expiration rule automates deletion at 7 years, avoiding manual cleanup.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is well-suited for unpredictable access patterns, but when the access pattern is well-known and predictable (active for 30 days, then rarely accessed), explicit lifecycle rules are more cost-effective. Intelligent-Tiering also charges a per-object monitoring fee that adds up at petabyte scale.
wrong_explanation_2: Storing petabytes in S3 Standard for 7 years is significantly more expensive than using tiered storage. S3 Standard pricing is appropriate for frequently accessed data, not for compliance archival.
wrong_explanation_3: Transitioning directly from S3 Standard to Glacier Deep Archive skips the 1-year compliance period where data is rarely but occasionally accessed. Glacier Deep Archive has retrieval times of 12–48 hours, which may be too slow for compliance access requests. S3 Standard-IA provides faster retrieval at a lower cost than Standard for this period.

scenario: A data engineering team runs an AWS Glue job that processes data from multiple S3 prefixes. The job should only run after all upstream data files have been uploaded to their respective prefixes. The upstream systems upload files independently and at different times. Which approach ensures the Glue job runs only after all required files are present?
correct_answer: Use AWS Step Functions with a parallel state to wait for S3 object creation events from all prefixes, then start the Glue job
wrong_answer_1: Schedule the Glue job to run at a fixed time after the latest expected upload
wrong_answer_2: Use an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 events to count uploaded files and start the Glue job when the count matches the expected number
wrong_answer_3: Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks to process files as they arrive
correct_explanation: AWS Step Functions can use a parallel state to wait for multiple S3 object creation events (via EventBridge) from different prefixes. Once all expected events are received, the workflow proceeds to start the Glue job. This provides a declarative, event-driven solution that ensures all required input data is present before processing begins.
wrong_explanation_1: Scheduling the Glue job at a fixed time after the latest expected upload introduces a race condition. If any upstream system is delayed, the Glue job will start with incomplete data and fail or produce incorrect results.
wrong_explanation_2: While a Lambda function triggered by S3 events can count uploaded files and start the Glue job when the count is correct, this requires custom state management (e.g., storing counts in DynamoDB) and custom logic. Step Functions provides a more declarative and maintainable solution.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed to avoid reprocessing. They do not wait for multiple files to arrive or coordinate the start of the job based on the presence of all required input files.

scenario: A developer wants to update a production Lambda function and gradually shift traffic to the new version while retaining the ability to instantly roll back. The developer wants to route 5% of traffic to the new version initially. Which Lambda feature should the developer use?
correct_answer: Lambda alias with weighted traffic routing between two published versions.
wrong_answer_1: Lambda environment variables to toggle between code paths.
wrong_answer_2: Route 53 weighted routing between two Lambda function URLs.
wrong_answer_3: API Gateway stage variables pointing to different Lambda versions.
correct_explanation: Lambda aliases can be configured with a routing-config that splits traffic between two published versions by weight. Setting the alias to route 5% to the new version and 95% to the current version enables gradual rollout. Rolling back is instant — update the alias weight to 100% on the stable version. An alias can point to a maximum of two versions simultaneously.
wrong_explanation_1: Environment variables can toggle code paths within a single deployed version, but both code paths exist in the same deployment package. This does not provide true version isolation or the ability to instantly roll back to a separately published version.
wrong_explanation_2: Route 53 weighted routing between Lambda function URLs is not a supported or recommended pattern for Lambda traffic shifting. Lambda aliases with weighted routing are the native, purpose-built mechanism for this use case.
wrong_explanation_3: API Gateway stage variables can reference different Lambda versions, but they route all traffic for a given stage to one version — they do not support percentage-based traffic splitting between two versions within the same stage.

scenario: A developer is building a REST API using Amazon API Gateway with Lambda proxy integration. The API has a caching TTL of 300 seconds configured on the stage. A mobile client needs to bypass the cache and always retrieve the latest data from the Lambda function for a specific request. What should the client include in the request to force a cache bypass?
correct_answer: Cache-Control: max-age=0 header
wrong_answer_1: Cache-Control: no-store header
wrong_answer_2: X-Bypass-Cache: true header
wrong_answer_3: Pragma: no-cache header
correct_explanation: API Gateway allows clients to invalidate a cached response for individual requests by including the Cache-Control: max-age=0 header. When API Gateway receives this header from an authorized client, it bypasses the cache and forwards the request directly to the Lambda integration, then replaces the existing cache entry with the fresh response.
wrong_explanation_1: Cache-Control: no-store is a valid HTTP cache directive that instructs caches not to store the response, but API Gateway specifically requires max-age=0 to trigger per-request cache invalidation. The no-store directive is not recognized by API Gateway for this purpose.
wrong_explanation_2: X-Bypass-Cache is a custom header with no meaning in API Gateway. API Gateway does not recognize custom headers as cache invalidation signals — only the standard Cache-Control: max-age=0 header triggers this behavior.
wrong_explanation_3: Pragma: no-cache is a legacy HTTP/1.0 directive. API Gateway does not use the Pragma header for cache invalidation. The Cache-Control: max-age=0 header is the correct mechanism for per-request cache bypass in API Gateway.

scenario: A developer needs to set up HTTPS between viewers and a CloudFront distribution that serves a web application. The origin is an Application Load Balancer. The developer also wants to ensure that traffic between CloudFront and the ALB origin is encrypted. Which TWO configurations are required? (Select the answer that covers both.)
correct_answer: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy to HTTPS Only, and set the Origin Protocol Policy to HTTPS Only.
wrong_answer_1: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy to HTTPS Only, and use a self-signed certificate on the ALB.
wrong_answer_2: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and configure the ALB to use its default SSL certificate.
wrong_answer_3: Associate a WAF web ACL with the CloudFront distribution and enable HTTPS on the ALB listener.
correct_explanation: End-to-end HTTPS requires two separate configurations: the Viewer Protocol Policy controls encryption between viewers and CloudFront edge locations, and the Origin Protocol Policy controls encryption between CloudFront and the origin (ALB). Both must be set to HTTPS Only for full end-to-end encryption. The ALB must have a valid SSL certificate from ACM or a trusted CA.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudFront does not support self-signed certificates on custom origins. The ALB must use a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager or a trusted third-party certificate authority. A self-signed certificate will cause CloudFront to reject the origin connection.
wrong_explanation_2: ALBs do not have a 'default SSL certificate' — a certificate must be explicitly provisioned and attached to the HTTPS listener. Additionally, 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' only addresses the viewer-to-CloudFront leg; the Origin Protocol Policy must also be configured for the CloudFront-to-ALB leg.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS WAF protects against web application attacks but does not configure encryption protocols. Enabling HTTPS on the ALB listener alone does not configure CloudFront to use HTTPS when communicating with the origin — the Origin Protocol Policy must be explicitly set.

scenario: Which architectural pattern describes a model that first ENCODES an input sequence into a latent representation and then DECODES it into an output sequence — useful for translation and summarization?
correct_answer: Encoder-decoder architecture
wrong_answer_1: Convolutional architecture
wrong_answer_2: Random forest
wrong_answer_3: Linear regression
correct_explanation: Encoder-decoder architectures process an input sequence into a latent representation (encoder) and then generate an output sequence (decoder). They underlie many sequence-to-sequence tasks including machine translation and summarization.
wrong_explanation_1: Convolutional architectures are designed for spatial input like images, not for sequence-to-sequence translation.
wrong_explanation_2: Random forests are ensemble decision-tree models; they are not encoder-decoder networks.
wrong_explanation_3: Linear regression is not a sequence model.

scenario: An ML team needs to deploy a SageMaker model endpoint that requires GPU-accelerated inference but wants to minimize costs by sharing GPU resources across multiple endpoints. Which SageMaker feature enables GPU resource sharing across multiple inference workloads?
correct_answer: SageMaker Elastic Inference
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker multi-model endpoints
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference
wrong_answer_3: SageMaker Batch Transform with GPU instances
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Elastic Inference allows you to attach a fractional GPU accelerator to any SageMaker endpoint instance type. This enables GPU-accelerated inference at a fraction of the cost of a full GPU instance, as the GPU resources are shared across multiple workloads in the AWS infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker multi-model endpoints share CPU/memory resources across multiple models on a single instance but do not provide GPU resource sharing across endpoints. They are designed for cost reduction through model consolidation, not GPU sharing.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference does not support GPU acceleration. It runs on managed CPU infrastructure and is not suitable for GPU-accelerated inference workloads.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker Batch Transform with GPU instances allocates a dedicated GPU instance for the duration of the batch job. It does not share GPU resources across multiple endpoints and is designed for offline batch inference, not real-time serving.

scenario: A bank has a labeled dataset of past loan applications with a column indicating whether each applicant defaulted. The bank wants to train an ML model to predict defaults for new applicants. Which type of machine learning is most appropriate?
correct_answer: Supervised learning
wrong_answer_1: Unsupervised learning
wrong_answer_2: Reinforcement learning
wrong_answer_3: Self-supervised pre-training
correct_explanation: Supervised learning trains a model on labeled examples — input features paired with a known target (defaulted: yes/no). The trained model can then predict the target for new, unlabeled examples. The presence of historical labels is the defining signal.
wrong_explanation_1: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction). It does not predict a known target like default vs no-default.
wrong_explanation_2: Reinforcement learning trains agents through rewards from interacting with an environment. There is no interactive environment in a default-prediction task.
wrong_explanation_3: Self-supervised pre-training generates pseudo-labels from the data itself for tasks like LLM training. It is not the standard approach for tabular classification with explicit labels.

scenario: A company runs long SageMaker training jobs that sometimes fail partway through due to spot instance interruptions. The team wants to reduce training costs by using Spot Instances while ensuring that training can resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch. Which SageMaker feature enables this?
correct_answer: SageMaker Managed Spot Training with checkpoint configuration
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with early stopping
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Pipelines with retry policies
wrong_answer_3: SageMaker Processing jobs with Spot Instances
correct_explanation: SageMaker Managed Spot Training uses EC2 Spot Instances to reduce training costs by up to 90%. When configured with a checkpoint S3 path, the training job saves checkpoints periodically. If a Spot Instance is interrupted, SageMaker automatically resumes training from the last checkpoint on a new instance, avoiding full restarts.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with early stopping stops individual training jobs when the validation metric stops improving. It does not use Spot Instances or provide checkpoint-based resumption after interruptions.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Pipelines retry policies can retry a failed pipeline step, but they restart the training job from scratch rather than resuming from a checkpoint. This does not address the cost of restarting long training jobs.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker Processing jobs support Spot Instances for data processing workloads, but they are not designed for model training with checkpoint-based resumption. Managed Spot Training is the feature specifically designed for training job interruption recovery.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes the key DIFFERENCE between generative AI models and traditional discriminative ML models?
correct_answer: Generative models produce new content (text, images, audio); discriminative models predict labels or values for inputs
wrong_answer_1: Generative models do not require training data
wrong_answer_2: Generative models are always smaller than discriminative models
wrong_answer_3: Discriminative models can only handle numeric input
correct_explanation: Generative models learn the distribution of training data and can produce new examples (e.g., text, images). Discriminative models learn boundaries between classes or fit regression curves — they predict labels or numeric values rather than synthesizing new content.
wrong_explanation_1: Generative models require substantial training data — typically more than discriminative models.
wrong_explanation_2: Many state-of-the-art generative models (LLMs, diffusion models) are very large.
wrong_explanation_3: Discriminative models handle text, images, and many input modalities, not just numeric.

scenario: A data scientist needs to build a model to predict customer churn for a subscription service. The dataset contains 50,000 labeled records with 40 features including demographics, usage patterns, and billing history. The team wants a model that is interpretable enough for the business team to understand which features drive churn. Which algorithm is most appropriate?
correct_answer: XGBoost
wrong_answer_1: Deep neural network (DNN)
wrong_answer_2: K-means clustering
wrong_answer_3: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
correct_explanation: XGBoost is a gradient boosting algorithm well-suited for tabular classification problems. It produces feature importance scores that make it interpretable for business stakeholders, handles mixed feature types well, and consistently achieves strong performance on structured datasets like this one.
wrong_explanation_1: A deep neural network can achieve high accuracy on tabular data but is generally considered a black-box model. It requires more data and tuning to outperform gradient boosting on structured tabular datasets, and it does not natively provide the feature importance interpretability the business team requires.
wrong_explanation_2: K-means clustering is an unsupervised algorithm used for grouping unlabeled data into clusters. Since the dataset has labeled churn outcomes, this is a supervised classification problem — k-means is not applicable.
wrong_explanation_3: PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique, not a predictive model. It cannot be used directly to predict churn and would reduce interpretability by transforming original features into abstract principal components.

scenario: A company uses Amazon EFS to provide shared storage for a fleet of EC2 instances running a content management system. A cost analysis shows that EFS costs are unexpectedly high. Investigation reveals that most files are accessed frequently for the first week after creation, then rarely accessed afterward. Which EFS configuration reduces storage costs for this access pattern?
correct_answer: Enable EFS Intelligent-Tiering or configure an EFS lifecycle policy to transition files to the EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage class after 7 days of no access.
wrong_answer_1: Switch from EFS Standard to EFS One Zone storage class to reduce costs by storing data in a single Availability Zone.
wrong_answer_2: Reduce the EFS throughput mode from Bursting to Provisioned to lower the throughput cost.
wrong_answer_3: Enable EFS compression to reduce the amount of data stored and lower storage costs.
correct_explanation: EFS Infrequent Access storage class costs significantly less per GB than EFS Standard. A lifecycle policy that transitions files after 7 days of no access matches the described pattern — files are in Standard during the active first week and automatically move to IA afterward. EFS Intelligent-Tiering automates this with no fixed transition period.
wrong_explanation_1: EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ, which reduces costs and is appropriate for non-critical data. However, it changes the durability and availability characteristics of the file system. The lifecycle policy approach reduces costs while maintaining the multi-AZ durability of EFS Standard.
wrong_explanation_2: EFS Provisioned Throughput charges for throughput regardless of usage, which typically increases costs for workloads that don't consistently use high throughput. Switching from Bursting to Provisioned would likely increase costs, not reduce them.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon EFS does not offer a built-in compression feature. Storage costs are based on the amount of data stored, and there is no EFS-level compression setting to enable.

scenario: A company runs an analytics workload that queries historical data stored in Amazon Redshift. The cluster runs 24/7 but queries are only executed during business hours (8 AM–6 PM weekdays). The company wants to reduce Redshift costs without losing the data or query history. Which solution provides the most cost reduction?
correct_answer: Use Amazon Redshift Serverless for the analytics workload, which charges only for the compute used during query execution and incurs no cost when idle.
wrong_answer_1: Pause the Redshift cluster outside business hours using the cluster pause/resume feature and resume it each morning.
wrong_answer_2: Resize the Redshift cluster to the smallest available node type to reduce hourly costs.
wrong_answer_3: Purchase Reserved Nodes for the Redshift cluster with a 1-year term to reduce the hourly node cost.
correct_explanation: Amazon Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales compute capacity for query execution and charges only for the Redshift Processing Units (RPUs) used during queries. When no queries are running, there is no compute charge. For a workload with long idle periods, this provides significantly lower costs than a provisioned cluster running 24/7.
wrong_explanation_1: Pausing and resuming a Redshift cluster is a valid cost optimization — paused clusters do not incur compute charges. However, resume time can take several minutes, and the process requires automation. Redshift Serverless provides a more seamless experience with no resume latency for query execution.
wrong_explanation_2: Resizing to the smallest node type reduces the hourly rate but the cluster still runs 24/7, incurring charges during all idle overnight and weekend hours. The cost reduction is modest compared to a consumption-based model.
wrong_explanation_3: Reserved Nodes reduce the hourly rate for provisioned nodes but charge for the full reservation period regardless of usage. For a cluster idle more than 60% of the time, reserved pricing still charges for all idle hours at the discounted rate.

scenario: A classification model returns both a predicted class and a numerical CONFIDENCE SCORE. How should the confidence score be interpreted in a responsible way?
correct_answer: As a relative indicator of the model's certainty that can support, but not replace, human review for high-stakes decisions
wrong_answer_1: As a guaranteed probability that the prediction is correct under all conditions
wrong_answer_2: As a measure of how popular the prediction is across users
wrong_answer_3: As a hyperparameter that can be tuned to improve accuracy
correct_explanation: Confidence scores are useful but imperfect indicators of certainty. They can be miscalibrated and should not be treated as guaranteed probabilities — especially in high-stakes settings where human review remains valuable.
wrong_explanation_1: Many model confidence scores are not strictly calibrated and cannot be treated as exact probabilities.
wrong_explanation_2: Confidence scores are not based on user popularity.
wrong_explanation_3: Confidence scores are model outputs, not hyperparameters.

scenario: A development team needs to centrally create, manage, and rotate symmetric encryption keys used by Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, and AWS Lambda. Which service should the team use?
correct_answer: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Secrets Manager
wrong_answer_2: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
wrong_answer_3: AWS CloudHSM
correct_explanation: AWS KMS is the managed service for creating, controlling, and rotating cryptographic keys used to encrypt data across most AWS services including S3, EBS, and Lambda. It provides integrated key management with native AWS service integration.
wrong_explanation_1: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets such as database passwords or API keys. It does not manage data-encryption keys for service-level encryption.
wrong_explanation_2: ACM provisions and manages TLS/SSL certificates for use with AWS services. It is for transport-layer security, not data encryption keys.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudHSM provides dedicated hardware security modules for customers with strict regulatory requirements. KMS is the default and more commonly used managed service for encryption keys.

scenario: An IT governance team wants to publish a portfolio of approved CloudFormation-based products (e.g., a standard hardened Windows server, a vetted analytics stack) for internal developers to launch in a controlled, repeatable way. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS Service Catalog
wrong_answer_1: AWS Marketplace
wrong_answer_2: AWS re:Post
wrong_answer_3: AWS CodeArtifact
correct_explanation: AWS Service Catalog lets administrators publish a portfolio of approved CloudFormation-based products. End users in the organization can launch those products in a controlled, repeatable way, while administrators retain governance over what is offered.
wrong_explanation_1: Marketplace catalogs third-party software for general AWS customers. It is not the internal-approved-portfolio service.
wrong_explanation_2: re:Post is a community Q&A site, not a launchable product catalog.
wrong_explanation_3: CodeArtifact stores build artifacts (npm, Maven, PyPI). It is not a CloudFormation portfolio service.

scenario: A company wants to migrate a tightly coupled monolithic application to a microservices architecture on AWS. The application currently uses direct function calls between components. The solutions architect wants to introduce asynchronous communication between services while maintaining the ability to replay events if a downstream service fails and needs to reprocess historical data. Which service should the architect use?
correct_answer: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which retains records for up to 365 days and allows consumers to replay events from any point in the retention window.
wrong_answer_1: Use Amazon SQS Standard queues, which retain messages for up to 14 days and support at-least-once delivery.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon SNS to publish events to all downstream services simultaneously with guaranteed delivery.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the sequence of service calls and retry failed steps automatically.
correct_explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams retains records for up to 365 days and allows multiple independent consumers to read from the stream at different positions. If a downstream service fails, it can reset its iterator to an earlier position and replay all events from that point. This replay capability is a key differentiator from SQS, which deletes messages after they are consumed.
wrong_explanation_1: SQS messages are deleted after they are successfully consumed. SQS does not support replaying already-consumed messages — once a message is processed and deleted, it cannot be retrieved. The 14-day retention only applies to unconsumed messages.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon SNS delivers messages to subscribers at the time of publication but does not store messages for replay. If a subscriber is unavailable when a message is published, the message is lost (unless an SQS queue is used as the subscriber). SNS has no replay capability.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Step Functions orchestrates workflows with retry logic but is not a streaming or messaging service. It does not provide event replay capability for historical data reprocessing by independent consumers.

scenario: A company wants to fine-tune a foundation model on PROPRIETARY documents that it does NOT own copyright to. Which limitation or risk MUST the company consider?
correct_answer: Intellectual property and licensing — using third-party copyrighted data without rights can expose the company to legal risk
wrong_answer_1: Top-P inference parameter must be set to 1
wrong_answer_2: Foundation models have no concept of intellectual property
wrong_answer_3: Fine-tuning automatically clears any legal claim
correct_explanation: Training or fine-tuning on data the company does not have rights to can violate copyright, licensing, or contractual terms. Companies must ensure they have appropriate rights to use the data — a core consideration of responsible AI and AWS's Acceptable Use Policy.
wrong_explanation_1: Top-P is an inference parameter and is unrelated to legal-rights considerations.
wrong_explanation_2: Intellectual property protections still apply to data used by ML pipelines.
wrong_explanation_3: Fine-tuning does not transfer or clear licensing rights.

scenario: A company runs a video transcoding service where jobs are submitted via a web interface and processed by worker EC2 instances. Jobs vary in duration from 5 minutes to 4 hours. The company wants the architecture to automatically scale the number of workers based on the number of pending jobs in the queue. Which scaling approach should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Use an SQS queue for job submissions and configure an Auto Scaling group for the worker instances with a custom CloudWatch metric based on the SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible attribute to drive scaling.
wrong_answer_1: Use target tracking scaling on the Auto Scaling group based on CPU utilization of the worker instances.
wrong_answer_2: Use scheduled scaling to add worker instances during business hours when most jobs are submitted.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Batch to manage the worker fleet, which automatically scales compute resources based on the number of submitted jobs.
correct_explanation: Scaling based on SQS queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible) directly reflects the amount of pending work. A custom CloudWatch metric derived from queue depth divided by the number of running instances (backlog per instance) allows the Auto Scaling group to scale out when jobs accumulate and scale in when the queue drains. This is the recommended pattern for queue-based worker scaling.
wrong_explanation_1: CPU-based scaling reacts to current worker load, not pending work. If workers are processing long jobs, CPU may be high even when no new jobs are queued. Conversely, if workers are idle waiting for I/O, CPU may be low even with a large backlog. Queue depth is a more accurate signal for this workload.
wrong_explanation_2: Scheduled scaling is appropriate for predictable traffic patterns. Video transcoding job submissions are unpredictable and do not follow a fixed schedule, making scheduled scaling ineffective for this use case.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Batch is a valid alternative for managed batch computing, but the question asks about scaling an existing EC2-based worker architecture. AWS Batch would require migrating the worker application to a containerized or managed job format.

scenario: A small business wants on-demand access to vetted AWS-certified experts for one-off projects, paying via their AWS bill. Which AWS resource matches this gig-style engagement model?
correct_answer: AWS IQ
wrong_answer_1: AWS Professional Services
wrong_answer_2: AWS Managed Services (AMS)
wrong_answer_3: AWS re:Post
correct_explanation: AWS IQ connects customers with AWS-certified third-party experts for short-term, scoped projects. Payments are processed through the customer's AWS bill, and the marketplace model fits gig-style engagements.
wrong_explanation_1: Professional Services is a paid AWS-employed consulting team. It is not the gig marketplace AWS IQ is.
wrong_explanation_2: AMS provides ongoing operations management for production workloads — much larger in scope than a gig project.
wrong_explanation_3: re:Post is free community Q&A, not a hire-an-expert marketplace.

scenario: A data engineering team runs an Amazon Redshift cluster that processes analytical queries. The team wants to monitor query performance, identify slow queries, and track which users are running the most resource-intensive queries. Which Redshift feature provides detailed query performance metrics and execution history?
correct_answer: Query monitoring in the Redshift console and system tables (STL and SVL views)
wrong_answer_1: Amazon CloudWatch Logs
wrong_answer_2: AWS CloudTrail
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Athena query history
correct_explanation: Amazon Redshift provides query monitoring through the Redshift console and system tables (STL and SVL views). These views contain detailed information about query execution, including query text, execution time, rows processed, and user information. You can query these system tables to identify slow queries and analyze performance.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon CloudWatch Logs can store Redshift logs, but it does not provide the structured query performance metrics and execution history that Redshift system tables offer. CloudWatch Logs are better suited for log aggregation and searching, not detailed query analysis.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS CloudTrail logs API calls made to Redshift for auditing purposes, such as cluster creation or configuration changes. It does not log query execution details or performance metrics.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Athena query history tracks queries run in Athena, not Redshift. Athena and Redshift are separate services with independent query execution engines and monitoring systems.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to encrypt data in transit between an Amazon EMR cluster and Amazon S3. The security team requires that all data transferred between these services uses TLS encryption. Which configuration enforces this?
correct_answer: Enable EMR in-transit encryption using an EMR security configuration with TLS certificates
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3) on the destination bucket
wrong_answer_2: Configure a VPC endpoint for S3 to route traffic through the private AWS network
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket
correct_explanation: Amazon EMR security configurations support in-transit encryption using TLS certificates for data moving between EMR nodes and between EMR and S3. This ensures all data in transit is encrypted using TLS, meeting the security team's requirement.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3) encrypts data at rest in S3. It does not encrypt data in transit between EMR and S3 — that requires TLS configuration on the EMR side.
wrong_explanation_2: A VPC endpoint for S3 routes traffic through the AWS private network, keeping it off the public internet. While this improves network security, it does not enforce TLS encryption of the data in transit.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload speeds by routing through CloudFront edge locations. It does not configure TLS encryption for EMR-to-S3 data transfers.

scenario: A data engineering team processes customer data from multiple source systems and loads it into Amazon Redshift. After loading, they discover that some customer records have duplicate email addresses, which should be unique. The team wants to implement automated data quality checks to detect duplicates before loading data into Redshift. Which AWS service provides automated duplicate detection?
correct_answer: AWS Glue Data Quality rules
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Redshift unique constraints
wrong_answer_2: AWS Lambda function with custom validation logic
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Athena query with GROUP BY and HAVING clauses
correct_explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality allows you to define rules that validate data against constraints, including uniqueness checks. You can create a rule that checks for duplicate email addresses and configure the Glue job to fail or flag records that violate the rule before loading data into Redshift.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Redshift unique constraints enforce uniqueness at the database level, but they cause the load operation to fail when duplicates are encountered. They do not detect duplicates before loading or provide automated quality checks in the ETL pipeline.
wrong_explanation_2: Using a Lambda function with custom validation logic can detect duplicates, but it requires writing and maintaining custom code. AWS Glue Data Quality provides a declarative, no-code approach to defining and enforcing data quality rules.
wrong_explanation_3: Running an Athena query with GROUP BY and HAVING clauses can identify duplicates, but it requires manual query execution and does not integrate with the automated ETL pipeline. Glue Data Quality rules run automatically as part of the ETL job.

scenario: A team wants humans to grade the LINGUISTIC QUALITY of an LLM's open-ended marketing copy — including coherence and creativity — using consistent rubrics, then aggregate those judgments. Which evaluation approach is MOST appropriate?
correct_answer: Human-in-the-loop evaluation
wrong_answer_1: Automatic evaluation using ROUGE only
wrong_answer_2: Automatic evaluation using BLEU only
wrong_answer_3: Mean squared error
correct_explanation: When evaluating open-ended subjective qualities like creativity and coherence, human judgment with structured rubrics is more reliable than automatic metrics. Bedrock model evaluation supports human-in-the-loop evaluation precisely for these qualities.
wrong_explanation_1: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap and does not capture creativity or coherence judgments.
wrong_explanation_2: BLEU is for machine translation precision; it is not suited to subjective marketing-copy quality.
wrong_explanation_3: Mean squared error is a regression metric for numerical predictions, not text quality.

scenario: Which of the following is INCLUDED in the AWS Basic Support plan available to all AWS customers at no additional cost?
correct_answer: Customer service, documentation, whitepapers, AWS re:Post, and a limited set of Trusted Advisor checks
wrong_answer_1: 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers via phone and chat
wrong_answer_2: A dedicated Technical Account Manager (TAM)
wrong_answer_3: Concierge Support for billing and account questions
correct_explanation: Basic Support is free and includes 24/7 access to customer service for account/billing questions, documentation, whitepapers, AWS re:Post, and a limited set of core Trusted Advisor checks. Technical support from Cloud Support Engineers requires a paid plan.
wrong_explanation_1: 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers begins with Business Support, not Basic.
wrong_explanation_2: Dedicated TAMs are exclusive to Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise Support plans.
wrong_explanation_3: Concierge Support is exclusive to Enterprise Support, not Basic.

scenario: A company runs a web application using AWS Lambda functions behind Amazon API Gateway. During peak hours, Lambda invocations spike to 10,000 per minute. During off-peak hours, invocations drop to near zero. The company wants to optimize Lambda costs. Which approach reduces Lambda costs for this usage pattern?
correct_answer: Lambda pricing is based on the number of requests and duration — no action is needed to optimize costs for variable workloads, as Lambda automatically scales to zero when idle and charges only for actual invocations.
wrong_answer_1: Purchase Lambda Savings Plans with a 1-year commitment to reduce the per-invocation cost during peak hours.
wrong_answer_2: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency for all functions to reduce cold start latency and improve cost efficiency.
wrong_answer_3: Increase the Lambda function memory allocation to the maximum to reduce execution duration and lower costs.
correct_explanation: Lambda's serverless pricing model charges only for actual invocations and execution duration — there is no charge when functions are idle. For highly variable workloads that drop to near zero during off-peak hours, Lambda's pay-per-use model is already cost-optimized. No additional purchasing commitments are needed.
wrong_explanation_1: Lambda Savings Plans provide a discount on Lambda usage in exchange for a consistent spend commitment. For workloads with near-zero off-peak usage, a usage commitment may not be cost-effective — the commitment must be met regardless of actual usage.
wrong_explanation_2: Lambda Provisioned Concurrency pre-warms function instances to eliminate cold starts, but it charges for the provisioned concurrency continuously, even when no invocations occur. For a workload that drops to near zero off-peak, Provisioned Concurrency would add significant idle costs.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing memory allocation increases the per-GB-second cost rate. While more memory can reduce execution duration, the net effect on cost depends on the workload. Arbitrarily maximizing memory without profiling the function is not a cost optimization strategy.

scenario: A company stores raw data in Amazon S3 Standard. After 30 days, the data is rarely accessed but must be retained for 7 years for compliance. After 1 year, the data is almost never accessed. The team wants to minimize storage costs while meeting retention requirements. Which S3 lifecycle configuration achieves this?
correct_answer: Transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, then to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year
wrong_answer_1: Transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
wrong_answer_2: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for all objects
wrong_answer_3: Copy objects to a second S3 bucket with lower redundancy after 30 days
correct_explanation: S3 Standard-IA is cost-effective for infrequently accessed data that still needs occasional retrieval within milliseconds. After 1 year when access is almost never needed, transitioning to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval provides the lowest cost for long-term retention while still allowing retrieval within minutes to hours for compliance audits.
wrong_explanation_1: Transitioning to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after only 30 days is overly aggressive. Deep Archive has a minimum storage duration of 180 days and retrieval times of up to 12 hours — if the data needs to be accessed occasionally in the first year, this would be impractical.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns and is a good general-purpose option, but it charges a monitoring fee per object. For a known access pattern (rarely accessed after 30 days, almost never after 1 year), explicit lifecycle rules with Glacier are more cost-effective.
wrong_explanation_3: Copying objects to a second S3 bucket does not reduce storage costs — it doubles them. S3 does not have a 'lower redundancy' standard storage class that reduces costs through reduced durability.

scenario: A data engineering team needs to grant an AWS Glue ETL job access to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS account and write query results to an Amazon Athena workgroup. The team wants to follow the principle of least privilege. Which approach provides the minimum required permissions?
correct_answer: Create an IAM role with policies granting s3:GetObject on the source bucket and athena:StartQueryExecution on the workgroup, then attach the role to the Glue job
wrong_answer_1: Attach the AWS managed policy AmazonS3FullAccess to the Glue job's IAM role
wrong_answer_2: Create an S3 bucket policy that allows public read access to the source bucket
wrong_answer_3: Use the AWS Glue service role with administrator access
correct_explanation: Creating an IAM role with specific permissions for s3:GetObject on the source bucket and athena:StartQueryExecution on the workgroup follows the principle of least privilege. The role grants only the permissions necessary for the Glue job to perform its tasks, minimizing security risk.
wrong_explanation_1: The AWS managed policy AmazonS3FullAccess grants full access to all S3 buckets in the account, which violates the principle of least privilege. The Glue job only needs read access to a specific bucket, not full access to all S3 resources.
wrong_explanation_2: Creating an S3 bucket policy that allows public read access exposes the data to anyone on the internet, which is a significant security risk. The Glue job should use IAM role-based access, not public bucket policies.
wrong_explanation_3: Using an IAM role with administrator access grants far more permissions than necessary and violates the principle of least privilege. The Glue job should have only the specific permissions it needs to read from S3 and write to Athena.

scenario: An organization wants its engineers to earn AWS certifications and pursue role-based learning paths through official AWS-published curricula. Which AWS resource is the canonical place to enroll in these courses?
correct_answer: AWS Training and Certification (AWS Skill Builder)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Marketplace
wrong_answer_2: AWS re:Post
wrong_answer_3: AWS Professional Services
correct_explanation: AWS Training and Certification — including the AWS Skill Builder platform — offers role-based learning paths, free digital courses, paid classroom training, and the certification exams themselves. It is the canonical AWS learning resource.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Marketplace catalogs third-party software products, not AWS training curricula.
wrong_explanation_2: re:Post is a community Q&A site, not a structured learning curriculum.
wrong_explanation_3: Professional Services is a paid consulting team, not a learning platform.

scenario: A team wants to trace requests through their application to identify which downstream service is causing latency. The application uses Lambda functions that call DynamoDB and an external payment API. Which AWS X-Ray environment variables does Lambda automatically set to enable trace context propagation?
correct_answer: _X_AMZN_TRACE_ID and AWS_XRAY_CONTEXT_MISSING
wrong_answer_1: AWS_XRAY_TRACING_NAME and AWS_XRAY_DEBUG_MODE
wrong_answer_2: AUTO_INSTRUMENT and AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS
wrong_answer_3: XRAY_TRACE_ID and AWS_XRAY_SAMPLING_RATE
correct_explanation: _X_AMZN_TRACE_ID contains the tracing header including the sampling decision, trace ID, and parent segment ID — Lambda sets this automatically when X-Ray tracing is enabled. AWS_XRAY_CONTEXT_MISSING determines the X-Ray SDK's behavior when trace context is unavailable; Lambda sets this to LOG_ERROR by default. These two variables are the ones Lambda manages automatically for X-Ray integration.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS_XRAY_TRACING_NAME is used by the X-Ray SDK to set a service name for segments — it is an application-level configuration, not set automatically by Lambda. AWS_XRAY_DEBUG_MODE configures the SDK to output debug logs to the console without a logging library — also not set automatically by Lambda.
wrong_explanation_2: AUTO_INSTRUMENT is used by the X-Ray SDK for Django Framework only to record subsegments for built-in database and template rendering operations. AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS exposes the X-Ray daemon's address and is set by Lambda, but it is not one of the two primary trace context variables. AUTO_INSTRUMENT is not set by Lambda automatically.
wrong_explanation_3: XRAY_TRACE_ID and AWS_XRAY_SAMPLING_RATE are not valid X-Ray environment variable names used by Lambda. The correct trace ID variable is _X_AMZN_TRACE_ID (with the underscore prefix).

scenario: A company needs to migrate 50 TB of training data from an on-premises file server to Amazon S3. The on-premises environment has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection already in place. The team wants a managed service that handles data integrity verification, bandwidth throttling, and automatic retries during the transfer. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
correct_answer: AWS DataSync
wrong_answer_1: AWS Snowball Edge
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
wrong_answer_3: AWS Storage Gateway
correct_explanation: AWS DataSync is a managed data transfer service that automates moving data between on-premises file systems and AWS storage. It performs automatic data integrity verification using checksums, supports bandwidth throttling to avoid saturating the Direct Connect link, and handles automatic retries on failure — making it ideal for this managed transfer scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Snowball Edge is a physical device for offline data transfer, used when network bandwidth is insufficient. With a 10 Gbps Direct Connect already in place, a network-based transfer via DataSync is faster and more appropriate than shipping a physical device.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload speeds by routing through CloudFront edge locations over the public internet. Since a Direct Connect connection is already available, DataSync over Direct Connect provides a more reliable and potentially faster path.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Storage Gateway provides hybrid cloud storage integration for on-premises applications to access AWS storage. It is designed for ongoing hybrid access patterns, not for one-time bulk data migration.

scenario: A non-profit organization is evaluating moving its donation processing system to AWS. Leadership wants to understand which benefit of the AWS Cloud most directly enables the organization to focus its limited engineering staff on building features rather than maintaining infrastructure.
correct_answer: Reduced operational overhead through managed services
wrong_answer_1: Unlimited free service credits for non-profits
wrong_answer_2: Guaranteed elimination of all security responsibilities
wrong_answer_3: Mandatory enrollment in AWS Enterprise Support
correct_explanation: Managed AWS services (RDS, Lambda, S3, etc.) handle patching, scaling, replication, and infrastructure maintenance on behalf of customers. This frees engineering staff to invest time in building product features rather than running infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS offers some credits and programs for non-profits, but unlimited free credits are not a standard offering. The core value proposition for small teams is managed services, not free credits.
wrong_explanation_2: Security on AWS is a shared responsibility model. AWS handles security of the cloud, but customers retain responsibility for security in the cloud (their data, IAM, configurations).
wrong_explanation_3: Enterprise Support is a paid option, not a mandatory feature. Customers choose the support plan that fits their needs.

scenario: A team is building an application that stores sensitive health records in DynamoDB. Regulatory requirements mandate that the data be encrypted at rest using a key that the company controls and can revoke at any time. Which DynamoDB encryption configuration satisfies this requirement?
correct_answer: Configure DynamoDB to use a customer managed key (CMK) in AWS KMS for encryption at rest.
wrong_answer_1: Configure DynamoDB to use AWS owned keys for encryption at rest.
wrong_answer_2: Configure DynamoDB to use the AWS managed key (aws/dynamodb) for encryption at rest.
wrong_answer_3: Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) to protect data from accidental deletion or corruption.
correct_explanation: Customer managed keys (CMKs) give the company full control over the key policy, rotation schedule, and the ability to disable or schedule deletion of the key. Disabling the CMK immediately prevents DynamoDB from decrypting the data, effectively revoking access. This satisfies both the company-controlled key and revocation requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS owned keys are managed entirely by AWS and are not visible or controllable by the customer. The company cannot disable, rotate, or revoke AWS owned keys — they do not satisfy the requirement for company-controlled keys with revocation capability.
wrong_explanation_2: The AWS managed key (aws/dynamodb) is created by AWS on behalf of the customer and appears in the customer's KMS key list. However, the customer cannot disable it or control its rotation schedule. It cannot be used to revoke access to the data.
wrong_explanation_3: DynamoDB PITR provides continuous backups enabling point-in-time table restoration. It is a data recovery feature, not an encryption or access control mechanism. It does not address the requirement for company-controlled encryption keys.

scenario: A company stores application log files in Amazon S3. Logs from the past 7 days are queried frequently by the operations team. Logs between 8 and 90 days old are queried occasionally for incident investigations. Logs older than 90 days must be retained for 3 years for compliance but are almost never accessed. The company wants to minimize storage costs. Which S3 lifecycle configuration should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Store new logs in S3 Standard for 7 days, transition to S3 Standard-IA after 7 days, transition to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 days, and expire objects after 3 years.
wrong_answer_1: Store all logs in S3 Standard for 3 years to ensure consistent access performance for all log queries.
wrong_answer_2: Store new logs in S3 Standard for 7 days, then transition directly to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.
wrong_answer_3: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for all logs and let AWS automatically move objects between tiers based on access patterns.
correct_explanation: This lifecycle policy precisely matches each storage tier to the access pattern: S3 Standard for frequent 7-day access, S3 Standard-IA for occasional access during the 8–90 day window (lower cost, millisecond retrieval), and S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for compliance archival with rare but immediate access needs. The 3-year expiration automates deletion.
wrong_explanation_1: Storing all logs in S3 Standard for 3 years is significantly more expensive than tiered storage. S3 Standard pricing is appropriate only for frequently accessed data — using it for compliance archives wastes money on storage that is almost never accessed.
wrong_explanation_2: Transitioning directly to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days skips the occasional-access window (8–90 days). Glacier Deep Archive has retrieval times of 12–48 hours, which is unsuitable for incident investigations that require timely access to logs.
wrong_explanation_3: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is well-suited for unpredictable access patterns, but this scenario has a well-defined and predictable access pattern. Explicit lifecycle rules are more cost-effective here, and Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-object monitoring fee that adds up for large volumes of small log files.

scenario: A team is evaluating a foundation model that can accept both text and images as input and produce text descriptions. Which term BEST describes this kind of model?
correct_answer: Multimodal model
wrong_answer_1: Linear model
wrong_answer_2: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
wrong_answer_3: Convolutional neural network (CNN) only
correct_explanation: Multimodal models handle more than one modality of data (e.g., text + image + audio) and can map across modalities — for example, taking an image as input and producing a text caption. Modern foundation models increasingly support multimodal input.
wrong_explanation_1: Linear models do not span multiple modalities like images and text.
wrong_explanation_2: RNNs are a single architecture family; multimodality is defined by input/output type, not architecture.
wrong_explanation_3: CNNs alone are not enough to caption images with natural language descriptions — multimodal foundation models combine vision and language capability.

scenario: A machine learning team needs to run weekly batch inference on 10 million customer records stored in S3 to generate personalized product recommendations. The inference job takes approximately 4 hours. The team does not need real-time responses. Which SageMaker deployment option is most cost-effective for this use case?
correct_answer: SageMaker Batch Transform
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker real-time inference endpoint
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference
wrong_answer_3: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference with a persistent endpoint
correct_explanation: SageMaker Batch Transform is designed for offline batch inference on large datasets. It spins up instances, processes the entire dataset, writes results to S3, and then terminates the instances — charging only for the duration of the job. For weekly batch jobs on millions of records with no real-time requirement, Batch Transform is the most cost-effective option.
wrong_explanation_1: A real-time inference endpoint keeps instances running continuously, incurring 24/7 costs even when not processing requests. For a weekly batch job, this would be significantly more expensive than Batch Transform.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Serverless Inference is designed for sporadic real-time requests, not for processing 10 million records in a single batch job. It has payload size limits and is not optimized for large-scale batch processing.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference handles individual requests asynchronously and is designed for long-running single predictions, not for processing millions of records as a batch. A persistent endpoint would also incur continuous costs.

scenario: A machine learning team is implementing a CI/CD pipeline for their SageMaker model. They want to automatically trigger model retraining whenever new training data is uploaded to a specific S3 prefix. Which AWS service should be used to detect the S3 upload event and trigger the retraining pipeline?
correct_answer: Amazon EventBridge with an S3 event notification rule
wrong_answer_1: AWS CloudTrail with a CloudWatch alarm
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
wrong_answer_3: AWS Config with a remediation action
correct_explanation: Amazon EventBridge can receive S3 event notifications (such as object creation in a specific prefix) and route them to targets like SageMaker Pipelines or Step Functions to trigger retraining. This is the standard event-driven pattern for automating ML pipeline triggers based on data arrival.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS CloudTrail records API calls for auditing. While CloudTrail can log S3 PutObject events, using CloudTrail with CloudWatch alarms to trigger pipelines is more complex and less direct than using EventBridge with native S3 event notifications.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor detects data drift and model quality degradation on deployed endpoints. It does not monitor S3 for new data uploads or trigger retraining pipelines.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config monitors resource configuration changes for compliance purposes. It is not designed to detect S3 data uploads or trigger ML retraining pipelines.

scenario: A company uses Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to retrain their fraud detection model weekly. After each training run, the team wants to automatically register the new model in a central repository, track its version, and require a manual approval step before it is deployed to production. Which SageMaker feature supports model versioning and approval workflows?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
wrong_answer_2: Amazon S3 versioning
wrong_answer_3: AWS CodeArtifact
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry provides a central repository for registering, versioning, and managing ML models. It supports approval workflows where models can be set to 'PendingManualApproval' status, requiring a human reviewer to approve before the model is deployed to production. It integrates natively with SageMaker Pipelines.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon SageMaker Experiments tracks training runs and their associated metrics and parameters. It does not provide model versioning, approval workflows, or a deployment-ready model registry.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon S3 versioning tracks versions of objects stored in S3 buckets. While model artifacts are stored in S3, S3 versioning does not provide ML-specific metadata, approval workflows, or integration with SageMaker deployment pipelines.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS CodeArtifact is a package management service for software artifacts like npm, Maven, and PyPI packages. It is not designed for managing ML model versions or approval workflows.

scenario: A company runs a SaaS application that serves thousands of customers. Each customer's data is isolated in a separate VPC. The company wants to allow customers to access the SaaS application's API privately from their own VPCs without the traffic traversing the public internet, and without requiring VPC peering or VPN connections between the company and each customer. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Expose the SaaS API as an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer. Customers create VPC interface endpoints in their own VPCs to connect to the service privately.
wrong_answer_1: Create VPC peering connections between the SaaS provider VPC and each customer VPC.
wrong_answer_2: Deploy the SaaS API behind an internet-facing ALB and use HTTPS with mutual TLS to secure the connection from customer VPCs.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Transit Gateway to connect all customer VPCs and the SaaS provider VPC in a hub-and-spoke topology.
correct_explanation: AWS PrivateLink allows service providers to expose services to consumers privately without VPC peering, VPN, or internet exposure. The provider creates an endpoint service backed by an NLB. Each customer creates a VPC interface endpoint in their VPC that connects to the provider's endpoint service over the AWS private network. This scales to thousands of customers without managing peering connections.
wrong_explanation_1: VPC peering requires a separate peering connection for each customer, which does not scale to thousands of customers. It also gives customers network-level access to the provider's VPC, which is broader than necessary for API access.
wrong_explanation_2: An internet-facing ALB routes traffic over the public internet, which violates the requirement for private connectivity. Mutual TLS provides authentication but does not make the connection private.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Transit Gateway connecting all customer VPCs to the provider VPC would give customers network-level access to the provider's entire VPC and to each other (unless carefully managed with route tables). It also requires the provider to manage Transit Gateway attachments for thousands of customers.

scenario: A company runs a web application on a fleet of On-Demand EC2 instances behind an ALB. AWS Cost Explorer shows that the application has run at a consistent baseline of 10 instances for the past 12 months, with occasional spikes to 20 instances. The company wants to reduce EC2 costs while maintaining the ability to handle spikes. Which purchasing strategy minimizes cost?
correct_answer: Purchase Savings Plans or Reserved Instances to cover the 10-instance baseline, and use On-Demand or Spot Instances to cover the additional capacity during spikes.
wrong_answer_1: Purchase Reserved Instances for all 20 instances to cover both baseline and peak capacity.
wrong_answer_2: Use only Spot Instances for all instances to maximize savings across both baseline and spike capacity.
wrong_answer_3: Use On-Demand Instances for all instances and apply for an Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) to reduce costs.
correct_explanation: The optimal strategy for variable workloads is to cover the predictable baseline with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances (up to 72% discount) and handle variable spike capacity with On-Demand or Spot Instances. This minimizes commitment costs while maintaining flexibility for unpredictable demand.
wrong_explanation_1: Purchasing Reserved Instances for all 20 instances means paying for 10 reserved instances that are only used during spikes. The unused reservation hours during non-peak periods represent wasted spend with no return.
wrong_explanation_2: Spot Instances can be interrupted with 2-minute notice. Using Spot for the entire baseline fleet of a production web application introduces unacceptable availability risk — a Spot interruption event could terminate all baseline instances simultaneously.
wrong_explanation_3: On-Demand Instances for all capacity is the most expensive option. Enterprise Discount Programs require significant committed spend and are negotiated at the enterprise level — they are not a self-service cost optimization tool.

scenario: Which risk is MOST associated with generative AI being used to create realistic but false articles, photos, or videos at scale?
correct_answer: Misinformation and disinformation
wrong_answer_1: Increased latency on small models
wrong_answer_2: Higher token throughput on small models
wrong_answer_3: Reduced vocabulary size
correct_explanation: Generative AI lowers the cost of producing realistic content. At scale, this can be misused to produce convincing misinformation or disinformation — a major societal risk that responsible AI policies (and AWS's own AUP) specifically address.
wrong_explanation_1: Latency on small models is an operational matter, not a societal risk.
wrong_explanation_2: Token throughput is a performance metric, not a societal risk.
wrong_explanation_3: Vocabulary size is a model property, not a misinformation risk.

scenario: An enterprise's AWS Organization includes 80 AWS accounts. The security team wants to apply different SCP guardrails to development accounts versus production accounts without managing each account individually. Which Organizations feature supports this grouping?
correct_answer: Organizational Units (OUs)
wrong_answer_1: IAM groups
wrong_answer_2: Resource groups
wrong_answer_3: VPC route tables
correct_explanation: Organizational Units (OUs) are containers in AWS Organizations used to group accounts. SCPs and other policies can be attached at the OU level so they apply uniformly to all accounts within the OU — for example, a Prod OU and a Dev OU.
wrong_explanation_1: IAM groups contain IAM users within a single account. They do not group AWS accounts.
wrong_explanation_2: Resource groups group AWS resources within an account; they do not group accounts.
wrong_explanation_3: VPC route tables control network routing within a VPC, unrelated to organizational account grouping.

scenario: A data engineering team stores sensitive data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The security team requires that all data be encrypted at rest using a customer-managed KMS key. The team wants to enable encryption with minimal changes to the application code. Which approach enables encryption at rest with a customer-managed key?
correct_answer: Enable DynamoDB encryption at rest and specify a customer-managed KMS key in the table settings
wrong_answer_1: Encrypt data in the application before writing to DynamoDB
wrong_answer_2: Use DynamoDB Streams to encrypt data as it is written
wrong_answer_3: Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery
correct_explanation: DynamoDB supports encryption at rest using AWS KMS. You can enable encryption when creating a table or update an existing table to use a customer-managed KMS key. DynamoDB automatically encrypts and decrypts data using the specified key, requiring no changes to application code.
wrong_explanation_1: Encrypting data in the application before writing to DynamoDB (client-side encryption) provides encryption at rest, but it requires significant changes to application code to handle encryption and decryption. DynamoDB's native encryption at rest is simpler and requires no code changes.
wrong_explanation_2: DynamoDB Streams capture changes to items in a table for processing by downstream applications. Streams do not encrypt data at rest in the table itself.
wrong_explanation_3: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery enables continuous backups for disaster recovery. It does not encrypt data at rest in the table. Encryption at rest must be enabled separately.

scenario: A company uses Amazon Aurora MySQL for its production database. The database must be available across multiple AWS Regions for disaster recovery, with an RPO of under 1 minute and an RTO of under 1 minute. Which Aurora feature meets these requirements?
correct_answer: Enable Aurora Global Database, which replicates data to a secondary region with typical replication lag under 1 second and supports managed failover in under 1 minute.
wrong_answer_1: Create an Aurora cross-region read replica and promote it manually if the primary region fails.
wrong_answer_2: Use AWS Database Migration Service to continuously replicate the Aurora database to a second region.
wrong_answer_3: Enable Aurora Multi-AZ and configure automated backups with cross-region copy.
correct_explanation: Aurora Global Database uses dedicated replication infrastructure to replicate data from the primary region to up to five secondary regions with typical lag under 1 second. In the event of a regional failure, a secondary region can be promoted to primary in under 1 minute using managed planned or unplanned failover, meeting both the RPO and RTO requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Aurora cross-region read replicas use Aurora's standard replication, which has higher replication lag than Global Database. Promotion is also a manual process that requires application reconfiguration, making it difficult to achieve a sub-1-minute RTO.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS DMS is designed for database migration, not for ongoing low-latency replication as a DR solution. It introduces additional infrastructure complexity and does not provide the sub-second replication lag or managed failover capabilities of Aurora Global Database.
wrong_explanation_3: Aurora Multi-AZ provides high availability within a single region, not across regions. Cross-region backup copies provide data durability but require restoring a new cluster from backup, which takes significantly longer than 1 minute.

scenario: Which AWS-designed silicon is optimized for low-cost, high-performance INFERENCE of large ML models?
correct_answer: AWS Inferentia (Inf1/Inf2 instances)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trainium (Trn1 instances)
wrong_answer_2: AWS Graviton
wrong_answer_3: AWS Nitro
correct_explanation: AWS Inferentia is custom AWS silicon optimized for ML inference. Inf1 and Inf2 instances offer competitive price-performance for inference workloads compared to GPU instances.
wrong_explanation_1: Trainium is optimized for TRAINING, not inference. Trn1 instances target training workloads.
wrong_explanation_2: Graviton is general-purpose ARM-based AWS silicon, not specifically optimized for ML inference.
wrong_explanation_3: Nitro is the AWS hypervisor and hardware platform; it is not an ML accelerator.

scenario: A data engineering team runs an Amazon EMR cluster to process large datasets. The cluster runs batch jobs overnight and sits idle during the day. The team wants to automatically terminate the cluster after all jobs complete to reduce costs. Which EMR feature should they enable?
correct_answer: Auto-termination with an idle timeout
wrong_answer_1: EMR Managed Scaling
wrong_answer_2: Spot Instance allocation strategy
wrong_answer_3: EMR cluster cloning
correct_explanation: EMR auto-termination automatically terminates a cluster after it has been idle for a specified period. You can configure an idle timeout (e.g., 1 hour), and EMR will terminate the cluster if no jobs are running and no new jobs are submitted within that time. This reduces costs by ensuring clusters do not run unnecessarily.
wrong_explanation_1: EMR Managed Scaling automatically adds or removes instances based on workload, but it does not terminate the entire cluster. The cluster continues to run with a minimum number of instances, incurring costs even when idle.
wrong_explanation_2: Spot Instance allocation strategy optimizes the use of Spot Instances to reduce costs, but it does not terminate the cluster when idle. Spot Instances can reduce per-hour costs but do not eliminate costs when the cluster is not processing jobs.
wrong_explanation_3: EMR cluster cloning creates a copy of an existing cluster configuration for launching new clusters. It does not automatically terminate clusters or reduce costs for idle clusters.

scenario: A developer is using AWS SAM to deploy a serverless application and needs to embed a nested application from the AWS Serverless Application Repository into the SAM template. Which SAM resource type should the developer use?
correct_answer: AWS::Serverless::Application
wrong_answer_1: AWS::Serverless::Function
wrong_answer_2: AWS::Serverless::LayerVersion
wrong_answer_3: AWS::Serverless::Api
correct_explanation: AWS::Serverless::Application is the SAM resource type used to embed a nested application from the AWS Serverless Application Repository or from an S3 bucket. It allows serverless applications to be composed of reusable components defined as separate applications.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS::Serverless::Function defines a Lambda function and its event sources. It is used to declare individual functions, not to embed entire nested applications from the Serverless Application Repository.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS::Serverless::LayerVersion defines a Lambda Layer containing shared libraries or runtime dependencies. It is used to package reusable code, not to embed nested applications.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS::Serverless::Api defines an API Gateway REST API resource. It is used for advanced API configuration scenarios, not for embedding nested applications.

scenario: An ML platform team wants to store computed features so they can be reused across multiple model training jobs and also retrieved with low latency during real-time inference. The team needs to ensure that the same feature values used during training are available at inference time to prevent training-serving skew. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this requirement?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
wrong_answer_1: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Aurora
wrong_answer_3: Amazon S3 with a metadata catalog
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store provides both an online store for low-latency real-time feature retrieval and an offline store backed by S3 for training. Features are written once and read from both stores, ensuring that training and inference use identical feature values — directly preventing training-serving skew.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides low-latency key-value lookups but has no offline store for training, no feature versioning, and no native SageMaker integration. Replicating features between a Redis cache and an S3 training store would require custom engineering to maintain consistency.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon Aurora is a managed relational database optimized for transactional workloads. It can serve low-latency reads but does not provide an offline training store, feature versioning, or built-in SageMaker integration for preventing training-serving skew.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon S3 with a metadata catalog can store feature data for training but does not provide the sub-millisecond online serving latency required for real-time inference. A separate serving layer would be needed, reintroducing the risk of training-serving skew.

scenario: A healthcare company needs to transfer 200 TB of historical patient records from an on-premises NAS to Amazon S3 to build a training dataset. The on-premises environment has a 1 Gbps internet connection, and the transfer must complete within 5 days. The data is sensitive and must be encrypted in transit. Which AWS service is the most appropriate for this transfer?
correct_answer: AWS Snowball Edge
wrong_answer_1: AWS DataSync over the internet
wrong_answer_2: S3 Transfer Acceleration
wrong_answer_3: AWS Direct Connect
correct_explanation: At 200 TB over a 1 Gbps connection, a network transfer would take approximately 18+ days at full utilization — well beyond the 5-day window. AWS Snowball Edge is a physical data transfer device that can move petabyte-scale data offline. It encrypts data at rest and in transit, and AWS ships it directly to the destination region, meeting both the timeline and security requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS DataSync over a 1 Gbps internet connection cannot transfer 200 TB within 5 days. At theoretical maximum throughput, 200 TB would take over 18 days, making this option infeasible for the given timeline.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload speeds by routing through CloudFront edge locations, but it still relies on the existing internet connection. It cannot overcome the fundamental bandwidth constraint of a 1 Gbps link for 200 TB in 5 days.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated network connection but takes weeks to provision. It would not be available within the 5-day transfer window and is more appropriate for ongoing connectivity rather than a one-time bulk migration.

scenario: A company deployed a SageMaker endpoint 6 months ago. The team wants to establish a baseline of the model's current prediction behavior and then continuously compare future predictions against this baseline to detect when the model's output distribution shifts. Which SageMaker Model Monitor capability supports this?
correct_answer: Model quality monitoring with a baseline created from captured predictions
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker Clarify bias detection with a pre-training baseline
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Debugger with a custom rule comparing output tensors
wrong_answer_3: Amazon CloudWatch anomaly detection on the endpoint invocation count metric
correct_explanation: SageMaker Model Monitor's model quality monitoring can create a baseline from captured predictions and ground truth labels, then continuously compare future predictions against this baseline to detect shifts in output distribution. This enables detection of model degradation over time.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Clarify bias detection analyzes a static dataset for bias metrics before or after training. It does not continuously monitor live prediction distributions against a baseline on a deployed endpoint.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Debugger monitors tensor values during training jobs, not prediction distributions on deployed endpoints. It cannot compare live inference outputs against a historical baseline.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudWatch anomaly detection on invocation count detects unusual traffic patterns (e.g., sudden spikes or drops in request volume). It does not analyze the content or distribution of model predictions.

scenario: Which AWS-hosted embedding model is commonly used to convert text into vectors for RAG pipelines on Amazon Bedrock?
correct_answer: Amazon Titan Embeddings
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Polly
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Transcribe
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Comprehend Medical
correct_explanation: Amazon Titan Embeddings (available on Bedrock) produce vector embeddings for text, used for semantic search and RAG. Bedrock also exposes other embedding model options from providers like Cohere.
wrong_explanation_1: Polly is text-to-speech, not an embedding model.
wrong_explanation_2: Transcribe is speech-to-text, not an embedding model.
