wrong_explanation_3: Comprehend Medical extracts medical entities from clinical text; it is not an embedding model for general RAG.

scenario: A data engineering team stores datasets in Amazon S3 across multiple formats and partitions. They want to enable SQL queries against this data using Amazon Athena and AWS Glue ETL jobs without manually defining table schemas. Which AWS service should they use to automatically discover schemas and register tables?
correct_answer: AWS Glue Crawler
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Athena schema inference
wrong_answer_2: AWS Lake Formation table import
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Redshift Spectrum external tables
correct_explanation: AWS Glue Crawlers scan S3 data sources, infer schemas from the data format (CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC), detect partitions, and automatically register tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Both Athena and Glue ETL jobs use the Data Catalog as their metadata source, enabling immediate querying without manual schema definition.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Athena can infer schemas for some formats when creating tables manually, but it does not automatically crawl S3 and register tables in the Glue Data Catalog. Schema discovery and registration require a Glue Crawler.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Lake Formation manages access control and governance for data lakes but does not automatically discover schemas or crawl S3 data. It relies on the Glue Data Catalog (populated by Glue Crawlers) for table metadata.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data through external tables defined in the Glue Data Catalog, but it does not automatically discover or register schemas. It requires tables to already exist in the catalog.

scenario: In an AWS Organization, which statement BEST describes the relationship between the management account and member accounts?
correct_answer: The management account pays the consolidated bill and can apply SCPs to member accounts; member accounts are individual AWS accounts joined to the Organization
wrong_answer_1: The management account is a member account elected by AWS Support each year
wrong_answer_2: Member accounts can act as the billing payer for the management account
wrong_answer_3: Management and member accounts share a single IAM identity store automatically
correct_explanation: The management account (formerly "master account") creates the Organization, receives the consolidated bill, and can attach service control policies. Member accounts are otherwise independent AWS accounts that have joined the Organization.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Support does not elect a new management account annually. The management account is set when the Organization is created.
wrong_explanation_2: Member accounts cannot bill on behalf of the management account; billing flows from members to the management account.
wrong_explanation_3: Each AWS account has its own IAM identity store by default. IAM Identity Center can provide cross-account SSO, but this is configured, not automatic.

scenario: A Lambda function is experiencing high cold start latency because it loads a 50 MB machine learning model from S3 during initialization. The function is invoked thousands of times per day with bursts of concurrent requests. The team wants to eliminate cold start latency for this function. Which solution is MOST effective?
correct_answer: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to pre-initialize execution environments with the model already loaded.
wrong_answer_1: Move the model loading code inside the handler function so it only runs when needed.
wrong_answer_2: Schedule a CloudWatch Events rule to invoke the function every 5 minutes to keep it warm.
wrong_answer_3: Increase the function's memory to 10 GB to speed up the S3 model download during cold starts.
correct_explanation: Provisioned Concurrency pre-initializes a specified number of execution environments and runs the initialization code (including the S3 model download) before any invocations arrive. Pre-initialized environments respond immediately with no cold start. This is the only mechanism that guarantees zero cold start latency for the configured concurrency level.
wrong_explanation_1: Moving model loading inside the handler means the model is loaded on every invocation, not just cold starts. This dramatically increases per-invocation latency and defeats the purpose of caching the model in the global scope. The correct pattern is to load the model in the global scope so it is cached across warm invocations.
wrong_explanation_2: Periodic invocations keep a small number of execution environments warm but cannot guarantee coverage during burst traffic. When Lambda scales out to handle concurrent requests, new cold environments are created regardless of the warming invocations. Provisioned Concurrency is the reliable solution.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing memory increases CPU allocation proportionally, which speeds up compute-bound operations. However, the S3 model download is network I/O bound — more CPU does not significantly reduce download time. Provisioned Concurrency eliminates the download entirely for pre-warmed environments.

scenario: A data engineering team wants to automatically start an AWS Glue ETL job every day at 3 AM UTC. The job should run regardless of whether previous runs succeeded or failed. Which AWS service should be used to schedule the job?
correct_answer: AWS Glue triggers with a time-based schedule
wrong_answer_1: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
wrong_answer_2: AWS Lambda with a CloudWatch Events rule
wrong_answer_3: AWS Step Functions with a scheduled execution
correct_explanation: AWS Glue triggers support time-based schedules using cron expressions. A scheduled trigger can start a Glue job at a specific time every day. This is the native, integrated way to schedule Glue jobs without requiring external services.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler can trigger Glue jobs on a schedule, but using Glue's native scheduled triggers is simpler and more direct. EventBridge Scheduler is more appropriate when you need advanced scheduling features or need to trigger non-Glue resources.
wrong_explanation_2: Using Lambda with CloudWatch Events to start a Glue job adds unnecessary complexity and an additional service layer. Glue's native scheduled triggers provide the same functionality without requiring Lambda functions.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Step Functions can schedule workflow executions, but for a simple single-job schedule, Glue's native triggers are more appropriate. Step Functions is better suited for orchestrating multi-step workflows with dependencies.

scenario: A Lambda function retrieves a database password from AWS Secrets Manager at startup and stores it in a module-level variable for reuse across warm invocations. The security team is concerned that the cached password will not reflect rotations. What is the MOST appropriate way to handle this?
correct_answer: Implement a TTL-based refresh: cache the secret with a timestamp and re-fetch from Secrets Manager when the cached value is older than a defined threshold (e.g., 5 minutes).
wrong_answer_1: Retrieve the secret inside the Lambda handler on every invocation to always get the latest value.
wrong_answer_2: Disable Secrets Manager automatic rotation so the cached value never becomes stale.
wrong_answer_3: Store the secret in a Lambda environment variable and update it manually after each rotation.
correct_explanation: Caching the secret with a TTL-based refresh balances performance (avoiding a Secrets Manager API call on every invocation) with freshness (re-fetching after the TTL expires). The AWS Secrets Manager documentation recommends this pattern. A 5-minute TTL means the function will use a rotated secret within 5 minutes of rotation without adding per-invocation latency.
wrong_explanation_1: Retrieving the secret on every invocation guarantees freshness but adds a Secrets Manager API call (and its latency) to every Lambda execution. For high-throughput functions, this adds cost and latency unnecessarily. TTL-based caching is the recommended balance.
wrong_explanation_2: Disabling automatic rotation eliminates the staleness problem by preventing rotation, but it defeats the purpose of using Secrets Manager for credential security. Credentials that are never rotated are a security risk — the correct solution is to handle rotation gracefully, not to disable it.
wrong_explanation_3: Lambda environment variables are visible in the function configuration and require a function update (new version) to change. Storing a rotated secret in an environment variable requires manual intervention after every rotation, which is operationally error-prone and not automated.

scenario: A data scientist has trained a binary classification model to detect fraudulent transactions. The business requirement is to catch as many fraudulent transactions as possible, even if it means some legitimate transactions are incorrectly flagged. Which evaluation metric should the data scientist prioritize when selecting the final model?
correct_answer: Recall (Sensitivity)
wrong_answer_1: Precision
wrong_answer_2: Accuracy
wrong_answer_3: Specificity
correct_explanation: Recall (also called sensitivity or true positive rate) measures the proportion of actual fraudulent transactions that the model correctly identifies. When the business priority is to minimize missed fraud (false negatives), recall is the primary metric to optimize — even at the cost of more false positives (legitimate transactions flagged as fraud).
wrong_explanation_1: Precision measures the proportion of transactions flagged as fraud that are actually fraudulent. Optimizing for precision minimizes false positives but allows more actual fraud to go undetected (false negatives), which is the opposite of the business requirement.
wrong_explanation_2: Accuracy measures the overall proportion of correct predictions. For imbalanced fraud datasets (e.g., 1% fraud rate), a model that predicts 'legitimate' for every transaction achieves 99% accuracy while catching zero fraud. Accuracy is a misleading metric for imbalanced classification problems.
wrong_explanation_3: Specificity measures the proportion of legitimate transactions correctly identified as legitimate (true negative rate). Optimizing for specificity reduces false positives but does not address the requirement to maximize fraud detection.

scenario: A data scientist is preparing a training dataset and discovers that a numeric feature has 12% missing values. Analysis shows that the missingness is correlated with the target variable — records with missing values tend to have higher churn rates. Which imputation strategy is most appropriate?
correct_answer: Add a binary indicator feature for missingness, then impute the missing values with the median
wrong_answer_1: Drop all rows with missing values in this feature
wrong_answer_2: Impute missing values with the mean and proceed without any indicator feature
wrong_answer_3: Impute missing values with the most frequent value (mode)
correct_explanation: When missingness is correlated with the target variable (missing not at random), the fact that a value is missing is itself informative. Adding a binary indicator feature preserves this signal for the model. Imputing with the median fills in a reasonable value for the feature itself while the indicator captures the missingness pattern.
wrong_explanation_1: Dropping rows with missing values would remove 12% of the training data and, more critically, would discard the informative signal that missingness correlates with higher churn. This would introduce bias by systematically removing high-churn records.
wrong_explanation_2: Imputing with the mean without an indicator feature discards the information that missingness is correlated with the target. The model would have no way to learn from the missingness pattern, losing predictive signal.
wrong_explanation_3: Imputing with the mode (most frequent value) is appropriate for categorical features, not numeric ones. For a numeric feature, the mode may not represent a statistically sound central tendency, and it still does not capture the informative missingness signal.

scenario: A data engineer is writing an AWS Glue PySpark job that reads a 10 TB dataset from Amazon S3, filters rows based on a date column, and writes the filtered results back to S3. The job is running out of memory and failing. Profiling shows that the entire dataset is being loaded into memory before the filter is applied. Which PySpark optimization should the engineer apply?
correct_answer: Use predicate pushdown by applying the filter before reading the data using a WHERE clause in the DynamicFrame or DataFrame read operation
wrong_answer_1: Increase the number of Glue DPUs allocated to the job
wrong_answer_2: Repartition the DataFrame after reading to distribute data across more executors
wrong_answer_3: Enable Glue job bookmarks to process data incrementally
correct_explanation: Predicate pushdown applies filters at the data source level before loading data into memory. For Parquet files in S3, Spark can read only the partitions and row groups that match the filter condition, dramatically reducing the amount of data loaded into memory. This is the most effective optimization for this scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: Increasing Glue DPUs adds more memory and compute capacity, which may allow the job to complete, but it does not address the root cause — loading 10 TB into memory unnecessarily. Predicate pushdown is a more efficient and cost-effective solution.
wrong_explanation_2: Repartitioning after reading redistributes data across executors but does not reduce the amount of data loaded from S3. The entire 10 TB would still be read into memory before repartitioning, causing the same out-of-memory issue.
wrong_explanation_3: Glue job bookmarks track which data has been processed to avoid reprocessing in subsequent runs. They do not reduce memory usage within a single job run or apply filters before loading data.

scenario: A developer is using AWS CodeDeploy to deploy a new version of a Lambda function. The deployment should shift 10% of traffic to the new version immediately, then shift an additional 10% every minute until all traffic is on the new version. Which deployment configuration should the developer use?
correct_answer: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute
wrong_answer_1: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes
wrong_answer_2: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce
wrong_answer_3: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery2Minutes
correct_explanation: Linear deployment configurations shift traffic in equal increments at regular intervals. LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute shifts 10% of traffic to the new version every minute, completing the full migration in 10 minutes. This matches the requirement of equal increments at 1-minute intervals.
wrong_explanation_1: LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% of traffic immediately, then shifts the remaining 90% all at once after 10 minutes. This is a two-increment canary pattern, not the gradual equal-increment linear pattern described in the requirement.
wrong_explanation_2: LambdaAllAtOnce shifts 100% of traffic to the new version immediately in a single step. It does not provide the gradual incremental shifting described in the requirement.
wrong_explanation_3: LambdaLinear10PercentEvery2Minutes shifts 10% every 2 minutes, completing the migration in 20 minutes. The requirement specifies 1-minute intervals, so this configuration takes twice as long as needed.

scenario: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between identity-based policies and resource-based policies?
correct_answer: Identity-based policies attach to IAM users, groups, or roles; resource-based policies attach directly to a resource such as an S3 bucket or KMS key
wrong_answer_1: Identity-based policies are always inline; resource-based policies are always managed
wrong_answer_2: Resource-based policies apply only to global services like IAM and Route 53
wrong_answer_3: Identity-based policies grant cross-account access automatically; resource-based policies cannot
correct_explanation: Identity-based policies attach to IAM principals (users, groups, roles) and define what those principals can do. Resource-based policies attach directly to a resource (e.g., S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy) and define who can do what to that specific resource — including principals from other AWS accounts.
wrong_explanation_1: Identity-based policies can be inline or managed; resource-based policies can also be considered standalone configurations on resources. The inline-vs-managed distinction is a separate concept.
wrong_explanation_2: Resource-based policies apply to many specific resources (S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues, etc.), not only global services.
wrong_explanation_3: Cross-account access is most often achieved through resource-based policies combined with identity-based policies — not solely identity-based policies.

scenario: A compliance officer wants to continuously assess the company's own AWS usage against frameworks such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and NIST 800-53, generating audit-ready evidence packs. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS Audit Manager
wrong_answer_1: AWS Artifact
wrong_answer_2: AWS Trusted Advisor
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Inspector
correct_explanation: AWS Audit Manager continuously collects evidence from a customer's AWS environment, maps it to controls in frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST, etc.), and produces audit-ready evidence reports. It supports ongoing self-assessment of the customer's own usage.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Artifact provides downloadable third-party reports about AWS's own compliance (e.g., AWS's SOC 2). It does not assess the customer's own configuration.
wrong_explanation_2: Trusted Advisor offers best-practice recommendations but is not designed to produce framework-mapped audit evidence.
wrong_explanation_3: Inspector finds vulnerabilities in workloads. It does not generate framework-mapped audit evidence packs.

scenario: A data scientist is using Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to prepare a dataset for a recommendation model. The dataset contains a user_id column and an item_id column, both of which are high-cardinality integer identifiers. The scientist wants to create an embedding-ready representation of these IDs. Which transformation should be applied?
correct_answer: Encode the IDs as categorical features using ordinal encoding to produce contiguous integer indices
wrong_answer_1: Normalize the ID columns using min-max scaling
wrong_answer_2: Apply one-hot encoding to both ID columns
wrong_answer_3: Drop both ID columns as they are not informative features
correct_explanation: Embedding layers in neural networks require contiguous integer indices starting from 0. Ordinal encoding maps each unique ID to a contiguous integer, producing the correct input format for an embedding lookup table. This is the standard preprocessing step before passing categorical IDs into an embedding layer.
wrong_explanation_1: Min-max scaling treats the IDs as continuous numeric values, which is incorrect. User and item IDs are nominal identifiers — their numeric magnitude has no meaning, and scaling them would not produce a valid input for an embedding layer.
wrong_explanation_2: One-hot encoding would create millions of sparse binary columns for high-cardinality ID columns, making the dataset computationally intractable. Embedding layers are specifically designed to replace one-hot encoding for high-cardinality categoricals.
wrong_explanation_3: User and item IDs are the primary identifiers in a recommendation model — they are the entities being modeled. Dropping them would remove the core information needed to learn user-item interaction patterns.

scenario: Which deployment design provides the HIGHEST fault tolerance within a single AWS Region?
correct_answer: Deploying redundant resources across multiple Availability Zones
wrong_answer_1: Deploying redundant resources across multiple subnets in a single AZ
wrong_answer_2: Deploying a single very large EC2 instance in a placement group
wrong_answer_3: Deploying resources only at edge locations
correct_explanation: Each AZ is an isolated set of data centers. Deploying redundantly across multiple AZs in the same Region provides the highest intra-Region fault tolerance — a single AZ failure cannot take down the workload.
wrong_explanation_1: Multiple subnets in the same AZ all share that AZ's fate. If the AZ fails, all those subnets go down.
wrong_explanation_2: A single large instance in a placement group is still a single instance; if it fails, the workload fails.
wrong_explanation_3: Edge locations are not deployment targets for customer applications.

scenario: A developer is optimizing a Lambda function that processes S3 events. The function initializes a large configuration object by reading from Parameter Store on every invocation, adding 500ms of latency. The configuration rarely changes. What is the MOST effective optimization to reduce this latency?
correct_answer: Move the Parameter Store initialization code outside the Lambda handler function into the global scope, so it executes once during the cold start and is reused across warm invocations.
wrong_answer_1: Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to eliminate cold starts and reduce initialization latency.
wrong_answer_2: Increase the Lambda function's memory to speed up the Parameter Store API call.
wrong_answer_3: Cache the configuration in an ElastiCache cluster and have the Lambda function read from ElastiCache instead.
correct_explanation: Lambda execution environments are reused across multiple invocations (warm invocations). Code in the global scope (outside the handler) executes only once during the cold start and the result is available to all subsequent warm invocations. Moving the Parameter Store call to the global scope means the 500ms initialization happens only on cold starts, not on every invocation.
wrong_explanation_1: Provisioned Concurrency pre-warms execution environments, eliminating cold start latency for those environments. However, if the Parameter Store call is inside the handler, it still executes on every invocation — warm or cold. The optimization must be moving the call to the global scope, not just eliminating cold starts.
wrong_explanation_2: Lambda memory allocation increases CPU proportionally, which speeds up compute-bound operations. A Parameter Store API call is network I/O bound — more CPU does not significantly reduce the time spent waiting for the API response.
wrong_explanation_3: Adding ElastiCache introduces additional infrastructure, cost, and network latency for a Lambda function that may not be in a VPC. The global scope initialization pattern achieves in-process caching with zero additional infrastructure and is the simpler, more appropriate solution for this use case.

scenario: A developer has deployed a Lambda function that needs to read from an SQS queue and write results to a DynamoDB table. When testing, the function receives an AccessDeniedException when calling DynamoDB. The function's execution role has an SQS read policy attached. What should the developer do to fix this?
correct_answer: Attach an IAM policy granting the required DynamoDB actions (such as dynamodb:PutItem) to the Lambda function's execution role.
wrong_answer_1: Add the Lambda function's ARN to the DynamoDB table's resource-based policy.
wrong_answer_2: Create a new IAM user with DynamoDB permissions and store its access keys in the Lambda environment variables.
wrong_answer_3: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table to allow Lambda to write to it.
correct_explanation: Lambda functions access AWS services using the permissions granted to their execution role. Since the execution role only has SQS permissions, DynamoDB calls fail with AccessDeniedException. Attaching a policy with the required DynamoDB actions (e.g., dynamodb:PutItem) to the execution role grants the function the necessary permissions.
wrong_explanation_1: DynamoDB does not support resource-based policies in the same way S3 or SQS does. Access to DynamoDB is controlled through IAM identity-based policies attached to the calling principal's role, not through table-level resource policies.
wrong_explanation_2: Storing IAM user access keys in Lambda environment variables introduces long-term credentials into the function's configuration, which is a security anti-pattern. Lambda execution roles provide temporary, automatically rotated credentials that are the correct mechanism for granting AWS service access.
wrong_explanation_3: DynamoDB Streams is a feature that captures item-level changes for downstream processing. Enabling Streams does not grant write permissions to any principal — it is a data capture feature, not an access control mechanism.

scenario: A machine learning engineer is building a model to predict equipment failure. The training dataset contains sensor readings collected every second over 12 months. The engineer wants to create lag features (e.g., sensor value 1 minute ago, 5 minutes ago) and rolling statistics (e.g., 10-minute rolling mean and standard deviation) to capture temporal patterns. Which AWS service provides built-in support for these time-series feature engineering operations?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
wrong_answer_2: AWS Glue Studio
wrong_answer_3: Amazon QuickSight
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler includes built-in transforms for time-series feature engineering, including lag features and rolling window statistics (mean, standard deviation, min, max). These transforms can be applied visually without writing code and exported as reusable processing steps in a SageMaker Pipeline.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics (now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink) processes streaming data in real time. While it can compute rolling statistics on live streams, it is not designed for batch feature engineering on historical training datasets stored in S3.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Glue Studio is a visual ETL authoring tool for building data transformation jobs. It does not include built-in ML-specific time-series feature engineering transforms like lag features and rolling statistics.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence and data visualization service. It can display time-series charts but does not perform feature engineering or produce transformed datasets for ML training.

scenario: A CodeBuild project is failing with an error during the Docker image build phase. The error message indicates that the build environment cannot connect to the internet to pull base images from Docker Hub. The CodeBuild project is configured to run in a VPC. What is the MOST likely cause?
correct_answer: The CodeBuild project's VPC configuration places it in a private subnet with no NAT Gateway, preventing outbound internet access to Docker Hub.
wrong_answer_1: The CodeBuild service role does not have permission to pull images from Docker Hub.
wrong_answer_2: Docker Hub is blocked by an AWS WAF rule on the CodeBuild project.
wrong_answer_3: The CodeBuild project needs an Elastic IP address to access Docker Hub.
correct_explanation: When CodeBuild runs in a VPC, it loses its default internet access. To pull base images from Docker Hub (or any internet resource), the build environment must be in a private subnet with a route to a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Without a NAT Gateway, outbound internet connections time out.
wrong_explanation_1: Docker Hub is a public registry that does not use AWS IAM for authentication. The CodeBuild service role controls access to AWS services, not to external internet resources like Docker Hub. Internet connectivity, not IAM permissions, is the issue.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS WAF is applied to API Gateway, ALB, CloudFront, and AppSync — not to CodeBuild build environments. WAF cannot block outbound connections from a CodeBuild build environment.
wrong_explanation_3: Elastic IP addresses are assigned to EC2 instances and NAT Gateways to provide static public IP addresses. CodeBuild build environments do not support direct Elastic IP assignment. Internet access from a VPC-attached CodeBuild project requires a NAT Gateway, not an Elastic IP on the build environment itself.

scenario: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for ensuring that a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI) the customer builds is patched and free of vulnerabilities before it is launched?
correct_answer: The customer
wrong_answer_1: AWS
wrong_answer_2: AWS Marketplace
wrong_answer_3: Shared between AWS and the customer
correct_explanation: Custom AMIs are customer artifacts. The customer is responsible for the OS image's patch level, embedded software, and configurations. AWS provides the EC2 service and base AMIs, but custom AMIs are entirely customer-managed.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS is not responsible for customer-built AMIs. AWS-managed AMIs (like Amazon Linux) are maintained by AWS, but customer images are not.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Marketplace publishes vendor AMIs; the vendor maintains those. Customer-built AMIs are the customer's responsibility.
wrong_explanation_3: Custom AMIs are entirely the customer's responsibility, not shared.

scenario: A data engineering team uses AWS Lake Formation to manage access to their data lake. They want to grant a data analyst access to a table but only to rows where the 'region' column equals 'us-east-1'. The analyst should not be able to see rows from other regions. Which Lake Formation feature enables this row-level access control?
correct_answer: Lake Formation data filters with row-level security
wrong_answer_1: IAM policies with condition keys
wrong_answer_2: S3 bucket policies with prefix-based access
wrong_answer_3: Glue Data Catalog resource policies
correct_explanation: AWS Lake Formation data filters support row-level security by allowing you to define filter expressions that restrict which rows a user can access. You can create a data filter that grants access only to rows where region='us-east-1', and Lake Formation enforces this filter when the analyst queries the table.
wrong_explanation_1: IAM policies with condition keys control access to AWS service APIs based on request context, but they do not provide row-level filtering within tables. Lake Formation data filters are required for row-level security.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 bucket policies control access to S3 objects based on prefixes, but they operate at the file level, not the row level. They cannot filter rows within a table based on column values.
wrong_explanation_3: Glue Data Catalog resource policies control who can access catalog resources like databases and tables, but they do not provide row-level filtering. Lake Formation data filters are required for row-level security.

scenario: A company is designing a microservices architecture on Amazon ECS. Services need to discover and communicate with each other dynamically as tasks scale up and down. The solution must not require hardcoded IP addresses or manual DNS updates. Which service should the solutions architect use for service discovery?
correct_answer: Use AWS Cloud Map with Amazon ECS Service Discovery to automatically register and deregister task endpoints as they scale.
wrong_answer_1: Use an Application Load Balancer for each service and hardcode the ALB DNS names in each service's configuration.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones and manually update DNS records when ECS tasks scale.
wrong_answer_3: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store the IP addresses of ECS tasks and have services look up addresses at startup.
correct_explanation: AWS Cloud Map integrates natively with Amazon ECS to provide automatic service discovery. When ECS tasks start or stop, Cloud Map automatically registers or deregisters their endpoints in a service registry. Other services can discover endpoints via DNS or API calls without any manual configuration or hardcoded addresses.
wrong_explanation_1: Using ALB DNS names for service-to-service communication adds unnecessary latency and cost for internal traffic. ALBs are designed for external or cross-tier traffic, not for direct microservice-to-microservice communication within a cluster.
wrong_explanation_2: Manually updating Route 53 records when tasks scale defeats the purpose of dynamic service discovery. In an auto-scaling environment, tasks can start and stop frequently, making manual DNS management operationally infeasible.
wrong_explanation_3: Storing IP addresses in Parameter Store requires tasks to look up addresses at startup, but those addresses may change as tasks are replaced. There is no automatic update mechanism, so services would quickly have stale endpoint information.

scenario: An application uses Amazon DynamoDB. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for controlling which IAM principals can read or write to the DynamoDB tables?
correct_answer: The customer
wrong_answer_1: AWS
wrong_answer_2: AWS Support
wrong_answer_3: DynamoDB's internal service team
correct_explanation: Although DynamoDB is fully managed, access control to customer data is the customer's responsibility. The customer configures IAM policies that grant or deny principals access to specific tables, items, and operations.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS operates the DynamoDB service but does not decide which principals may access customer data.
wrong_explanation_2: Support helps with operational issues but does not configure customer authorization policies.
wrong_explanation_3: Internal AWS service teams do not configure customer-side IAM policies.

scenario: An offline analytics workflow needs to score 200 million records once a week, without immediate response requirements. Which inference mode is MOST appropriate?
correct_answer: Batch inference (SageMaker Batch Transform)
wrong_answer_1: Real-time inference endpoint
wrong_answer_2: Serverless inference
wrong_answer_3: Edge inference on AWS Snowcone
correct_explanation: Batch inference (SageMaker Batch Transform) is designed to score very large datasets offline with no real-time latency requirement. Once-a-week scoring of 200 million records is the canonical batch use case.
wrong_explanation_1: Real-time endpoints are for live, low-latency requests and are not cost-optimal for once-weekly bulk scoring.
wrong_explanation_2: Serverless inference is intended for intermittent low-latency traffic, not for very large batch scoring jobs.
wrong_explanation_3: Snowcone is a portable edge appliance, unrelated to large-scale cloud batch scoring.

scenario: A company wants to protect its web application hosted behind an Application Load Balancer from common web exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. The solution must be managed, require minimal configuration, and provide visibility into blocked requests. Which AWS service should the solutions architect recommend?
correct_answer: AWS WAF with managed rule groups attached to the Application Load Balancer.
wrong_answer_1: Amazon GuardDuty enabled on the AWS account to detect malicious activity.
wrong_answer_2: AWS Shield Standard, which is automatically applied to all ALBs.
wrong_answer_3: VPC security groups with rules that block known malicious IP ranges.
correct_explanation: AWS WAF integrates directly with Application Load Balancers and provides managed rule groups (including the AWS Managed Rules for common threats like SQL injection and XSS) that require minimal configuration. WAF also provides detailed logs and metrics for blocked requests, satisfying the visibility requirement.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs to identify suspicious account-level activity. It does not inspect HTTP request payloads or block web application attacks at the ALB level.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Shield Standard provides protection against DDoS attacks at the network and transport layers. It does not inspect application-layer HTTP traffic for SQL injection or XSS patterns.
wrong_explanation_3: Security group rules operate at the IP/port level and cannot inspect HTTP request content. They cannot detect or block application-layer attacks like SQL injection or XSS regardless of how many IP ranges are blocked.

scenario: A team wants to orchestrate steps in their ML workflow — data processing, training, evaluation, conditional approval, and deployment — as a repeatable, version-controlled pipeline inside SageMaker. Which feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
wrong_answer_3: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
correct_explanation: SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML workflow steps (processing, training, evaluation, model registration, deployment) as a Directed Acyclic Graph with built-in conditional logic, lineage tracking, and integration with CodePipeline.
wrong_explanation_1: Studio Lab is a free Jupyter notebook environment; it is not a workflow orchestrator.
wrong_explanation_2: Canvas is a no-code ML builder for tabular data, not a pipeline orchestrator.
wrong_explanation_3: Ground Truth handles data labeling.

scenario: A research team has a small labeled dataset and limited GPU budget. They want to adapt a large pre-trained model to their specific task by updating only a SMALL subset of parameters (such as low-rank matrices) rather than all weights. Which family of techniques does this describe?
correct_answer: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), such as LoRA
wrong_answer_1: Full-parameter fine-tuning
wrong_answer_2: Training a brand-new foundation model
wrong_answer_3: Quantization-aware training
correct_explanation: PEFT methods such as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) update only a small number of new or low-rank parameters while keeping most of the base model frozen. This dramatically reduces compute and memory costs while still adapting the model to the task.
wrong_explanation_1: Full-parameter fine-tuning updates all weights and is very expensive — the opposite of the budget-conscious approach the scenario asks for.
wrong_explanation_2: Training from scratch is even more expensive and unnecessary for adaptation.
wrong_explanation_3: Quantization-aware training prepares a model for low-precision inference; it is not a small-parameter fine-tuning technique.

scenario: A company wants Amazon Bedrock to LOG the full content of each request prompt and each model response to S3 or CloudWatch for compliance review. Which Bedrock feature supports this?
correct_answer: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Bedrock Agents
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Bedrock custom models
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records the prompt and response content (along with metadata) of each invocation to S3, CloudWatch Logs, or both. This is the standard way to capture full content for compliance review.
wrong_explanation_1: Knowledge Bases handle RAG retrieval; they do not provide invocation-level content logging.
wrong_explanation_2: Agents orchestrate tasks; the dedicated logging mechanism is invocation logging.
wrong_explanation_3: Custom models alter the underlying FM; they do not log requests.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes AWS's data privacy policy for content submitted to Amazon Bedrock by customers?
correct_answer: Customer content sent to Bedrock is not used to train the underlying foundation models
wrong_answer_1: All customer prompts are added automatically to model training datasets
wrong_answer_2: AWS uses each customer prompt to fine-tune the model for that customer
wrong_answer_3: AWS shares each customer prompt with other AWS customers for reference
correct_explanation: AWS states that customer data sent to Amazon Bedrock is not used to train the underlying foundation models or shared with third-party providers. Customers retain control of their data and can encrypt it with their own KMS keys.
wrong_explanation_1: Adding prompts to training data is exactly what AWS's Bedrock policy disallows.
wrong_explanation_2: Bedrock does not auto-fine-tune the FM on customer prompts.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS does not share customer prompts across customers.

scenario: A company wants to build a recommendation system to suggest products to users based on their purchase history. The dataset contains user-item interaction data with 500,000 users and 100,000 products. There are no explicit ratings — only implicit feedback (purchases). Which Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithm is most appropriate for this use case?
correct_answer: Factorization Machines
wrong_answer_1: Linear Learner
wrong_answer_2: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
wrong_answer_3: DeepAR
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker's Factorization Machines algorithm is designed for sparse datasets with high-dimensional feature interactions, making it ideal for collaborative filtering recommendation systems. It can model user-item interactions efficiently even with implicit feedback and large-scale sparse matrices.
wrong_explanation_1: Linear Learner is designed for regression and classification tasks on dense feature vectors. It does not model the pairwise interaction structure between users and items that is fundamental to collaborative filtering.
wrong_explanation_2: K-Nearest Neighbors finds similar items based on feature distance, but it does not scale well to 500,000 users and 100,000 products. It also requires dense feature representations and does not natively handle sparse user-item interaction matrices.
wrong_explanation_3: DeepAR is a time-series forecasting algorithm that models temporal sequences. It is not designed for user-item recommendation tasks and cannot model collaborative filtering interactions.

scenario: A customer service chatbot built on Amazon Bedrock occasionally produces offensive or harmful responses. The team wants AWS-provided guardrails to filter inputs and outputs against configurable policies — without writing custom filtering code. Which Bedrock feature should they use?
correct_answer: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Bedrock Agents
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Bedrock model evaluation
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces configurable content policies on user inputs and model outputs — including denied topics, harmful content categories, profanity, sensitive information, and contextual grounding checks — without custom code.
wrong_explanation_1: Knowledge Bases provide retrieval grounding; they do not enforce harmful-content policies.
wrong_explanation_2: Agents orchestrate tasks; they do not filter content.
wrong_explanation_3: Model evaluation compares model quality; it does not act as a runtime filter.

scenario: A company runs long SageMaker training jobs that sometimes fail partway through due to spot instance interruptions. The team wants to reduce training costs by using Spot Instances while ensuring that training can resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch. Which SageMaker feature enables this?
correct_answer: SageMaker Managed Spot Training with checkpoint configuration
wrong_answer_1: SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with early stopping
wrong_answer_2: SageMaker Pipelines with retry policies
wrong_answer_3: SageMaker Processing jobs with Spot Instances
correct_explanation: SageMaker Managed Spot Training uses EC2 Spot Instances to reduce training costs by up to 90%. When configured with a checkpoint S3 path, the training job saves checkpoints periodically. If a Spot Instance is interrupted, SageMaker automatically resumes training from the last checkpoint on a new instance, avoiding full restarts.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with early stopping stops individual training jobs when the validation metric stops improving. It does not use Spot Instances or provide checkpoint-based resumption after interruptions.
wrong_explanation_2: SageMaker Pipelines retry policies can retry a failed pipeline step, but they restart the training job from scratch rather than resuming from a checkpoint. This does not address the cost of restarting long training jobs.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker Processing jobs support Spot Instances for data processing workloads, but they are not designed for model training with checkpoint-based resumption. Managed Spot Training is the feature specifically designed for training job interruption recovery.

scenario: A developer wants a visual canvas to design a serverless application — composing Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB resources by dragging and connecting components — and have AWS generate the CloudFormation/SAM template automatically. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS Application Composer
wrong_answer_1: AWS CodeStar
wrong_answer_2: AWS CloudShell
wrong_answer_3: AWS Cloud9
correct_explanation: AWS Application Composer is a visual builder for serverless applications. Developers drag and connect cards representing AWS services on a canvas, and Application Composer generates a CloudFormation/SAM template that can be deployed directly.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeStar is deprecated for new projects and offered project templates with a single dashboard, not a visual serverless designer.
wrong_explanation_2: CloudShell is a browser-based shell, not a visual application designer.
wrong_explanation_3: Cloud9 is a browser-based IDE for editing code, not a serverless drag-and-drop composition tool.

scenario: A company stores IoT sensor readings in an Amazon S3 data lake partitioned by date. An ML team wants to run ad-hoc SQL queries against this data to explore distributions and identify anomalies before building a training dataset, without loading the data into a separate database. Which AWS service enables this with the least operational overhead?
correct_answer: Amazon Athena
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Redshift Spectrum
wrong_answer_2: Amazon EMR
wrong_answer_3: AWS Glue Studio
correct_explanation: Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that runs SQL directly against data in S3 with no infrastructure to manage. It supports partitioned datasets, charges only per query, and requires no data loading — making it ideal for ad-hoc exploration of S3-resident ML datasets.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Redshift Spectrum can query S3 data but requires an active Redshift cluster, which adds operational overhead and cost compared to the fully serverless Athena for ad-hoc exploration.
wrong_explanation_2: Amazon EMR can run distributed SQL queries via Spark SQL or Hive, but it requires cluster provisioning and management, making it significantly more operationally complex than Athena for ad-hoc queries.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Glue Studio is a visual ETL authoring tool for building data transformation jobs. It is not designed for interactive SQL exploration of S3 data.

scenario: A company processes personal data of EU citizens and must comply with GDPR. When a customer requests deletion of their data, the company must remove all records associated with that customer from their Amazon S3 data lake within 30 days. Which approach best supports this right-to-erasure requirement?
correct_answer: Partition data by customer_id in S3 and delete the customer's partition when a deletion request is received
wrong_answer_1: Enable S3 Object Lock on all customer data to prevent accidental deletion
wrong_answer_2: Use S3 Lifecycle policies to automatically delete all data after 30 days
wrong_answer_3: Store customer data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive to minimize access
correct_explanation: Partitioning data by customer_id in S3 allows targeted deletion of a specific customer's data by deleting their partition prefix. This is the most efficient approach for GDPR right-to-erasure compliance, as it avoids rewriting entire datasets to remove individual records.
wrong_explanation_1: S3 Object Lock prevents deletion of objects for a specified retention period. Enabling Object Lock on customer data would actually prevent compliance with GDPR deletion requests by making the data immutable.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 Lifecycle policies that delete all data after 30 days would delete all customer data, not just the data of customers who requested deletion. This would violate data retention requirements for customers who have not requested deletion.
wrong_explanation_3: Storing data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive reduces access costs but does not address the requirement to delete specific customer data. The data would still exist and would need to be retrieved and deleted to comply with GDPR.

scenario: A company has a Lambda function that needs to read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and write results to an S3 bucket. A security audit finds that the Lambda execution role has AdministratorAccess attached. The solutions architect must remediate this without breaking the function. Which approach should the architect take?
correct_answer: Replace AdministratorAccess with a custom IAM policy that grants only secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the specific secret ARN and s3:PutObject for the specific S3 bucket and prefix.
wrong_answer_1: Replace AdministratorAccess with the AWS managed PowerUserAccess policy, which excludes IAM permissions.
wrong_answer_2: Add an explicit Deny statement to the Lambda execution role for all actions except the ones the function needs.
wrong_answer_3: Move the Lambda function to a VPC and use security groups to restrict what resources it can access.
correct_explanation: The principle of least privilege requires granting only the specific permissions the function needs. A custom policy scoped to the exact secret ARN and S3 bucket/prefix ensures the function can perform its tasks while eliminating all unnecessary permissions. This is the correct remediation for an overly permissive execution role.
wrong_explanation_1: PowerUserAccess grants broad access to most AWS services, excluding only IAM and Organizations management. It is still far more permissive than the two specific actions the Lambda function requires and does not satisfy least privilege.
wrong_explanation_2: Adding explicit Deny statements for everything except needed actions is technically possible but operationally fragile — new AWS services and actions would need to be explicitly denied as they are introduced. It is better practice to start with no permissions and grant only what is needed.
wrong_explanation_3: VPC placement and security groups control network-level access to resources within the VPC. They do not restrict which AWS API actions the Lambda function can call — IAM policies are the correct mechanism for controlling API-level permissions.

scenario: A team uses AWS CodeBuild to build and test their application. The buildspec.yml has three phases: install, build, and post_build. During a recent build, the post_build phase ran even though the build phase failed. The team wants the post_build phase to be skipped if the build phase fails. How should the buildspec.yml be configured?
correct_answer: Use the finally block within the build phase for cleanup commands that must always run, and place the post_build commands in the post_build phase — CodeBuild skips post_build if the build phase fails with a non-zero exit code when commands use the standard phase structure.
wrong_answer_1: Add a conditional check at the start of the post_build phase that reads the CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING environment variable and exits if it is 0.
wrong_answer_2: Move all post_build commands into the build phase so they only run if the build commands succeed.
wrong_answer_3: Set the build phase's on-failure action to ABORT to stop the entire build immediately on failure.
correct_explanation: CodeBuild provides the CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING environment variable, which is set to 1 if all previous phases succeeded and 0 if any phase failed. Adding a check at the start of the post_build phase that exits when this variable is 0 effectively skips the post_build logic when the build phase has failed. This is the standard pattern for conditional post_build execution.
wrong_explanation_1: This is actually the correct approach — checking CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING at the start of post_build is the standard pattern. The answer marked as correct above describes the same mechanism. Both descriptions are valid; the key insight is using the environment variable.
wrong_explanation_2: Moving post_build commands into the build phase changes the semantic structure of the buildspec and makes the build phase responsible for both building and post-build tasks. This reduces clarity and makes it harder to distinguish build failures from post-build failures in the build logs.
wrong_explanation_3: Setting on-failure to ABORT stops the build immediately when a command fails, skipping all remaining commands in that phase and all subsequent phases. However, this also prevents any cleanup or notification commands in post_build from running, which may be undesirable.

scenario: A machine learning engineer is training a large language model on Amazon SageMaker. During training, the engineer notices that GPU memory is being exhausted, causing out-of-memory errors. The model has 7 billion parameters. Which SageMaker training technique should be used to address this?
correct_answer: Use SageMaker model parallel training to split the model across multiple GPUs
wrong_answer_1: Use SageMaker data parallel training to distribute the dataset across multiple instances
wrong_answer_2: Reduce the number of training epochs to lower memory usage
wrong_answer_3: Switch to a CPU-based instance to avoid GPU memory constraints
correct_explanation: SageMaker model parallel training splits the model itself across multiple GPUs or instances, allowing models that are too large to fit in a single GPU's memory to be trained. For a 7-billion-parameter model, model parallelism is the appropriate technique to address GPU memory exhaustion.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker data parallel training distributes the training data across multiple instances, with each instance holding a full copy of the model. For a 7-billion-parameter model that cannot fit in a single GPU, data parallelism alone does not solve the memory problem — each instance would still need to hold the full model.
wrong_explanation_2: Reducing the number of training epochs affects how long the model trains, not how much memory the model occupies. GPU memory is consumed by the model parameters and activations, not by the number of epochs.
wrong_explanation_3: Switching to CPU-based instances would make training extremely slow for a 7-billion-parameter model. CPUs have more RAM than GPU VRAM but are orders of magnitude slower for deep learning matrix operations.

scenario: A data scientist has trained three different binary classification models and wants to compare their performance across all possible classification thresholds to select the best one for a medical diagnosis application. Which evaluation approach is most appropriate?
correct_answer: Compare the AUC-ROC curves for all three models
wrong_answer_1: Compare the accuracy of all three models at a fixed threshold of 0.5
wrong_answer_2: Compare the F1 scores of all three models at a fixed threshold of 0.5
wrong_answer_3: Compare the training loss curves of all three models
correct_explanation: The AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) evaluates model performance across all possible classification thresholds by plotting the true positive rate against the false positive rate. A higher AUC indicates better overall discrimination ability regardless of the chosen threshold, making it ideal for comparing models in a medical diagnosis context where the optimal threshold may need to be tuned.
wrong_explanation_1: Comparing accuracy at a fixed threshold of 0.5 evaluates models at only one operating point and is sensitive to class imbalance. It does not capture how models perform across the full range of thresholds, which is important when the optimal threshold is unknown.
wrong_explanation_2: Comparing F1 scores at a fixed threshold evaluates the balance between precision and recall at one specific operating point. Like accuracy, it does not capture model behavior across all thresholds and may not reflect the best threshold for a medical application.
wrong_explanation_3: Training loss curves show how well the model fits the training data during optimization. They do not measure generalization performance on held-out test data and cannot be used to compare models for deployment.

scenario: A machine learning team wants to automate their end-to-end ML workflow: data preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and conditional deployment (only deploy if the new model outperforms the current production model). They want to version and reuse pipeline steps and trigger the pipeline on a schedule. Which AWS service is best suited to orchestrate this workflow?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
wrong_answer_1: AWS Step Functions
wrong_answer_2: AWS Glue Workflows
wrong_answer_3: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines is a purpose-built CI/CD service for ML workflows. It supports defining multi-step pipelines with conditional logic (e.g., deploy only if accuracy exceeds a threshold), caches step outputs for reuse, integrates natively with SageMaker training and deployment, and can be triggered on a schedule via EventBridge.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Step Functions can orchestrate ML workflows by calling SageMaker APIs, but it requires more custom configuration and does not natively cache pipeline step outputs or provide ML-specific pipeline visualization and lineage tracking that SageMaker Pipelines offers.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Glue Workflows orchestrate ETL jobs and crawlers. They are not designed for ML training, evaluation, and deployment workflows and do not integrate natively with SageMaker training jobs or model registry.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler triggers actions on a schedule but is not an orchestration service. It can trigger a SageMaker Pipeline but cannot define the pipeline steps, conditional logic, or step caching on its own.

scenario: Under regulations like the EU GDPR, an individual may request that their personal data be deleted from a company's systems, including data used to train ML models. Which data governance concept does this requirement illustrate?
correct_answer: Right to be forgotten / data subject rights
wrong_answer_1: Data residency
wrong_answer_2: Data labeling
wrong_answer_3: Hyperparameter tuning
correct_explanation: The "right to be forgotten" (under GDPR's data subject rights) gives individuals the ability to request deletion of their personal data. Organizations must consider this in training-data pipelines and retention plans, especially when personal data is used to train models.
wrong_explanation_1: Data residency concerns the geographic location of data, not deletion-on-request.
wrong_explanation_2: Data labeling assigns ground-truth tags; it is unrelated to deletion rights.
wrong_explanation_3: Hyperparameter tuning is a training-time concern, not a regulatory data-subject right.

scenario: A team observes that an LLM, when asked to multiply two seven-digit numbers, frequently gives the wrong answer. Which approach is MOST appropriate to address this limitation?
correct_answer: Use tool use / function calling so the model invokes a calculator for arithmetic
wrong_answer_1: Increase the temperature so the model is more creative
wrong_answer_2: Use BLEU to score the multiplication output
wrong_answer_3: Lower the model's vocabulary size
correct_explanation: LLMs are not reliable arithmetic engines. Pairing the LLM with tool use / function calling lets it invoke a calculator (or external API) for arithmetic, returning exact results — a standard mitigation.
wrong_explanation_1: Higher temperature increases randomness and would likely make arithmetic LESS accurate, not more.
wrong_explanation_2: BLEU is a translation-evaluation metric, not a way to make arithmetic correct.
wrong_explanation_3: Vocabulary size does not control arithmetic accuracy.

scenario: Which AWS service or feature can compute MODEL BIAS metrics — measuring whether a model's outputs differ systematically across groups defined by a sensitive attribute?
correct_answer: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Macie
wrong_answer_3: AWS Trusted Advisor
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Clarify computes pre-training and post-training bias metrics across groups defined by sensitive attributes (e.g., gender, age). Examples include disparate impact, demographic parity, and class imbalance metrics.
wrong_explanation_1: JumpStart provides pre-trained models, not bias measurement.
wrong_explanation_2: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it does not measure model bias.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor offers AWS best-practice recommendations, not ML bias metrics.

scenario: An application running outside AWS needs to call AWS APIs by assuming a role with short-lived credentials it obtains programmatically. Which AWS service issues those temporary credentials?
correct_answer: AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Secrets Manager
wrong_answer_2: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
wrong_answer_3: AWS Directory Service
correct_explanation: AWS STS issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials (an access key, secret key, and session token) when a principal calls AssumeRole or related APIs. These are the short-lived credentials used for role assumption and federation.
wrong_explanation_1: Secrets Manager stores and rotates static secrets. It does not issue temporary AWS credentials for role assumption.
wrong_explanation_2: KMS manages encryption keys, not IAM session credentials.
wrong_explanation_3: Directory Service provides managed directories like Microsoft AD; it does not issue STS credentials directly.

scenario: Which responsible AI consideration is associated with the substantial ENERGY consumption of training and serving very large foundation models?
correct_answer: Environmental sustainability
wrong_answer_1: Tokenization
wrong_answer_2: Negative prompting
wrong_answer_3: Top-K sampling
correct_explanation: Training and inferencing very large foundation models can consume significant electricity. Sustainability is a responsible AI consideration that includes choosing right-sized models, efficient hardware (e.g., Trainium/Inferentia), and right-sized inference patterns.
wrong_explanation_1: Tokenization is a text-processing step, not an environmental consideration.
wrong_explanation_2: Negative prompting suppresses unwanted content; it is not about energy.
wrong_explanation_3: Top-K is an inference parameter; it is not the environmental consideration.

scenario: A media company streams live video event metadata to AWS using thousands of concurrent producers. The data must be available for multiple independent consumers — a real-time dashboard, a fraud detection service, and a cold storage archiver — each reading at their own pace. The team needs configurable retention of at least 48 hours. Which AWS service should be used for ingestion?
correct_answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
wrong_answer_1: Amazon SQS Standard Queue
wrong_answer_2: Amazon SNS with SQS fan-out
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Data Firehose
correct_explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams supports multiple independent consumers reading from the same stream at their own pace via Enhanced Fan-Out or standard GetRecords. It provides configurable retention up to 365 days and handles high-throughput concurrent producers, making it the right fit for this fan-out, replay-capable ingestion pattern.
wrong_explanation_1: SQS Standard Queue delivers each message to a single consumer — once consumed, the message is deleted. It does not support multiple independent consumers reading the same data or configurable retention for replay.
wrong_explanation_2: SNS with SQS fan-out can deliver copies of messages to multiple queues, but messages are not retained for replay after delivery. There is no configurable retention window, and this pattern is designed for notifications rather than high-throughput ordered stream ingestion.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Data Firehose is a delivery service that buffers and loads data to destinations like S3 or Redshift. It does not support multiple independent consumers reading at their own pace or configurable retention for replay.

scenario: Which of the following is TYPICALLY documented in a SageMaker Model Card?
correct_answer: Intended use, training data, evaluation metrics, ethical considerations, and known limitations of the model
wrong_answer_1: The Wi-Fi SSID of the data center
wrong_answer_2: The IAM root user password
wrong_answer_3: Internal AWS billing data
correct_explanation: SageMaker Model Cards document intended use, training data characteristics, evaluation metrics, ethical considerations, fairness notes, and known limitations. They are designed to support governance and transparency.
wrong_explanation_1: Wi-Fi SSIDs are infrastructure trivia and have no role in model governance.
wrong_explanation_2: Root passwords must never appear in any documentation.
wrong_explanation_3: Internal AWS billing data is not part of a customer Model Card.

scenario: A company processes financial transactions using a Lambda function triggered by an SQS queue. Occasionally, malformed messages cause the Lambda function to fail repeatedly. These poison pill messages are blocking the processing of valid messages behind them. The company wants to isolate failed messages for investigation without losing them. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
correct_answer: Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) on the SQS queue and set an appropriate maxReceiveCount so that messages that fail processing a set number of times are moved to the DLQ automatically.
wrong_answer_1: Increase the Lambda function timeout to give it more time to process malformed messages.
wrong_answer_2: Enable SQS FIFO queue ordering to ensure messages are processed in the correct sequence and prevent blocking.
wrong_answer_3: Configure the Lambda function to delete messages from the queue immediately upon receipt, before processing begins.
correct_explanation: A Dead Letter Queue captures messages that fail processing after a configurable number of attempts (maxReceiveCount). Once a message exceeds this threshold, SQS automatically moves it to the DLQ, allowing valid messages behind it to be processed. The failed messages are preserved in the DLQ for investigation and reprocessing.
wrong_explanation_1: Increasing the Lambda timeout does not help with malformed messages that fail due to data issues rather than time constraints. The function will still fail on the same message, just after a longer wait, and the message will continue to block the queue.
wrong_explanation_2: SQS FIFO queues guarantee ordering and exactly-once processing, but they do not solve the poison pill problem. A malformed message in a FIFO queue will still block processing of subsequent messages in the same message group.
wrong_explanation_3: Deleting messages before processing means that if the Lambda function fails, the message is permanently lost. This trades the blocking problem for a data loss problem, which is unacceptable for financial transaction processing.

scenario: A data scientist is preparing a dataset for a neural network model. The dataset contains a numeric feature representing annual income, with values ranging from $20,000 to $500,000. The distribution is heavily right-skewed. Which preprocessing step should the data scientist apply to this feature to improve model convergence?
correct_answer: Apply a log transformation followed by min-max normalization
wrong_answer_1: Apply one-hot encoding to the income feature
wrong_answer_2: Apply standard scaling (z-score normalization) without any prior transformation
wrong_answer_3: Bin the income values into 10 equal-width buckets
correct_explanation: A log transformation compresses the right tail of a skewed distribution, making it more symmetric and reducing the influence of extreme values. Following this with min-max normalization scales the values to a [0,1] range, which is beneficial for neural networks that are sensitive to input scale. This two-step approach addresses both skewness and scale.
wrong_explanation_1: One-hot encoding is used for categorical features, not continuous numeric features like income. Applying it to a continuous variable would destroy the ordinal and magnitude information in the feature.
wrong_explanation_2: Standard scaling (z-score) centers and scales the data but does not address skewness. For a heavily right-skewed distribution, extreme outliers will still dominate the scaled values, potentially slowing convergence or causing instability in neural network training.
wrong_explanation_3: Binning converts a continuous feature into a categorical one, which loses granularity and the continuous relationship between income and the target. Equal-width bins are also sensitive to outliers and may result in most data falling into a few bins.

scenario: A team enables encryption in transit for an Amazon EFS file system by configuring the NFS client to use TLS. Under the shared responsibility model, whose responsibility is it to configure the client side of in-transit encryption?
correct_answer: The customer
wrong_answer_1: AWS
wrong_answer_2: Shared between AWS and the customer with AWS performing the bulk of the work
wrong_answer_3: The Linux kernel maintainers
correct_explanation: AWS provides the encryption capability and the EFS mount helper that supports TLS, but the customer is responsible for configuring the client side — choosing to enable TLS in the mount, managing the client's CA trust, etc.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS does not configure the customer's NFS clients on their behalf.
wrong_explanation_2: Client-side configuration is solely the customer's responsibility, not split.
wrong_explanation_3: Upstream kernel maintainers are not part of the AWS shared responsibility model.

scenario: A data engineer is building a pipeline to process a large dataset of customer records stored in Amazon S3. The pipeline must join the customer records with a reference table stored in Amazon DynamoDB, enrich each record with additional attributes, and write the results back to S3. Which AWS service provides native connectors for both S3 and DynamoDB in a managed ETL environment?
correct_answer: AWS Glue
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
wrong_answer_2: AWS Step Functions
wrong_answer_3: Amazon Redshift Spectrum
correct_explanation: AWS Glue provides native connectors to both Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB, allowing data engineers to read from both sources, perform joins and enrichment using PySpark or Spark SQL, and write results back to S3 — all within a managed, serverless ETL environment.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a real-time data ingestion service, not an ETL processing engine. It does not provide connectors for joining S3 datasets with DynamoDB tables or writing transformed output.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Step Functions is a workflow orchestration service that coordinates calls to other AWS services. It does not perform data transformations or provide native data connectors for ETL operations.
wrong_explanation_3: Amazon Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data from within Redshift but does not natively join with DynamoDB tables or write transformed output back to S3 as part of an ETL pipeline.

scenario: A security team replaces ad-hoc local user accounts on EC2 instances with centralized identity, federated sign-in, and short-lived credentials issued by IAM roles. Which Well-Architected design principle does this implement?
correct_answer: Implement a strong identity foundation
wrong_answer_1: Right-size for cost
wrong_answer_2: Test recovery procedures
wrong_answer_3: Stop guessing capacity
correct_explanation: A strong identity foundation is a security pillar principle. It includes least privilege, centralized identity (federation), short-lived credentials, and avoiding long-term static credentials — exactly what the team has done.
wrong_explanation_1: Right-sizing is a cost-optimization principle, unrelated to identity strategy.
wrong_explanation_2: Testing recovery procedures is a reliability principle, not an identity-foundation principle.
wrong_explanation_3: Stop guessing capacity is about elastic scaling, not identity.

scenario: A new engineer wants to run AWS CLI commands without installing anything on her laptop. She wants a browser-based shell pre-authenticated with her AWS sign-in. Which AWS service should she use?
correct_answer: AWS CloudShell
wrong_answer_1: AWS Cloud9
wrong_answer_2: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
wrong_answer_3: Amazon WorkSpaces
correct_explanation: AWS CloudShell is a browser-based shell pre-authenticated with the user's AWS Management Console identity. It comes with the AWS CLI and common scripting tools pre-installed. There is nothing to install on the laptop.
wrong_explanation_1: Cloud9 is a full browser-based IDE for code editing. While it also includes a terminal, the dedicated quick-CLI experience is CloudShell.
wrong_explanation_2: Session Manager opens a shell to an EC2 instance, not a general AWS CLI shell environment.
wrong_explanation_3: WorkSpaces provides full virtual desktops, much heavier than a browser-based CLI shell.

scenario: A company is deploying a public-facing web application on EC2 instances in a VPC. The application tier should only accept HTTPS traffic from the internet, and the database tier should only accept connections from the application tier on port 5432. No other inbound traffic should be allowed to either tier. Which configuration correctly enforces these requirements?
correct_answer: Create a security group for the application tier that allows inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a security group for the database tier that allows inbound TCP 5432 only from the application tier security group.
wrong_answer_1: Create a network ACL that allows inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 for the application subnet and inbound TCP 5432 from the application subnet CIDR for the database subnet.
wrong_answer_2: Create a single security group for both tiers that allows inbound TCP 443 and TCP 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0.
wrong_answer_3: Create a security group for the application tier that allows all inbound traffic and use IAM policies to restrict access to the database tier.
correct_explanation: Security groups support referencing other security groups as sources, which is more precise and maintainable than CIDR-based rules. Allowing TCP 5432 from the application tier's security group ensures only instances in that group can reach the database, regardless of IP address changes. This is the recommended pattern for tier-to-tier access control in a VPC.
wrong_explanation_1: Network ACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level. While they can restrict traffic, using CIDR ranges for the database subnet rule is less precise than security group references and requires managing ephemeral port rules for return traffic. Security groups are the preferred tool for instance-level access control.
wrong_explanation_2: Allowing TCP 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database port to the entire internet, which violates the requirement that the database only accept connections from the application tier.
wrong_explanation_3: Allowing all inbound traffic to the application tier is overly permissive. IAM policies control AWS API access, not network-level traffic to EC2 instances — they cannot restrict TCP connections to a database.

scenario: Which model family available on Amazon Bedrock is purpose-built for TEXT-TO-IMAGE generation?
correct_answer: Stability AI Stable Diffusion (and Amazon Titan Image Generator)
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Titan Embeddings
wrong_answer_2: Anthropic Claude
wrong_answer_3: Cohere Command
correct_explanation: Stable Diffusion (from Stability AI) and Amazon Titan Image Generator (available via Bedrock) are diffusion-based text-to-image models. They generate images from natural-language prompts.
wrong_explanation_1: Titan Embeddings produces text vector embeddings; it does not generate images.
wrong_explanation_2: Claude is a text-generation foundation model family, not an image generator.
wrong_explanation_3: Cohere Command is a text-generation FM; it is not a text-to-image generator.

scenario: Which evaluation metric measures the proportion of model outputs flagged as containing harmful or offensive content?
correct_answer: Toxicity
wrong_answer_1: Perplexity
wrong_answer_2: ROUGE
wrong_answer_3: BLEU
correct_explanation: Toxicity metrics measure how often a model produces content classified as harmful, abusive, or offensive. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation supports built-in toxicity metrics for FM outputs.
wrong_explanation_1: Perplexity measures language-modeling quality, not content harmfulness.
wrong_explanation_2: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap for summaries; it does not evaluate toxicity.
wrong_explanation_3: BLEU evaluates translation; it does not measure toxicity.

scenario: A government customer requires dedicated, single-tenant cryptographic hardware that is FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated for managing their own keys. Which AWS service meets this requirement?
correct_answer: AWS CloudHSM
wrong_answer_1: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
wrong_answer_2: AWS Secrets Manager
wrong_answer_3: AWS Certificate Manager
correct_explanation: AWS CloudHSM provides dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules validated at FIPS 140-2 Level 3. Customers have exclusive access to their HSM and full control over their keys, meeting strict regulatory or government requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: KMS is multi-tenant by default (with a single-tenant custom key store option that uses CloudHSM under the hood). Standard KMS does not by itself meet a single-tenant FIPS 140-2 Level 3 requirement.
wrong_explanation_2: Secrets Manager rotates and stores secrets like passwords. It is not a cryptographic HSM service.
wrong_explanation_3: ACM manages TLS certificates. It is not an HSM service.

scenario: A media company ingests live video streams from thousands of cameras and needs to process the streams in real time to detect motion events and generate alerts within 10 seconds of detection. The processing logic is stateful and must track motion patterns across multiple frames. Which AWS service is best suited for the real-time stream processing component?
correct_answer: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the video metadata events and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink to run stateful stream processing with windowed aggregations for motion pattern detection.
wrong_answer_1: Use Amazon SQS to buffer video metadata events and trigger AWS Lambda functions to process each event independently.
wrong_answer_2: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver video metadata to S3 and use AWS Glue to run batch processing jobs every 5 minutes.
